**In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful**

**Tafsir (exegesis) of Surat al-Hajj.** It is Meccan, except for three verses: His saying, ﴿These two are adversaries﴾ [al-Hajj: 19], up to the end of three verses. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Mujahid. It is also reported from Ibn Abbas that they are four verses, [the exception being] His saying ﴿the punishment of the Burning﴾ [al-Hajj: 22]. Al-Dahhak and Ibn Abbas also said: "It is Madinan," and Qatada said the same, except for four verses: "And We did not send before you any messenger or prophet" [al-Hajj: 52] up to ﴿the punishment of a barren day﴾ [al-Hajj: 55]. These are Meccan. Al-Naqqash counted what was revealed at Madina as ten verses. The majority said: the surah is mixed, containing both Meccan and Madinan parts. This is the most sound view, because the verses indicate this: "O people" (ya ayyuha al-nas) is Meccan [meaning most of it is Meccan], and "O you who believe" (ya ayyuha alladhina amanu) is Madinan. Al-Ghaznawi said: It is one of the marvels of surahs. It was revealed by night and by day, while traveling and while at home, Meccan and Madinan, in time of peace and in time of war, abrogating and abrogated, clear (muhkam) and allegorical (mutashabih), with differing counts [of verses].

I say: Concerning its merit, there is what al-Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni related from Uqbah ibn Amir, who said: I said, "O Messenger of God, has the Surat al-Hajj been given merit by containing two prostrations?" He (ﷺ) said: "Yes, and whoever does not prostrate for them, let him not recite them." This is the wording of al-Tirmidhi. He said: This is a good hadith, but its chain of narration is not strong. The scholars differed on this. It is related from Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him) and Ibn Umar that they both said: "Surat al-Hajj has been given merit by containing two prostrations." Ibn al-Mubarak, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq hold this view. Some considered that it contains only one prostration, and this is the view of Sufyan al-Thawri. Al-Daraqutni related from Abd Allah ibn Tha'laba, who said: I saw Umar ibn al-Khattab make two prostrations in al-Hajj. I said: "In the dawn prayer?" He said: "In the dawn prayer."

**(In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)**

**In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful**

﴿O people, fear your Lord. Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing.﴾ (1)

[[al-Ruqma: a pale mark arising on the foreleg of an animal.]] Al-Tirmidhi related from Imran ibn Husayn that when the Prophet (ﷺ) received: "O people, fear your Lord. Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing," up to His saying "but the punishment of God is severe," (the Prophet) said: this verse was revealed to him while he was on a journey. He said: "Do you know which day that is?" They said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "That is the day when God will say to Adam: 'Send forth the contingent of the Fire.' He will say: 'O Lord, what is the contingent of the Fire?' He will say: 'Nine hundred and ninety-nine to the Fire, and one to Paradise.'" The Muslims then began to weep, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Be near to the truth and aim right, for no prophethood has ever occurred without a period of ignorance (jahiliyya) preceding it." He said: "The number will be taken from the ignorant, and if it is complete (well and good), otherwise it will be completed from the hypocrites. Your likeness and that of the nations is only like the ruqma in the foreleg of a beast, or like the mole (al-shama) in the flank of a camel." [[al-Shama: a mark differing from the body in which it is.]] Then he said: "I truly hope that you will be a quarter of the people of Paradise," so they proclaimed takbir. Then he said: "I truly hope that you will be a third of the people of Paradise," so they proclaimed takbir. Then he said: "I truly hope that you will be half of the people of Paradise," so they proclaimed takbir. (The narrator) said: I do not know whether he said "two-thirds" or not. He said: This is a good, sound hadith, and it has been related through more than one route from al-Hasan from Imran ibn Husayn. In it: the people despaired, to the point that they did not show a smile. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw this, he said: "Act and rejoice, for by Him in whose hand is my soul, you are with two creations which, whenever they have been with anything, have multiplied it: Gog and Magog, and those of the children of Adam and the children of Iblis who have died." He said: Some of what the people were feeling was lifted from them, and he said: "Act and rejoice, for by Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, you are among the people only like the mole in the flank of a camel, or like the ruqma in the foreleg of a beast." He said: This is a good, sound hadith.

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may God be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God Most High says: 'O Adam!' He says: 'At Your service, and good fortune is in Your hands.' He says: 'Bring forth the contingent of the Fire.' He says: 'What is the contingent of the Fire?' He says: 'Out of every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine.'" [[In some copies: "nine hundred and ninety-nine," with the accusative as object and the nominative as predicate.]] He said: "That is the time when the child grows gray, and every pregnant woman lays down her burden, and you see people intoxicated, though they are not intoxicated, but the punishment of God is severe." He said: This was hard on them, and they said: "O Messenger of God, which of us is that man?" He said: "Rejoice, for from Gog and Magog there are a thousand, and from you one man." He mentioned the hadith in a manner similar to what preceded in the hadith of Imran ibn Husayn.

Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas mentioned, saying: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Nafi' related to us, who said: Salama related to us, who said: Abd al-Razzaq related to us, who said: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, from Anas ibn Malik (may God be pleased with him), who said: "O people, fear your Lord. Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing," up to "but the punishment of God is severe." He said: It was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was on a journey, so he raised his voice with it until his companions gathered around him. Then he said: "Do you know what day this is? This is the day when God, Mighty and Majestic, says to Adam (ﷺ): 'O Adam, arise and send forth the contingent of the people of the Fire: out of every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine to the Fire, and one to Paradise.'" This weighed heavily on the Muslims, so the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Be steadfast and aim right, and rejoice, for by Him in whose hand is my soul, you are among the people only like the mole in the flank of a camel, or like the ruqma in the foreleg of a donkey. With you are two creations which, whenever they have been with anything, have multiplied it: Gog and Magog, and those of the unbelieving jinn and humans who have perished."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O people, fear your Lord﴾. The intended address of this call is the responsible (mukallafun), meaning: fear Him by not abandoning His commands, and by not transgressing His prohibitions. Taqwa (God-consciousness, guarding oneself) is wariness of what is disliked, and its meaning has already been fully discussed at the beginning of al-Baqara, so there is no point in repeating it. The meaning is: guard yourselves through obedience to Him against His punishment.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing﴾. Zalzala (convulsion) is intense movement, and from it is His saying: ﴿and they were shaken until the Messenger and those who believed with him said﴾ [al-Baqara: 214]. The root of the word is from zalla 'an al-mawdi', meaning it departed from the place and moved. And zalzala Allah qadamahu means God made his foot move. This term is used to express the awesomeness of a thing. It is said: it is the well-known earthquake which is one of the signs of the Hour, occurring in this world before the Day of Resurrection. This is the view of the majority. It has also been said: this convulsion will occur in the middle of the month of Ramadan, and after it will be the rising of the sun from its west. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 2:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the day you see it﴾

The pronoun in "tarawnaha" (you see it) refers, according to the majority, to the earthquake (zalzalah). This is strengthened by His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Every nursing mother will be distracted from what she nursed, and every pregnant woman will drop her burden﴾. Nursing and pregnancy belong only to the worldly life. Another group said: the earthquake is on the Day of Resurrection, and they cited the hadith of Imran ibn Husayn which we have mentioned, in which it says: "Do you know what day that is? ..." and the hadith. This is also what the context of Muslim's report in the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri indicates.

His saying, "tadhhalu" (is distracted), meaning tashtaghilu (becomes preoccupied), as stated by Qutrub. He recited:

"Striking [[In the original: "bi-darb", corrected from Ibn Hisham's Sirah. Before it:

We have killed you for its interpretation, as we killed you for its revelation.

The verse is by Abdullah ibn Rawahah, who recited it while leading the camel of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when he entered Mecca for the Umrat al-Qada'. See Ibn Hisham's Sirah.]] that removes the skull from its resting place, and distracts the close friend from his close friend."

It was also said: forgets. It was also said: is heedless. It was also said: consoles itself; the meanings are close.

"What she nursed" (ʿamma arḍaʿat): al-Mubarrad said: "ma" here has the sense of the verbal noun, meaning she is distracted from nursing. He said: This indicates that this earthquake is in the world, since after resurrection there is no pregnancy and nursing. Unless it is said: whoever died pregnant will be resurrected pregnant and will drop her burden from the terror; and whoever died nursing will be resurrected likewise. It is said: this is like the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿A Day that will make children grey-haired﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 17]. [[See vol. 19, p. 47.]]

It was said: it occurs with the first blast. It was said: it occurs at the establishment of the Hour, until people stir from their graves at the second blast.

It is possible that the earthquake in the verse is an expression for the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Misfortune and adversity touched them, and they were shaken﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214]. [[See vol. 3, p. 33 onwards.]] And as the prayer of the Prophet, upon him be peace: "O Allah, defeat them and shake them."

The benefit of mentioning the terror of that day is to urge preparation for it and readiness through righteous deeds.

Calling the earthquake "a thing" (shay') is either because its occurrence is certain, so it is made easy to name it a thing although it does not yet exist, since certainty resembles existing things. Or it is according to its outcome: that is, when it occurs it is a great thing. It is as if the name was not applied now; rather the meaning is that when it is, it is then a great thing, and therefore it distracts nursing mothers and makes people drunk, as He said: ﴿and you see people as drunk﴾, meaning from its terror and from the fear and alarm that overtakes them.

(﴿Yet they are not drunk﴾)

From wine. The people of meanings said: "and you see people as if they were drunk." This is supported by the reading of Abu Zur'ah Harim ibn 'Amr ibn Jarir ibn 'Abdullah: "wa-tara an-nas" with a dammah on the ta', meaning you think and it appears to you. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "sakra" without an alif; the rest read "sukara." Both are dialectal forms for the plural of sakran, like kaslā and kusālā.

Zalzalah: violent shaking. Dhuhul: heedlessness of a thing when something arises that preoccupies one from it, such as grief, pain, or something else. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is that she leaves her child because of the distress that has befallen her.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 3–4:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And among the people is one who disputes about Allah without knowledge, and follows every rebellious devil.﴾ (3) ﴿It has been decreed for him that whoever takes him as an ally, he will lead him astray and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze.﴾ (4) Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And among the people is one who disputes about Allah without knowledge.﴾ It was said: the one meant is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who said: "Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is not able to revive one who has decayed and become dust."

(And follows) i.e., in that statement of his.

(Every rebellious devil) mutaraddin (rebellious, defiant).

(It has been decreed for him that whoever takes him as an ally) Qatadah and Mujahid said: i.e., whoever takes the Shaytan as an ally.

(He will lead him astray and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 3–4:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And among the people is one who disputes about Allah without knowledge, and follows every rebellious devil.﴾ (3) ﴿It has been decreed for him that whoever takes him as an ally, he will lead him astray and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze.﴾ (4) Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And among the people is one who disputes about Allah without knowledge.﴾ It was said: the one meant is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who said: "Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is not able to revive one who has decayed and become dust."

(And follows) i.e., in that statement of his.

(Every rebellious devil) mutaraddin (rebellious, defiant).

(It has been decreed for him that whoever takes him as an ally) Qatadah and Mujahid said: i.e., whoever takes the Shaytan as an ally.

(He will lead him astray and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 5 (part 1 of 2):

Allah's words: "O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection" - up to His words "a specified term" - in this there are twelve issues.

The first issue: Allah's words, ﴿If you are in doubt about the Resurrection﴾. This is an argument addressed to the whole world from the first origination. His words "if you are in doubt" contain a conditional form. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "al-ba'th" with a fatha on the ayn (al-ba'ath). This is a dialect form of "al-ba'th" according to the Basran grammarians (al-Basriyyun). According to the Kufan grammarians (al-Kufiyyun), it is the lightened form of "ba'atha." The meaning is: O mankind, if you are in doubt about the re-creation.

﴿Indeed, We created you﴾, meaning We created your father, who is the origin of humankind, namely Adam, peace be upon him, ﴿from dust﴾.

﴿Then﴾ We created his offspring ﴿from a drop﴾, which is the seminal fluid. It was called "nutfah" because of its smallness, for it is a small quantity of water, though the term may also be applied to a large quantity of it. From this is the hadith: "Until a rider travels between the two nutfahs without fearing injustice," meaning the sea of the East and the sea of the West. "Al-nutf" means dripping: one says "natafa yantifu" and "yantufu." A "nutufah" night is one in which the rain constantly drips.

﴿Then from a clinging clot﴾, which is congealed blood. "Al-'alaq" is fresh blood, that is, still moist. It is said that it is blood that is very red.

﴿Then from a lump of flesh﴾, which is a small piece of flesh about the amount that can be chewed. From this is the hadith: "Verily, in the body there is a lump of flesh." These stages take four months. Ibn 'Abbas said: In the ten days after the four months the soul is breathed into it, and that is the waiting period of a woman whose husband has died: four months and ten days.

The second issue: Yahya ibn Zakariyya ibn Abi Za'idah narrated: Dawud related to us from 'Amir, from 'Alqamah, from Ibn Mas'ud and from Ibn 'Umar, that when the drop settles in the womb, an angel takes it in his palm and says: "O Lord, male or female? Wretched or blessed? What is the term and the trace [[al-athar: the term, so called because it follows the life span.]]? In what land will it die?" It is said to him: "Go to Umm al-Kitab (the Mother of the Book), for you will find in it the account of this drop." He goes and finds its account in Umm al-Kitab. Then it is formed, eats its provision, and walks in its traces. When its term comes, it is taken and buried in the place that was decreed for it. Then 'Amir recited: "O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, indeed We created you from dust."

In the Sahih, from Anas ibn Malik, who raised the hadith, he said: "Verily Allah has appointed an angel over the womb, and he says: 'O Lord, a drop! O Lord, a clot! O Lord, a lump!' When Allah wills to decree a creation," he said, "the angel says: 'O Lord, male or female? Wretched or blessed? What is the provision? What is the term?' and it is written thus in its mother's belly."

Also in the Sahih, from Hudhayfah ibn Asid al-Ghifari, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "When forty-two nights pass over the drop, Allah sends to it an angel who shapes it, creates its hearing, its sight, its skin, its flesh and its bones. Then he says: 'O Lord, male or female? ...'" and he mentioned the hadith.

Also in the Sahih, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ related to us, and he is the truthful and the one whose truthfulness is confirmed: "Verily, one of you is gathered together in his mother's belly for forty days, then he is a clot in a similar period, then he is a lump of flesh in a similar period. Then the angel is sent and breathes the soul into him, and he is commanded with four words: to write his provision, his term, his deeds, and whether he is wretched or blessed..." the hadith.

This hadith explains the earlier hadiths, for in it: "The creation of one of you is gathered in his mother's belly forty days as a drop, then forty days as a clot, then forty days as a lump of flesh, then the angel is sent and breathes the soul into him." These are four months, and within the ten days the angel breathes the soul, and this is the waiting period of the woman whose husband has died, as Ibn 'Abbas said.

His words "one of you is gathered together in his mother's belly" have been explained by Ibn Mas'ud. Al-A'mash was asked: What is gathered in the belly of his mother? He said: Khaythamah related to us, saying: 'Abd Allah said: When the drop falls into the womb and He wills to create a human from it, it flies into the skin of the woman under every nail and hair, then it remains for forty days, then it becomes blood in the womb. That is its gathering, and this is the time of its becoming a clot.

The third issue: Attributing creation and shaping to the angel is a metaphorical, not a literal, attribution. What the angel does regarding the formation of the lump happens at the time of shaping and fashioning, by the power, creation and origination of Allah. Do you not see that He, glory be to Him, has attributed the true creation to Himself and has cut off from it the connection of all creation? He says: ﴿And We certainly created you, then We fashioned you﴾ [al-A'raf: 11]. And He says: ﴿And We certainly created man from an extract of clay. Then We placed him as a drop in a firm place﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12-13]. And He says: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, indeed We created you from dust, then from a drop﴾. And Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿It is He who created you; then among you is a disbeliever and among you is a believer﴾ [al-Taghabun: 2]. Then He says: ﴿And He fashioned you and perfected your forms﴾ [Ghafir: 64]. And He says: ﴿Certainly We created man in the best stature﴾ [al-Tin: 4]. And He says: ﴿He created man from a clinging clot﴾ [al-'Alaq: 2]. Besides these verses, and what the decisive proofs indicate, that no one creates any of the created things except the Lord of the worlds.

The same applies to His words: "Then the angel is sent and breathes the soul into him," meaning that the breathing is a cause, while it is Allah who creates the soul and life in it. Likewise the same applies to all the customary causes, for they occur by the bringing into being of Allah, exalted is He, and not by anything else. So reflect upon this principle and hold fast to it, for in it is deliverance from the doctrines of the misguided naturalists [[In the original sources: al-tab'iyyin, the naturalists.]] and others.

The fourth issue: The scholars have not differed that the breathing of the soul into it occurs after one hundred and twenty days, which is the completion of four months and its entry into the fifth, as we have explained by the hadiths. On this basis one relies in the rulings needed concerning the establishment of paternity (istilhaq) when disputed, and in the obligation of maintenance (nafaqat) for the pregnancy of divorced women. This is because of certainty of the movement of the foetus in the womb. It has been said that this is the wisdom behind the waiting period of a woman after death being four months and ten days, and this entry into the fifth month establishes the clearing of the womb when this period has been reached without any pregnancy appearing.

The fifth issue: The drop is not certainly anything, and no ruling depends on it if the woman expels it while it has not gathered in the womb. It is as if it were in the loins of the man. If she expels a clot, we are certain that the drop has settled, gathered, and transformed into the first state by which it is established that it is a child. On this basis, the laying down of a clot or what is above it, a lump, is considered a delivery by which the womb is cleared, the waiting period is completed, and the status of an umm walad (a slave woman who has borne her master's child) is established for her. This is the view of Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, and his companions. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The miscarriage of a clot is not considered; what is considered is the appearance of the form and outline. If the outline is hidden and it is merely flesh, there are two opinions by transmission and derivation, and the explicitly stated view is that the waiting period is completed by it, but it does not make her an umm walad. They said: since the waiting period is completed by flowing blood, then by something else is more appropriate.

The sixth issue: Allah's words: ﴿formed and unformed﴾. Al-Farra' said: "Formed" means complete in its creation, and "unformed" means a miscarriage. Ibn al-A'rabi said: "Formed" means its creation has begun, and "unformed" means it has not yet been shaped. Ibn Zayd said: "Formed" is that in which Allah has created the head, the two hands and the two feet, and "unformed" is that in which nothing has been created.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: If we return to the root derivation, then the drop, the clot and the lump are all "formed," because all of them are Allah's creation. If we return to shaping, which is the limit of creation, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Then We produced it as another creation﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14], then that is what Ibn Zayd said.

I (al-Qurtubi) say: "Takhlīq" derives from "khalq" (creation), and it carries the sense of multiplicity. Whatever the stages follow one after another upon is created in one creation after another. When it is a drop, it is created, and for this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then We produced it as another creation﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14]. And Allah knows best.

It has also been said that His words "formed and unformed" refer to the child itself and not to the miscarriage: that is, among them is one whom the Lord, glory be to Him, completes in his lump and creates all his limbs, and among them is one who is immature, deficient, and incomplete.

It has been said: "formed" means that the woman gives birth at the completion of the term. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Formed" is what was alive, and "unformed" is a miscarriage. He said:

"Is weeping for the unformed?
Then where is your prudence, woe to you, and your modesty?"

The seventh issue: The scholars agreed that a slave woman becomes an *umm walad* (a mother of a child, whose master's child she bears and who gains certain rights) by miscarrying a fully formed fetus. According to Malik, al-Awza'i and others, she becomes one by a *mudghah* (a lump of flesh), whether or not it had taken shape. Malik said: "When it is known that it is a *mudghah*." Al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa said: "If some part of human form has become apparent in it, such as a finger or an eye or something else, then she is an *umm walad* for him."

The scholars agreed that a newborn who gives a cry (*istihlal*, raising the voice, i.e. showing signs of life) is prayed over. If he does not cry out, he is not prayed over according to Malik, Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i and others. It is narrated from Ibn Umar that he is prayed over, and this was said by Ibn al-Musayyib, Ibn Sirin and others. It is narrated from al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba that he used to command that a miscarried fetus (*siqt*) be prayed over, and he would say: "Name them, wash them, shroud them and perfume them, for God has honoured by Islam both your great and your small," and he would recite this verse: "﴿Indeed We created you from dust...﴾" up to "﴿...and unformed﴾."

Ibn al-Arabi said: "Perhaps al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba meant by *siqt* that whose form has become apparent; that is the one who is named, and whatever form has not become apparent has no existence." Some of the early scholars said: "He is prayed over from the time the soul is breathed into him and four months have been completed for him."

Abu Dawud narrated from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "If a child cries out (*istahalla*), he inherits." *Al-istihlal* means raising the voice. Thus every newborn for whom that occurred, or a movement, a sneeze or a breath, inherits, because there is in these a sign of life. This was the view of Sufyan al-Thawri, al-Awza'i and al-Shafi'i. Al-Khattabi said: "The best of this is the view of the people of opinion (the Hanafis)."

Malik said: "He has no inheritance, even if he moves or sneezes, so long as he has not cried out loudly." This was narrated from Muhammad ibn Sirin, al-Sha'bi, al-Zuhri and Qatadah.

The eighth issue: Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "What a woman expels of a *mudghah* or an *'alaqah* (a clot), or of what is known to be a child, if one strikes her belly, then for it is the *ghurrah* (a compensation equal to a slave or slave-girl valued at one-tenth of the full blood money)." Al-Shafi'i said: "There is nothing for it until some of its form has become apparent." Malik said: "If the fetus falls and does not cry out, then for it is the *ghurrah*. Whether it moved or sneezed, for it is always the *ghurrah*, until it cries out loudly, and then for it is the full blood money (*diyah*)." Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, and the rest of the jurists of the cities said: "If its life is known by movement, or by a sneeze, or by crying out, or by anything else by which its life is certainly established, then for it is the full blood money."

The ninth issue: The judge Isma'il mentioned that a woman's waiting period ('*iddah*) ends with a miscarried fetus that was placed (i.e. a stillborn), and he argued for it on the basis that it is a pregnancy. He said: Allah Most High said: "﴿And for those with child, their term is until they deliver their burden﴾" [[See vol. 18, p. 162 and following.]]. Judge Isma'il said: "The proof of this is that it inherits from its father, which indicates its existence as a created being, its being a child and a pregnancy." Ibn al-Arabi said: "None of these rulings attaches to it unless it has taken form."

I say: what we have mentioned about the etymology, and the saying of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace: "Indeed, each of you is gathered in his creation in his mother's belly," indicate the soundness of what we have said. Also, the one who miscarries a clot or a lump, when she casts it out, the term applies to the woman that she was pregnant and delivered what had settled in her womb, so the words of Allah Most High include her: "﴿And for those with child, their term is until they deliver their burden﴾" [al-Talaq: 4]. Also, she has brought forth the beginning of a child from a drop, embodied like a sketch, and this is clear.

The tenth issue: Ibn Majah narrated: Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah related to us, Khalid ibn Makhlad related to us, Yazid related to us from Abd al-Malik al-Nawfali, from Yazid ibn Ruman, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A miscarried child that I send ahead of me is dearer to me than a horseman I leave behind me [khalfi]." [[Addition from the Sunan of Ibn Majah.]] Al-Hakim also narrated it in *Ma'rifat 'Ulum al-Hadith* from Suhayl ibn Abi Salih, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, and he said: "Dearer to me than a thousand horsemen I leave behind me."

The eleventh issue: "﴿So that We may make clear to you﴾" means the perfection of Our power through Our varying you through the stages of your creation.

"﴿And We cause to remain in the wombs﴾" was read with the accusative *nuqirra* and *nukhrija*. Abu Hatim narrated it from Abu Zayd, from al-Mufaddal, from Asim. Abu Hatim said: "The accusative is by coordination (*'atf*)." Al-Zajjaj said: "*Nuqirru* is in the nominative only, because the meaning is not: 'We did that so that We might cause to remain in the wombs what We will'; rather Allah, Mighty and Majestic, created them to guide them to right direction and righteousness." It was also said: "The meaning is: so that We may make clear to them the matter of resurrection; so it is a parenthetical insertion between the two statements."

This group read it in the nominative, "*wa-nuqirru*," meaning "and We are causing to remain." This is the reading of the majority. It was also read: "*wa-yuqirru*" and "*yukhrijukum*" with the letter *ya*, and the nominative is acceptable on this reading. Ibn Wassab read "*ma nashā'u*" with a kasra on the nun.

The appointed term varies according to each individual fetus: there is one who miscarries, and there is one whose matter is completed and who comes out alive. He said "*mā nashā'u*" and did not say "*man nashā'u*," because it refers to the womb; that is, We cause to remain in the wombs what We will of the embryo and of the lump of flesh, which is inanimate, so He referred to it with the word *mā*.

The twelfth issue: His saying, Exalted is He: "﴿Then We bring you forth as infants﴾," meaning "as children (*atfāl*)," so it is a collective noun (*ism jins*). Also, the Arabs sometimes name the plural by the singular, as the poet said:

*They blame me about her love and reproach me,*
*and indeed the blamers are not princes over me.*

He did not say "*umarā'*" (princes). Al-Mubarrad said: "It is a noun used as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), like *al-ridā* and *al-'adl*, so it applies to the singular and the plural." Allah Most High said: "﴿...or children who have not yet attained knowledge of the private parts of women﴾" [[See p. 226 of this part and following.]] [al-Nur: 31]. Al-Tabari said: "It is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyīz*), like His saying: '﴿...but if they remit to you willingly a portion of it, then consume it﴾'" [al-Nisa': 4]. It was also said: the meaning is: "Then We bring out each one of you as a child." The word *tifl* applies from the time of a child's separation from the womb until puberty. The young of every wild animal is also a *tifl*. It is said: "a girl *tifl*," "two girls *tifl*," "girls *tifl*," "a boy *tifl*," "boys *tifl*." It is also said: "*tifl*," "*tiflah*," "*tiflān*," "*tiflatān*," and "*atfāl*." One does not say "*tiflāt*." *Atfalat al-mar'ah* means the woman became one with a child. *Al-muṭfilah* is the gazelle with her young, being recently given birth; likewise the she-camel. The plural is *maṭāfil* and *maṭāfīl*. *Al-ṭafl* (with a fatha on the ta) means tender and soft: one says "a soft girl (*jāriyah ṭafla*)," meaning tender, and "soft fingers (*banān ṭafl*)." *Ṭafala al-layl* means its darkness came on. *Al-ṭafal* (with fatha and sukun?) means after the afternoon prayer when the sun begins to set. *Al-ṭafal* also means rain. The poet said:

*To a depression (*wahd*)[[The *wahd* and *wahda* are the low-lying land, as if a pit.]] whose rain was the fine rain of al-Thurayya.*

"﴿Then that you may reach your maturity﴾": It was said that "*thumma*" is superfluous, like the "*wa*" in His saying: "﴿...until, when they reach it and its gates are opened...﴾" [al-Zumar: 73], because *thumma* is among the conjunctive particles like *wa*. "*Ashuddakum*" means the completion of your intellects and the culmination of your strength. Its explanation has already passed in *al-An'am* [[See vol. 7, p. 124.]].

"﴿And among you is one who is returned to the most abject age﴾" [al-Hajj: 5]: that is, the lowest and most degraded, which is senility and decrepitude until one does not understand. Therefore He said: "﴿so that he knows nothing after having known﴾." As He said in Surat Ya-Sin: "﴿And whomever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation﴾" [[See vol. 15, p. 38 and following.]] [Ya-Sin: 68].

The Prophet ﷺ used to supplicate and say: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from miserliness, and I seek refuge in You from cowardice, and I seek refuge in You from being returned to the most abject age, and I seek refuge in You from the trial of this world and the punishment of the grave." Al-Nasa'i narrated it from Sa'd, and he said: "He used to teach them to his sons as the teacher (*mukhtib*, a teacher) teaches the boys." [[Al-mukattib: the teacher.]] This meaning has already passed in *al-Nahl* [[See vol. 10, p. 140.]].

His saying, Exalted is He: "﴿And you see the earth lifeless (*hāmidah*)﴾": He mentioned a stronger proof for resurrection. In the first, He said: "﴿Indeed We created you from dust﴾," addressing a plural. In this second, He said: "﴿And you see the earth﴾," addressing a singular. So the wording is separated from the wording, but the meaning is connected in terms of the argument against those who deny resurrection.

*Hāmidah*: dry, not producing anything. This was said by Ibn Juraij. It was also said: *dārisah* (effaced). *Al-humūd* is effacement. Al-A'sha said:

*Qutaylah said: "What is wrong with your body, so pale,*
*and I see your garments worn out and effaced?"*

Al-Harawi said: "*Hāmidah*" means dry, having dust. Shamir said: "It is said: the plants of the earth withered (*hamada*) when they wore out and went away. And their voices withered (*hamadat*) when they became still. The lifelessness (*humūd*) of the earth means that there is no life in it, no plant, no shrub, and no rain has reached it." In a hadith: "until he almost withered (*yahmud*) from hunger," meaning perished. One says: the garment withered (*hamada*) when it wore out, and the fire withered (*hamadat*).

His saying, Exalted is He: "﴿Then when We send down water upon it, it stirs (*ihtazzat*)﴾," meaning it moved. *Al-ihtizāz* is intense movement. One says: "I shook the thing and it shook (*ihtazza*)," meaning I moved it and it moved. The driver (*al-hādī*) shook the camels with a chant (*hazīz*), and they stirred (*ihtazzat*) when they moved in their journey at his singing. And the star (*ihtazza*) in its falling, and a shooting star (*kawkab hāzz*). So the earth stirs with plants, because plants do not emerge from it until they displace part of it from part with a hidden displacement; so He called it *ihtizāz* metaphorically. It was also said: "its plants stirred," and the noun is omitted. Al-Mubarrad said: "Its *ihtizāz* is intensity of movement, as the poet said:

*She sways when she stands, and she quivers when she walks,*
*like the branch of the ban-tree stirring in green leaves.*

The *ihtizāz* is more apparent in plants than in the earth itself.

"*Wa-rabat*" means it rose and increased. It was also said: it swelled; the meaning is one, and its origin is increase. *Rabā al-shay' yarbū rabwan*: the thing increased. From it come *al-ribā* (usury) and *al-rabwah* (a hill). Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' and Khalid ibn Ilyas read "*wa-rabaʾat*," meaning it rose until it became like a lookout (*rabī'ah*), the one who guards a people from an elevated place. So he is *rābi'* and *rabī'ah* as an intensive form. Imru' al-Qays said:

*We sent a scout before that, one who hides himself,*
*like the wolf of the ghada tree, walking through the thicket and guarding himself.* [[*Al-mukhammal*: the one who conceals himself, moving and hiding so that the game does not sense him. *Al-ghadā*: a tree; the Arabs say: the most cunning of wolves is the wolf of the ghada, because it only mingles with people when it wants to raid. *Al-ḍarrā'* (with fatha and madd): the dense trees in the valley that conceal whoever enters. "Fulān yamshi al-ḍarrā'" means he walks hidden among the trees that conceal him.]]

"*Wa-anbatat*" means it brought forth.

"*Min kulli zawjin*" means of every kind (*lawn*).

"*Bahīj*" means beautiful, according to Qatadah: it delights whoever sees it. *Al-bahjah* is beauty; one says: a man of *bahjah*. *Bahuja* (with damma) *bahājah* and *bahjah*, so he is *bahīj*. *Abhajanī* means it pleased me by its beauty. Since He described the earth with producing vegetation, this shows that His saying "*ihtazzat wa-rabat*" refers to the earth and not to the plants. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 6–7:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth﴾. When He mentioned the dependence of existent things upon Him and their being subjected to His power and choice, in His saying, "O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection" — up to His saying — "beautiful," He said after that: "That is because Allah is the Truth, and He gives life to the dead, and He is Powerful over all things (6), and the Hour is coming, there is no doubt concerning it, and Allah will resurrect those in the graves" (7). By this, glorified and exalted is He, He draws attention to the fact that everything other than Him, although it truly exists, has no reality of its own, because it is subjected and directed. The true Truth (al-Haqq al-Haqiqi) is the Absolutely Existent, the Absolutely Self-Sufficient, and the existence of every existent thing is from the necessity of His existence. For this reason He said at the end of the surah: ﴿And that what they call upon besides Him is falsehood﴾ [al-Hajj: 62][[See p. 91 of this part.]]. Al-Haqq also means the existent, established, enduring one that does not change or cease, and that is Allah, Exalted is He. It is also said: "dhu al-haqq" (the one who holds the right) over His servants. And it is said: "al-Haqq" means "in His acts" (bi-ma'na fi af'alihi). Al-Zajjaj said: "That" (dhalika) is in the nominative position, i.e., the matter is what has been described and made clear to you.

(Bi-anna Allaha huwa al-Haqq) meaning: because Allah is the Truth. He also said: It is permissible for "dhalika" to be in the accusative, i.e., Allah did that because He is the Truth.

(Wa-annahu yuhyi al-mawta) meaning: by the fact that He (gives life to the dead), (wa-annahu 'ala kulli shay'in qadir) meaning: and by the fact that He is capable of whatever He wills.

(Wa-anna al-sa'ata atiyah) is coordinated with His saying "That is because Allah is the Truth" in terms of wording, and it is not coordinated in meaning, since one does not say "Allah did what was mentioned because the Hour is coming." Rather, a verb must be supposed to be implied by it, meaning: and so that they may know that the Hour is coming (la rayba fiha), meaning: there is no doubt.

(Wa-anna Allaha yab'athu man fi al-qubur) he means: for reward and punishment.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 22, verses 8–10:**

**Allah's words:** ﴿Among people is one who disputes about Allah without knowledge, or guidance, or an illuminating Book﴾ [22:8]. *Munir* means shining, with clear proof. It was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. It is also said that it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, according to Ibn 'Abbas. The majority hold that it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, like the first verse, so the two verses concern one group. The repetition is for emphasis in censure, as when you say to a man you are reproaching and rebuking: "You did this! You did this!" It is also possible that the repetition is because the verse describes him with an additional attribute in each verse, as if it said: "Al-Nadr ibn al-Harith disputes about Allah without knowledge and follows every rebellious devil, and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith disputes about Allah without knowledge, without guidance, and without an illuminating Book, to lead people astray from the way of Allah." This is like your saying: "Zayd insults me, and Zayd beats me," which is a meaningful repetition, as al-Qushayri said. It has also been said that about a dozen verses were revealed concerning him. The first verse refers to his denial of resurrection, and the second to his denial of prophethood and that the Qur'an is sent down from Allah. It has also been said that among al-Nadr ibn al-Harith's statements was that the angels are the daughters of Allah, and this is disputing about Allah, exalted is He. *Min* is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is in the phrase "and among people."

**(Thāniya ʿiṭfihi)** is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). It is interpreted in two meanings. The first: it is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: it refers to al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who twisted his neck out of arrogance and self-importance. The other meaning, which is the view of al-Farra': the sense is "Among people is one who disputes about Allah without knowledge, *thāniya ʿiṭfihi*," meaning turning away from the Remembrance, as recorded by al-Nahhas. Mujahid and Qatadah said: twisting his neck in disbelief. Ibn 'Abbas said: turning away from what he is called to, in disbelief. The meaning is one. Al-Awza'i related from Makhlad ibn Husayn, from Hisham ibn Hassan, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning Allah's words, "*thāniya ʿiṭfihi* to lead astray from the way of Allah," that he said: it refers to the people of innovation. Al-Mubarrad said: *al-ʿiṭf* is that which bends of the neck. Al-Mufaddal said: *al-ʿiṭf* is the side, and from it is the saying of people: "So-and-so looks into his *aʿṭāf*," that is, into his sides. The *ʿiṭfān* of a man are from the top of his head to his hip, and likewise the *ʿiṭfān* of anything are its two sides. It is said: "So-and-so turned his *ʿiṭf* away from me" when he turned away from you. So the meaning is: he turns away from the truth in his disputing and turns away from considering its speech. This is like Allah's words: ﴿Then he turns away arrogantly, as if he had not heard it﴾ [31:7]; and His words: ﴿They turn their heads﴾ [63:5]; and His words: ﴿He turns away and withdraws to his side﴾ [17:83]; and His words: ﴿He goes to his family, swaggering﴾ [75:33].

**(Li-yuḍilla ʿan sabīli Allāh)** means: away from obedience to Allah, exalted is He. It is also read *li-yaḍilla* with a fatha on the yā'. The lam is the lam of consequence (*lam al-ʿāqiba*), meaning: he disputes, and so he goes astray, like Allah's words: ﴿so that it would become for them an enemy and a source of grief﴾ [28:8], meaning: so it became for them such. A parallel is ﴿then, when a group of you associate others with their Lord, [so that] they may disbelieve﴾ [16:54–55].

**(Lahu fi al-dunya khizy)** means: humiliation and disgrace, through the foul mention that will be attached to him on the tongues of the believers until the Day of Resurrection, as He said: ﴿And do not obey every vile swearer﴾ [68:10] and the rest of the verse; and His words: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish﴾ [111:1]. It has also been said that *khizy* here means being killed, for the Prophet ﷺ killed al-Nadr ibn al-Harith on the day of Badr by execution, as mentioned earlier at the end of Surat al-Anfal.

**(Wa-nudhīquhu yawm al-qiyama ʿadhab al-ḥarīq)** means: the fire of Hell.

**(Dhālika bi-mā qaddamat yadāka)** means: it will be said to him in the Hereafter when he enters the Fire: "That punishment is because of what your hands sent forth of sins and disbelief." He expressed the whole by the hand, because the hand is what acts and strikes, and so it stands for the whole person. *Dhālika* here has the meaning of *hādhā* (this), as was mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

Mujahid and Qatadah said: twisting his neck in disbelief. Ibn 'Abbas said: turning away from what he is called to, in disbelief. The meaning is one. Al-Awza'i related from Makhlad ibn Husayn, from Hisham ibn Hassan, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning Allah's words, "*thāniya ʿiṭfihi* to lead astray from the way of Allah," that he said: it refers to the people of innovation. Al-Mubarrad said: *al-ʿiṭf* is that which bends of the neck. Al-Mufaddal said: *al-ʿiṭf* is the side, and from it is the saying of people: "So-and-so looks into his *aʿṭāf*," that is, into his sides. The *ʿiṭfān* of a man are from the top of his head to his hip, and likewise the *ʿiṭfān* of anything are its two sides. It is said: "So-and-so turned his *ʿiṭf* away from me" when he turned away from you. So the meaning is: he turns away from the truth in his disputing and turns away from considering its speech. This is like Allah's words: ﴿Then he turns away arrogantly, as if he had not heard it﴾ [31:7]; and His words: ﴿They turn their heads﴾ [63:5]; and His words: ﴿He turns away and withdraws to his side﴾ [17:83]; and His words: ﴿He goes to his family, swaggering﴾ [75:33].

**(Li-yuḍilla ʿan sabīli Allāh)** means: away from obedience to Allah, exalted is He. It is also read *li-yaḍilla* with a fatha on the yā'. The lam is the lam of consequence (*lam al-ʿāqiba*), meaning: he disputes, and so he goes astray, like Allah's words: ﴿so that it would become for them an enemy and a source of grief﴾ [28:8], meaning: so it became for them such. A parallel is ﴿then, when a group of you associate others with their Lord, [so that] they may disbelieve﴾ [16:54–55].

**(Lahu fi al-dunya khizy)** means: humiliation and disgrace, through the foul mention that will be attached to him on the tongues of the believers until the Day of Resurrection, as He said: ﴿And do not obey every vile swearer﴾ [68:10] and the rest of the verse; and His words: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish﴾ [111:1]. It has also been said that *khizy* here means being killed, for the Prophet ﷺ killed al-Nadr ibn al-Harith on the day of Badr by execution, as mentioned earlier at the end of Surat al-Anfal.

**(Wa-nudhīquhu yawm al-qiyama ʿadhab al-ḥarīq)** means: the fire of Hell.

**(Dhālika bi-mā qaddamat yadāka)** means: it will be said to him in the Hereafter when he enters the Fire: "That punishment is because of what your hands sent forth of sins and disbelief." He expressed the whole by the hand, because the hand is what acts and strikes, and so it stands for the whole person. *Dhālika* here has the meaning of *hādhā* (this), as was mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 11:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among mankind is one who worships Allah on an edge﴾. "Min" (مِنَ) is in the place of nominative case (raf') as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'), and the complete sense is "turned on his face," according to the reading of the majority, "he has lost." This verse is a report about the hypocrites. Ibn 'Abbas said: it refers to Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, who had embraced Islam before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ became manifest, but when revelation came to him, Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah apostatized. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: a man from the Jews embraced Islam, then his sight and his wealth were lost, so he considered Islam an omen of ill luck, came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "Release me from it!" He said: "Indeed Islam is not to be revoked." He said: "I have not found any good in this religion of mine! My sight has gone, my wealth and my children!" He said: "O Jew, indeed Islam refines men as fire refines the dross of iron, silver and gold," so Allah the Exalted revealed: "And among mankind is one who worships Allah on an edge." Isra'il narrated from Abu Husayn, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "And among mankind is one who worships Allah on an edge" — he said: a man would come to Madinah, and if his wife bore a boy and his mares foaled, he would say, "This is a good religion," but if his wife did not bear and his mares did not foal, he would say, "This is a bad religion." The commentators said: it was revealed concerning Bedouin Arabs who would come to the Prophet ﷺ and embrace Islam; if they gained prosperity they remained, and if hardship befell them they apostatized. It was said it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. Ibn Zayd and others said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites. The meaning of "on an edge" (ʿalā ḥarf) is "on doubt," as stated by Mujahid and others. Its reality is that he is on weakness in his worship, like the weakness of one standing on an unstable edge. The "harf" (حرف) of everything is its extremity, its brink and its boundary, and from it comes the "harf" of a mountain, which is its sharp summit. It was also said: "on an edge" means "on one aspect," namely that he worships Him in ease but not in adversity; and had they worshipped Allah with gratitude in ease and patience in adversity, they would not have worshipped Allah "on an edge." It was also said: "on an edge" means "on a condition," because Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah said to the Prophet ﷺ before his matter became manifest: "Pray to your Lord for Him to grant me wealth, camels, horses and children, so that I may believe in you and incline to your religion." He prayed for him, and Allah the Mighty and Majestic granted him what he wished. Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic willed to test him and examine him, and He knows him best; He took from him what He had granted him after he had embraced Islam, so he apostatized from Islam. Thereupon Allah, blessed and exalted, revealed concerning him: "And among mankind is one who worships Allah on an edge," meaning on a condition. Al-Hasan said: it is the hypocrite who worships Allah with his tongue but not his heart. In sum, this one who worships Allah "on an edge" is not wholly within it; and this is clarified by His saying: ﴿If good befalls him, he is content with it﴾, meaning soundness of body and ease of livelihood, he is pleased and remains upon his religion.

(﴿And if a trial befalls him﴾), that is, the opposite of that, of what he is tested by, (﴿he turns back upon his face﴾), that is, he apostatizes and returns to his former face, the disbelief in which he was.

(﴿He has lost the world and the Hereafter. That is the manifest loss﴾). Mujahid, Humayd ibn Qays, al-A'raj, al-Zuhri and Ibn Abi Ishaq — and it is narrated from Ya'qub — read "khasira al-dunya" with an alif (khasira as "khasira" in the accusative), as a circumstantial accusative (hal), and according to this reading one does not pause at "wajhihi." His loss of the world is that he gains no spoil and no praise, and his loss of the Hereafter is that he has no reward in it.

Allah the Exalted says: (He calls upon, besides Allah, that which neither harms him nor benefits him). That is, this one who turns back to disbelief worships an idol which neither benefits nor harms.

(That is the far-reaching error.) Al-Farra' said: "Al-tawil" (the far-reaching, i.e., extreme).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 13:

His saying, Exalted is He: (He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit) — meaning: this one who has turned on his face calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit, i.e., in the Hereafter, because by his worship he enters the Fire, and he never sees any benefit from it at all. But He said "whose harm is nearer than his benefit" as an elevated style of speech (tarfi'an lil-kalam), like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, either we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [[See vol. 14, p. 298.]] [Saba': 24]. It was also said: their worship of them implies that they will intercede for them tomorrow, as Allah, Exalted is He, said: "And they worship besides Allah that which neither harms them nor benefits them, and they say, 'These are our intercessors with Allah'" [10:18] [[See vol. 8, p. 321.]] [Yunus: 18]. And Exalted is He said: ﴿We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to Allah in position﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 232.]] [al-Zumar: 3].

Al-Farra', al-Kisa'i and al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the speech is an oath and a postponement, i.e., "By Allah, whose harm is nearer than his benefit (is the one he calls upon)." So the lam is placed out of its position. "Man" is in a position of accusative governed by "yad'u," and the lam is the answer to the oath. "Darruhu" is the subject (mubtada') and "aqrabu" is its predicate. Al-Nahhas criticized the postponement of the lam and said: "The lam does not have the flexibility that requires it to be either placed earlier or later." I say: the proper place of the lam is at the front, though it may be postponed. The poet said:

Khali la-anta, wa-man Jarir khal ... yanal al-'ala wa-yukrim al-akhwalaa

i.e., "Indeed you are my maternal uncle (la-khali anta)," and it has already been mentioned. Al-Nahhas: Ali ibn Sulayman related to us from Muhammad ibn Yazid, who said: "There is an ellipsis in the speech, and the meaning is: he calls upon the one whose harm is nearer than his benefit as a god (ilahan)." Al-Nahhas said: I think this statement is a mistake attributed to Muhammad ibn Yazid, because it has no meaning, since what follows the lam is a subject (mubtada'), so it is not permissible to put "ilah" in the accusative. I do not think Muhammad ibn Yazid's position is other than the saying of al-Akhfash, and it is the best of what has been said about the verse in my view, and Allah knows best. He said: "yad'u" has the meaning of "yaqulu" (says). "Man" is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, and the meaning is: he says to the one whose harm is nearer than his benefit: "his god." I say: al-Qushayri, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned this statement from al-Zajjaj, and al-Mahdawi from al-Akhfash, and he completed its grammatical analysis, saying: "yad'u" has the meaning of "yaqulu," "man" is a subject (mubtada'), "darruhu" is a second subject, "aqrabu" is its predicate, and the clause is the relative clause (silah) of "man," and the predicate of "man" is omitted, and the estimated meaning is: he says to the one whose harm is nearer than his benefit: "his god." A similar example is the saying of 'Antarah:

They call, "'Antar!", while the spears are like ropes of a well
in the chest of the dark-bay horse [[Al-ashtan: plural of shatan, which means well-ropes. Al-labban (with a fatha on the lam): the chest. Al-adham: the horse. He means that the spears in the chest of this horse are like the ropes of a well with buckets, because when a well is very deep, the bucket moves about in it, so two ropes are placed on it so that it does not move about.

(From the commentary on the Mu'allaqat).]]

Al-Qushayri said: The unbeliever who says, "The idol is my deity," does not say, "Whose harm is nearer than his benefit." Rather, the meaning is: the unbeliever says of the one whose harm is nearer than his benefit, according to the saying of the Muslims, "my deity and my god." It is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you magician, pray for us to your Lord﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 96.]] [al-Zukhruf: 49], i.e., "O you magician" according to those who call you a magician. Al-Zajjaj said: It is permissible that "yad'u" be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and in it there is a deleted pronoun (ha'), i.e., "that is the far error, he calls upon it," i.e., in the state of his calling upon it. So in "yad'u" there is a hidden pronoun, and one stops on "yad'u" on this view. His saying, "whose harm is nearer than his benefit," is a resumed statement (kalam mustan'af) in the nominative by inception (mubtada'), and its predicate is "labi'sa al-mawla" (wretched is the patron). This is because the lam is for oath and emphasis, so he placed it at the beginning of the speech. Al-Zajjaj said: It is also permissible that "dhalika" means "alladhi" (the one who), and it be in the accusative position by the governing of "yad'u" over it, i.e., "the one who is in the far error calls upon," as He said: "And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?" [20:17] [[See vol. 11, p. 186.]], i.e., "what is that which." Then His saying "whose harm" is a new subject (kalam mubtada'), and "labi'sa al-mawla" is the predicate of the subject. The estimated meaning of the verse according to this is: "He calls upon the one who is the far error," the object having been fronted, which is "alladhi," as you say, "Zaydan yadribu" (Zayd, he strikes). Abu 'Ali approved this. Al-Zajjaj claimed that the grammarians had overlooked this view, and he recited:

"Adas, what authority does 'Abbad have over you?
You have escaped, and this one you carry is a free man." [[This is the first of the verses of Yazid ibn Rabi'ah ibn Mufarrigh al-Himyari. 'Adas: a call to a mule to hurry. 'Abbad is the son of Ziyad, brother of 'Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad who fought al-Husayn ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, at Karbala. Ibn Mufarrigh satirized this 'Abbad, so he bore a grudge against him and shunned him; his brother 'Ubayd Allah seized him, imprisoned him and tortured him, and when his imprisonment lengthened, the people of Yemen came to Mu'awiyah and interceded for him, and he was released.

(See al-Shi'r wa al-Shu'ara' by Ibn Qutaybah and Khizanat al-Adab at the third witness after the three hundred and twenty-eighth after the four hundredth).]]

i.e., "and the one." Al-Zajjaj also said, and al-Farra' too: It is permissible that "yad'u" be repeated upon what precedes it, for the sake of intensifying this action which is calling, and it is not made transitive since you made it transitive first, i.e., "he calls upon, besides Allah, that which neither benefits him nor harms him, he calls," like "I struck Zayd, I struck," then the second "yad'u" is deleted, being sufficed by the first. Al-Farra' said: It is also permissible to read "lamman darruhu" with a kasra on the lam, i.e., "he calls to the one whose harm is nearer than his benefit," and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: "Because your Lord has inspired to her" [[See vol. 20, p. 149.]] [al-Zalzalah: 5], i.e., "to her." Al-Farra' also said, and al-Qaffal: the lam is extraneous (silah), i.e., "he calls upon whose harm is nearer than his benefit," i.e., "he worships him." It is also so in the reading of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud.

(Labi'sa al-mawla) i.e., in giving support (al-tanasur), (and wretched is the companion) i.e., the associate, the companion and the intimate. Mujahid said: he means the idol.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 14:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believed and did righteous deeds to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. When He mentioned the state of the polytheists, the hypocrites and the devils, He also mentioned the state of the believers in the Hereafter.

(Indeed, Allah does what He wills) meaning: He rewards whom He wills and punishes whom He wills. For the believers is Paradise, by the judgment of His true promise and by His grace; and for the disbelievers is the Fire, by what has preceded from His justice, not because the act of the Lord is conditioned by the acts of the servants.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 15:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever thinks that Allah will not help him in this world and the Hereafter, let him stretch out a rope to the sky⁠﴾. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: Among the best things said about it is that the meaning is: whoever thinks that Allah will not help Muhammad ﷺ, and that he (the one thinking) is able to cut off the victory which he (Muhammad) has been given.

﴿Let him stretch out a rope to the sky⁠﴾ means: let him seek a stratagem by which he may reach the sky.

﴿Then let him cut it off⁠﴾ means: then let him cut off the victory, if he is able to do so.

﴿Then let him look whether his scheme removes what enrages him⁠﴾. His scheme and stratagem is what enrages him of the victory of the Prophet ﷺ. The point of the statement is that if he is not able to scheme and devise in such a way, he will not reach the cutting off of the victory. Similarly, Ibn 'Abbas said: the pronoun in "Allah will help him" refers to Muhammad ﷺ. Although he has not been mentioned, the whole discourse indicates him, because faith is faith in Allah and in Muhammad ﷺ, and turning away from the religion is turning away from the religion which Muhammad ﷺ brought. That is: whoever, among those who oppose Muhammad ﷺ, and among those who worship Allah with a single doubt, thinks that we will not help Muhammad ﷺ, let him do such and such.

Also from Ibn 'Abbas: the pronoun refers to "man" (man), and the meaning is: whoever thinks that Allah will not provide for him, let him choke himself, let him kill himself, since there is no good in a life devoid of Allah's help. The "victory" (nasr) in this view means provision (rizq). The Arabs say: "Whoever gives me help, may Allah help him," meaning: whoever gives me, may Allah give him. From this is the Arab saying: "a land mansurah," meaning rained upon. Al-Faq'asi said:

"Indeed you do not give a man beyond his right,
nor do you own the cleft which the rain is its helper."

Similarly Ibn Abi Najih narrated from Mujahid, who said: "Whoever thinks that Allah will not help him," meaning: will not provide for him. This is also the saying of Abu 'Ubaydah. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the religion, and the meaning is: whoever thinks that Allah will not help His religion.

﴿With a rope⁠﴾ means: with a cord. The "sabab" is that by which one reaches something. ﴿To the sky⁠﴾ means: to the roof of the house. Ibn Zayd said: it is the well-known sky. The Kufans read "thumma layaqta'" with a sukun on the lam. Al-Nahhas said: this is weak in Arabic, because "thumma" is not like the waw and the fa', since it can be stopped upon and stands alone. In the reading of 'Abdullah: "fal-yaqta'hu thumma linazur hal yudhhibanna kaydahu ma yaghiz." It was said: "ma" is in the sense of "alladhi," meaning: whether his scheme removes that which enrages him, and the pronoun was dropped to make it lighter. It was also said: "ma" is in the sense of the verbal noun, meaning: whether his scheme removes his rage.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And thus did We send it down as clear signs﴾, meaning the Qur'an.

(And that Allah) i.e., and thus [it is that] Allah (guides whom He wills). He made the existence of guidance dependent upon His will, so He is the Guide, and there is no guide besides Him.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾, that is, in Allah and in Muhammad (ﷺ).

(And those who are Jews) — the Jews, who are those ascribed to the religion (millah) of Musa, peace be upon him.

(And the Sabians) — they are a people who worship the stars.

(And the Christians) — they are those ascribed to the religion of Isa.

(And the Magians) — they are the worshippers of fire, who hold that the world has two origins: light and darkness. Qatadah said: "The religions are five: four belong to Satan and one belongs to the Most Merciful." It has also been said: the Magians are originally the "nujus" (the impure), because of their religious practice of using impurities, and the mim and the nun interchange, as in al-ghaym and al-ghayn, and al-aym and al-ayn. All of this has already been discussed in full in al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 433].

(And those who associated partners) — they are the Arabs, the worshippers of idols.

(Indeed, Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection) — that is, He will decide and render judgment: the disbelievers will have the Fire, and the believers will have Paradise. It has also been said: this separation consists in making clear to them the truth from falsehood by a necessary knowledge, whereas in this world the truth is distinguished from falsehood through reflection and reasoning.

(Indeed, Allah is over all things a Witness) — that is, over the deeds of His creation, their movements and their words, so nothing of them escapes Him. Glory be to Him! The statement "Indeed, Allah will judge between them" is the predicate of "indeed" in "Indeed, those who believe," just as you say: "Indeed Zayd, indeed the good is with him." Al-Farra' said: "It is not permissible in speech to say 'Indeed Zayd, indeed his brother is departing,' and he claimed that it is permissible in the verse only because the sentence carries the meaning of a conditional, i.e., whoever believes and whoever becomes a Jew, or a Christian, or a Sabian, will be judged between them, and their reckoning is with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic." Abu Ishaq refuted this view of al-Farra' and found his statement that it is impermissible, "Indeed Zayd, indeed his brother is departing," repugnant. He said: "Because there is no difference between Zayd and alladhina (those who), and 'indeed' enters upon every subject, so you say 'Indeed Zayd, he is departing,' then you bring in another 'indeed' and say 'Indeed Zayd, indeed he is departing.'" And the poet said:

Indeed the caliph, indeed Allah has clothed him
With the garment of honor, by which the seals are brought (tarja).

[The variant reading is "tuzji" with zay and jim; al-izja' means driving. "Al-khawatim" is the plural of "al-khatam," a dialectal form of "al-khatim." He means that the rulers of the horizons send their seals to him out of fear of him, so their kingdom is added to his kingdom. This verse is from a qasidah by Jarir praising Abd al-Aziz ibn al-Walid ibn Abd al-Malik.

(From Khizanat al-Adab.)]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 18:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen that to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth﴾. This is the seeing of the heart, meaning: have you not seen with your heart and your intellect. The meaning of prostration (sujud) has already been discussed in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 1, p. 291.]], and the prostration of inanimate things in "al-Nahl".

"And the sun" is conjoined to "whoever". Likewise (and the moon, and the stars, and the mountains, and the trees, and the beasts, and many of mankind). Then He said: (and many have the punishment justly due to them). This is problematic in terms of i'rab (grammatical analysis): why was it not put in the accusative so that what the verb governs would be conjoined to what the verb governs, as in: ﴿and for the wrongdoers He has prepared a painful punishment﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 150.]] [al-Insan: 31]? Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' held that it would have been good to put it in the accusative, but the nominative was preferred because the meaning is "and many have refused prostration", so it is an inceptive clause (mubtada') and predicate (khabar), and the speech is complete at His saying "and many of mankind". It is also permissible for it to be conjoined, with prostration understood as humility and submission to the governance of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in weakness and strength, health and sickness, beauty and ugliness, and this encompasses everything. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative by supposing: "and He humiliated many, for whom the punishment is justly due", and the like. It was also said: the speech is complete at His saying "and the beasts", then He began: "and many of mankind" will be in Paradise, "and many have the punishment justly due to them". Likewise it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: (The meaning is: and many of mankind will be in Paradise, and many have the punishment justly due to them), recorded by Ibn al-Anbari. And Abu al-'Aliyah said: There is no star, nor moon, nor sun in the heavens except that it falls prostrate to Allah when it sets, then it does not turn back until it is permitted, and it returns from its rising-place. Al-Qushayri said: This has been reported in a connected (musnad) report concerning the sun, so this is a real prostration, and from its necessity is the composition of life and intellect in this one who prostrates. I say: The connected hadith to which he alluded was recorded by Muslim, and it will come in Surah "Ya Sin" at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the sun runs on to its resting place﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 26 onward.]] [Ya Sin: 38]. The meaning of prostration linguistically and in sense has already been discussed in al-Baqarah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever Allah humiliates, there is none to honour him﴾. That is: whoever Allah humiliates with wretchedness and disbelief, no one can remove the humiliation from him. Ibn 'Abbas said: Whoever neglects the worship of Allah goes to the Fire.

(Indeed Allah does what He wills): He means that their destination is the Fire, so there is no objection to Him from anyone. Al-Akhfash, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' related: "And whoever Allah humiliates, there is none to honour him", meaning honour (ikram).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 19–21:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾. Muslim transmitted from Qays ibn 'Abbad, who said: I heard Abu Dharr swear an oath that ﴿These two adversaries who dispute concerning their Lord﴾ was revealed concerning those who came forth on the day of Badr: Hamzah, 'Ali, 'Ubaydah ibn al-Harith, may Allah be pleased with them, and 'Utbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabi'ah, and al-Walid ibn 'Utbah. With this hadith Muslim (may Allah have mercy on him) concluded his book. Ibn 'Abbas said: These three verses were revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) in Madinah concerning three men from among the believers and three men from among the disbelievers, and he named them, as Abu Dharr mentioned. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Indeed I will be the first to kneel for contention before Allah on the Day of Resurrection, meaning his account of his duel with his two companions. It was recorded by al-Bukhari. This view was held by Hilal ibn Yasaf, 'Ata' ibn Yasar and others. 'Ikrimah said: The two adversaries refer to Paradise and Hell; they disputed, and Hell said: He created me for His punishment. And Paradise said: He created me for His mercy. I say: A hadith has also been related about the contention of Paradise and Hell, from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Paradise and Hell argued. This one said: The tyrants and the arrogant will enter me. And that one said: The weak and the needy will enter me. Allah, Exalted is He, said to this one: You are My punishment; I punish with you whom I will. And He said to that one: You are My mercy; I show mercy with you whom I will. And each of you will have its fill." Recorded by al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Tirmidhi, who said: a hasan sahih hadith. Ibn 'Abbas also said: They are the People of the Book, who said to the believers: We are closer to Allah than you, and older in scripture than you, and our Prophet came before your Prophet. The believers said: We are more entitled to Allah than you; we believe in Muhammad and we believe in your Prophet and in what was revealed to him of Scripture, while you know our Prophet and have abandoned him and disbelieved in him out of envy. So this was their dispute, and this verse was revealed concerning them. This is the view of Qatadah. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 22:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Every time they wish to get out of it﴾, that is, out of the Fire.

(They are returned into it) by being struck with the maqami' (iron hooks/rods). Abu Dhabyan said: It has been mentioned to us that they attempt to get out of the Fire when it surges and boils with them, and it throws those in it up to its highest gates, so they wish to leave, but the guardians (khazzan) return them into it with the maqami'. It was also said: when their distress in it becomes intense, they flee, and whoever reaches its edge, the angels return them into it with the maqami', and they say to them: ﴿Taste the punishment of the burning﴾, that is, the burning one, like "the painful" and "the agonizing." It was also said: al-HarIq (the burning) is a noun from al-ihtiraq (burning). One says "tahharaqa al-shay' bi'l-nar" and "ihtaraqa," and the noun is al-hurqah and al-hariq. Dhawq (tasting) is a contact through which the perception of taste is obtained; here it is used in an extended sense, and what is meant by it is their perception of pain.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 23:

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who have believed and done righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow.﴾ When He mentioned one of the two adversaries, who is the disbeliever, He mentioned the state of the other adversary, who is the believer.

(They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold) The "min" (من) is extra (ṣilah). This is according to the view of al-Akhfash and the Kufis, who permit the addition of "min" in an affirmative sentence. As for those who do not permit its addition in an affirmative sentence, some of them said it is partitive (lil-tab'id), some said it denotes the beginning (lil-ibtida'), and some said it is explanatory (bayaniyyah).

(Refer to al-Bahr al-Muhit and Ruh al-Ma'ani on the discussion of this verse.) "Al-asawir" is the plural of "uswirah," and "uswirah" has as its singular "siwar." It has three dialectal forms: the sīn with a ḍammah, the sīn with a kasrah, and "iswar." The exegetes said: since kings in this world wear bracelets and crowns, God has given that to the people of Paradise. None of the people of Paradise is without three bracelets on his hand: a bracelet of gold, a bracelet of silver, and a bracelet of pearls. He said here, and in Fatir [refer to vol. 14, p. ...]: ﴿of bracelets of gold and pearls﴾ [Fatir: 33], and He said in Surat al-Insan [refer to vol. 19, p. 141]: ﴿and they will be adorned with bracelets of silver﴾ [al-Insan: 21]. In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, who said: I heard my friend (ﷺ) say: "The ornament will reach the believer wherever the ablution reaches." It has also been said: women are adorned with gold and men with silver. But this is open to question, and the Qur'an refutes it.

("Wa-lu'lu'an") Nafi', Ibn al-Qa'qa', Shaybah and 'Asim recited here and in Surat al-Malaikah [refer to vol. 14, p. ...] "lu'lu'an" in the accusative case, meaning "and they will be adorned with pearls." They argued that it is written with an alif in all the codices here. Likewise Ya'qub, al-Jahdari and 'Isa ibn 'Umar recited it in the accusative here and in the genitive in "Fatir," following the codex, since it is written here with an alif and there without an alif. The rest [the Egyptian government's printed mushaf has it with an alif in both places] recited it in the genitive in both places. Abu Bakr did not hamz "al-lu'lu'" anywhere in the Qur'an; it is what is extracted from the sea from within the oyster shell. Al-Qushayri said: the intended meaning is the inlaying of the bracelet with pearls, and it is not far-fetched that there may be in Paradise a bracelet of pure pearl [al-musmat: that which is not mixed with anything else]. I say: this is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, indeed its explicit wording. Ibn al-Anbari said: whoever recites "lu'lu'" in the genitive pauses on it and does not pause on "adh-dhahab." Al-Sijistani said: whoever puts "al-lu'lu'" in the accusative, the sufficient pause is at "min dhahab," because the meaning is "and they will be adorned with pearls." Ibn al-Anbari said: this is not so, because when we put "al-lu'lu'" in the genitive we conjoin it to the wording of "al-asawir," and when we put it in the accusative we conjoin it to the sense of "al-asawir," as though we had said: "they will be adorned therein with bracelets and pearls," so it is in the accusative in the same position as it is in the genitive, and there is no sense in cutting it off from the first [in K: "from"].

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿and their clothing therein is silk﴾, meaning: all that they wear, of their bedding, their garments and their curtains, is silk, and it is far superior to what is in this world. Al-Nasa'i related on the authority of Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever wears silk in this world will not wear it in the Hereafter, whoever drinks wine in this world will not drink it in the Hereafter, and whoever drinks from vessels of gold and silver will not drink from them in the Hereafter." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The clothing of the people of Paradise, the drink of the people of Paradise and the vessels of the people of Paradise [are...]." If it is said: the Prophet (ﷺ) equated these three things and said that one is deprived of them in the Hereafter, so is he deprived of them when he enters Paradise? We say: Yes! If he does not repent of them, he is deprived of them in the Hereafter even if he enters Paradise, for hastening to what Allah has forbidden him in this world. It cannot be said: that deprivation applies only during the time he is punished in the Fire or through the long duration of his stay at the place of standing; as for when he enters Paradise, then no, because depriving one who is in Paradise of some of its pleasures is a kind of punishment and chastisement, and Paradise is not an abode of punishment, nor is there any chastisement in it in any way. We say: what you have mentioned is possible, were it not that there came what repels this possibility and rejects it from the apparent meaning of the hadith we have mentioned. And what the Imams related from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever drinks wine in this world and does not repent of it will be deprived of it in the Hereafter." The default is to hold to the apparent meaning until a text comes that repels it. Indeed, a text has come affirming the correctness of what we have mentioned, which is what Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi related in his Musnad: Hisham related to us from Qatadah from Dawud al-Sarraj from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever wears silk in this world will not wear it in the Hereafter, and even if he enters Paradise, the people of Paradise will wear it and he will not wear it." This is an explicit text, and its chain is sound. If "and even if he enters Paradise, the people of Paradise will wear it and he will not wear it" is from the words of the Prophet (ﷺ), then it is the utmost in clarity; and if it is from the words of the narrator as has been mentioned, then he is more knowledgeable about the wording and more apt about the circumstance, and such is not said by opinion. And Allah knows best. Likewise [the hadith] "whoever drinks wine and does not repent" and "whoever uses vessels of gold and silver."
