And just as one does not desire the station of one who is higher than him, and that is not a punishment, so likewise one does not desire the wine of Paradise nor its silk, and that is not a punishment. We have mentioned all of this in full in the book al-Tadhkirah, praise be to Allah, and we mentioned in it that the trees of Paradise and its fruits split open to yield the garments of Paradise, and we have mentioned it in the commentary on Surat al-Kahf [refer to vol. 10, p. 397].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 24:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they were guided to good speech﴾, meaning they were directed to it. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means "There is no god but Allah" and "All praise is for Allah." And it was said: it is the Qur'an. Then it was said: this is in the world, they were guided to the testimony (shahadah) and to the recitation of the Qur'an.

(﴿And they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy﴾), meaning to the path of Allah. The path of Allah is His religion, which is Islam. And it was said: they were guided in the Hereafter to good speech, which is "All praise is for Allah," because they will say tomorrow, "All praise is for Allah who guided us to this," "All praise is for Allah who has removed grief from us." In Paradise there is no idle talk and no falsehood, so whatever they say is good speech. They were also guided in Paradise to the path of Allah, since there is nothing in Paradise that opposes the command of Allah. And it was said: the good speech is what comes to them from Allah of good tidings. ﴿And they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy﴾, meaning to the way of Paradise.

**Ibn al-Qurtubi's commentary on Surah 22, verse 25 (part 1 of 2)**

There are seven issues (masa'il) here.

**The first issue:** God's words ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [others]﴾. The discourse returns to the idolaters of the Arabs when they barred the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from the Sacred Mosque in the year of al-Hudaybiyah. That is because no barring by them is known before that gathering, unless it is meant that they barred individuals from among the people, which did occur at the beginning of the mission (al-mab'ath). Al-sadd (barring) means prevention, so the sense is "and they bar." For this reason the future form is joined to the past (in the coordination of the verb ﴿and bar﴾, a present/future verb coordinated with a past verb) and it is acceptable. It has also been said that the waw is extra, so that "and bar" is the predicate (khabar) of "inna" (indeed). But this corrupts the intended meaning. The predicate is actually omitted and understood at God's words "and the desert dwellers" (al-bad), its implied sense being: they are the losers when they perish. The verb "and bar" comes in the future form because it is an action they continually maintain, just as God's words ﴿those who believe, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of God﴾ [al-Ra'd: 28] came in this way. It is as if He said: "Indeed, those who disbelieve, barring is among their habits." Had He said "those who disbelieve and barred," it would also have been permissible.

Al-Nahhas said: "In my book, from Abu Ishaq, he said: 'It is permissible, and this is the preferred view, that the predicate is ﴿We shall make them taste of a painful punishment﴾." Abu Ja'far said: "This is an error. I do not know what justification there is for it, because it has the predicate of 'inna' in a jussive form (jazm), and moreover it is the answer of a condition (jawab al-shart), and if it were the predicate of 'inna' the condition would remain without an answer. Especially since the verb in the condition is in the future, so it must have an answer."

**The second issue:** God's words ﴿and the Sacred Mosque﴾. It has been said that it refers to the Mosque itself, which is the apparent sense of the Qur'an, since He mentions nothing else. It has also been said that it refers to the entire Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), because the idolaters barred the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his companions from it in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, so he (ﷺ) stopped outside it. God said: ﴿and they barred you from the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Fath: 25], and He said: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Isra': 1]. This is correct, but here He mentioned the important point that was intended.

**The third issue:** God's words ﴿which We have made for the people﴾, meaning for prayer, circumambulation and worship. It is like His words ﴿Indeed, the first House established for the people﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 96].

﴿equal for the resident therein and the desert-dweller﴾. Al-'Akif means the one who stays and remains constantly. Al-Bad means the people of the desert and whoever comes to them. The meaning is: in honouring its sanctity and performing the rites there, the local and the one who comes from the lands are equal, so the people of Makkah have no greater right than the one who travels to it. It has been said that the equality applies only to its houses and dwellings: the one who lives in them is no more entitled than the newcomer who arrives at them. This is on the basis that the Sacred Mosque means the entire Sacred Precinct. This is the view of Mujahid and Malik, as transmitted from him by Ibn al-Qasim.

It is reported from 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas and a group that the one who arrives has the right to stay wherever he finds room, and the owner of the dwelling must lodge him, whether he wishes or refuses. Sufyan al-Thawri and others said this. This was also the practice in the early period: their houses had no doors until theft increased. A man then made a door, and 'Umar objected to him and said: "Will you lock a door in the face of the pilgrims to God's House?" He replied: "I only wanted to protect their goods from theft." So he left it, and the people began to make doors.

It is also reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him) that during the pilgrimage season he would order the doors of the houses of Makkah to be removed, so that whoever arrived could enter and settle wherever he wished. Tents would be pitched inside the houses.

It is reported from Malik that houses are not like the Mosque, and their residents have the right to refuse entry to others and to have exclusive use of them. This is the current practice, and this view was held by the majority of the community (in MS K: "the imams").

This disagreement rests on two foundations. The first is whether the houses of Makkah belong to their owners or to the people at large. The disagreement has two causes. The first is whether the conquest of Makkah was by force ('anwah), in which case it becomes spoils of war. But the Prophet (ﷺ) did not distribute it, and left it to its inhabitants and to those who came after them, just as 'Umar (may God be pleased with him) did with the land of al-Sawad, and he remitted the land tax (kharaj) for them, just as he (ﷺ) pardoned their captives and did not enslave them, out of kindness to them, unlike the rest of the disbelievers. Therefore it remains as it is: it may not be sold or rented, and whoever arrives first at a place has the better claim to it. This is the view of Malik, Abu Hanifah and al-Awza'i. Or its conquest was by treaty (sulh), which is the position of al-Shafi'i, in which case their dwellings remain in their hands, and they may dispose of their properties as they wish.

It is reported that 'Umar bought the house of Safwan ibn Umayyah for four thousand (dirhams) and made it a prison, and he was the first to imprison in Islam, as already explained in the verse about those who wage war in Surah al-Ma'idah (see vol. 6, p. 153). It is also reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) imprisoned someone on suspicion. Tawus disliked imprisonment in Makkah and used to say: "It is not fitting for a house of punishment to be in a house of mercy."

I say: the correct view is that of Malik, and the apparent sense of the established reports indicates that it was conquered by force. Abu 'Ubayd said: "We know of no city resembling Makkah." Al-Daraqutni transmitted from 'Alqamah ibn Nadlah, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) died, and Abu Bakr and 'Umar (may God be pleased with them both) were alive, and the dwellings of Makkah were not called anything but al-sawa'ib (free, unowned). Whoever needed shelter lodged there, and whoever was wealthy housed others." In another version 'Uthman is added. It is also transmitted from 'Alqamah ibn Nadlah al-Kinani, who said: "The houses of Makkah in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), Abu Bakr and 'Umar (may God be pleased with them both) were called al-sawa'ib; they were not sold. Whoever needed shelter lodged there, and whoever was wealthy housed others."

It is also transmitted from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "God Most High has made Makkah sacred, so the sale of its dwellings and the eating of their price is forbidden," and he said: "Whoever eats anything from the rent of the houses of Makkah is only eating fire." Al-Daraqutni said: "Abu Hanifah transmitted it as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report, and he erred in this; he also erred in saying 'Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Yazid, when it is in fact Ibn Abi Ziyad al-Haddah. The correct version is mawquf (ending with a Companion)." Al-Daraqutni also transmitted from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Makkah is a resting place (munakh); its dwellings may not be sold or rented." Abu Dawud transmitted from 'A'ishah (may God be pleased with her), who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of God, shall I build you a house or a structure at Mina to shade you from the sun?' He said: 'No, it is only a resting place for whoever arrives first.'"

Al-Shafi'i (may God be pleased with him) relied on God's words ﴿those who were expelled from their homes﴾ [al-Hajj: 40], attributing the homes to them. The Prophet (ﷺ) also said on the day of the conquest: "Whoever closes his door is safe, and whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe."

**The fourth issue:** Most readers read ﴿equal﴾ (sawa'un) in the nominative (raf'), as the subject (mubtada') of the sentence, with ﴿al-'akif﴾ as its predicate (khabar). It has also been said that the predicate is ﴿equal﴾, placed first, meaning: the resident therein and the desert-dweller are equal. This is the view of Abu 'Ali, and the meaning is: "that which We have made for the people as a qibla or a place of worship, the resident therein and the desert-dweller are equal."

Hafs, from 'Asim, read ﴿equal﴾ in the accusative (nasb), and this is the reading of al-A'mash. This too admits two possibilities. The first: it is the second object (maf'ul thani) of "made" (ja'ala), and ﴿al-'akif﴾ is raised by it because it is a verbal noun (masdar), which operates like an active participle (ism al-fa'il), since it means "equal." The second: it is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the pronoun in "We have made it."

One group read ﴿equal﴾ in the accusative, ﴿al-'akif﴾ in the genitive (khafd), and ﴿and the desert-dweller﴾ as a conjunct of "the people," the sense being: "that which We have made for the people, the resident and the desert-dweller."

Ibn Kathir's reading, both in pause and in continuation, is with the yā' (ي) in ﴿al-bādī﴾. Abu 'Amr paused without the yā' and joined with it. Nafi' read without the yā' both in continuation and in pause (Warsh transmitted from Nafi' the yā' in continuation but not in pause).

All agree on the equality within the Mosque itself, but they differ regarding Makkah, and we have already mentioned this.

**The fifth issue:** ﴿and whoever intends therein deviation with wrongdoing﴾ is a conditional clause (shart), and its answer is ﴿We shall make him taste of a painful punishment﴾. Ilhad (deviation) linguistically means inclining away, but God clarified that the deviation meant is with wrongdoing (zulm). There is disagreement about the wrongdoing. 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿and whoever intends therein deviation with wrongdoing﴾ that he said: "It is polytheism." 'Ata' said: "Polytheism and killing." It has also been said that it means hunting its pigeons, cutting its trees, and entering it without being in the state of ihram.

Ibn 'Umar said: "We used to say that deviation therein is for a person to say: 'No, by God!', 'Yes, by God!' and 'Certainly not, by God!'" For this reason he had two tents (fusțat), one in the non-sacred area (al-hill) and the other in the sacred precinct (al-haram). When he wished to pray he entered the tent of the sacred precinct, and when he wished to attend to some of his affairs he entered the tent of al-hill, to keep the sacred precinct free of such utterances, since God had magnified the sin therein.

Similarly 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As had two tents, one in al-hill and the other in the sacred precinct. When he wished to reprimand his family he did so in al-hill, and when he wished to pray he prayed in the sacred precinct. When he was asked about this he said: "We used to say that among deviation in the sacred precinct is saying 'No, by God!' and 'Yes, by God!' and sins are multiplied in Makkah just as good deeds are multiplied, so that a sin becomes two sins: one by the very act of disobedience, and the second by violating the sanctity of the sacred city." The sacred months are likewise. This has already been mentioned.

Abu Dawud transmitted from Ya'la ibn Umayyah that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Hoarding food in the sacred precinct is deviation therein." This is also the view of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. The general wording covers all of this.

**The sixth issue:** Some of the interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil), including al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd, held that this verse indicates that a person is punished for the sins he intends in Makkah even if he does not commit them. A similar report is transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Umar, who said: "If a man intended to kill another man in this House while he was at 'Adan Abyan (a town near the entrance of the Red Sea, which is called after Abyan, unlike 'Adan), God would punish him." I say: this is correct, and this meaning has been clarified in Surah ﴿Nun. By the pen﴾ [al-Qalam: 1], as will be explained there, God willing.

**The seventh issue:** The bā' in ﴿with deviation﴾ is extra (za'idah), like its extra use in God's words ﴿a tree that grows with oil﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 20] (see p. 14 of this part). On this basis they interpreted the poet's verse:

"We are the sons of Ja'dah, the companions of al-Falaj... we strike with the sword and hope for relief (bil-faraj)."

He meant: "we hope for relief (al-faraj)." Al-A'sha said:

"Our spears guaranteed the sustenance of our dependents."

meaning "sustenance." Another poet said (the speaker is Qays ibn Zuhayr al-'Absi, a pre-Islamic poet, from a rhyming ode he composed about a dispute between him and al-Rabi' ibn Ziyad al-'Absi; see *Khizanat al-Adab*, the thirty-sixth witness after six hundred):

"Has it not reached you, and the news spreads, of what the camels of the sons of Ziyad have met?"

meaning "what they met," with the bā' being extra; and this is common. Al-Farra' said: "I heard a Bedouin, and I asked him about something, and he said: 'I hope for that (arju bidhalika),' meaning 'I hope for that (arju dhalika).'" And another poet said:

"In a Yemeni valley whose bottom grows wild thyme (al-shatt), and whose lower part grows acacia and al-shabhan..."

"Ayy al-markh" (i.e., the sense of "ilhad" here is "al-markh," the act of deviating or the wrong-doing). This is the view of al-Akhfash, and in his understanding the meaning is: "And whoever intends in it deviation by wrongdoing." The Kufans said: the letter "ba'" (bi-) has entered because the meaning is "that he deviates" (bi-an yulhida), and the "ba'" with "an" may both be inserted and omitted. It is also permissible that the sense is: "And whoever desires people in it with deviation."

This deviation and wrongdoing gathers all sins, from disbelief down to minor offences. Because of the great sanctity of the place, Allah the Exalted threatened punishment for merely intending an evil deed within it. And whoever intends an evil deed but does not do it is not held to account for it, except in Makkah. This is the statement of Ibn Mas'ud and a group of the Companions and others, and we have mentioned it just above.

**Issue 1:** Concerning His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And when We settled Abraham in the place of the House﴾. That is, mention when We settled Abraham. One says *bawwa'tuhu manzilan* and *bawwa'tu lahu*, just as one says *makkantuka* and *makkantu laka* (both meaning "I established you"). So the *lam* in His words "*li-Ibrahim*" (for Abraham) is additional, for emphasis, like His words ﴿radifa lakum﴾ [An-Naml: 72] (See vol. 13, p. 230.). This is the view of al-Farra' (the grammarian). It has also been said that "*bawwa'na li-Ibrahim makan al-bayt*" means We showed him the original foundation so that he could build it. The House had been effaced by the Flood and other events. When the time of Abraham (peace be upon him) came, God commanded him to build it. He came to its location and began searching for a trace. God then sent a wind that uncovered the foundations of Adam (peace be upon him), and he set its foundations upon them, as was explained earlier in *al-Baqarah* (See vol. 2, p. 122.). It has also been said that "*bawwa'na*" [10: 93] is treated as a verb that takes the *lam* preposition, like *ja'alna* (We made), so the meaning is: We made for Abraham the place of the House a settled place. A poet said:

"How many a noble brother of mine
I laid in his niche-grave with my own hand."

**Issue 2:** The phrase "*an la tushrik*" (that you do not associate) addresses Abraham (peace be upon him), according to the majority. Ikrimah recited "*an la yushrika*" with the *ya'*, reporting the sense of the statement that was addressed to him. Abu Hatim said: On this reading the *kaf* must be in the subjunctive, meaning *li-'alla yushrik* (so that he would not associate). It has also been said that "*an*" is a lightened form of the heavy *anna*. It has been said that it is explanatory, and it has been said that it is superfluous, like ﴿falamma an ja'a al-bashir﴾ [Yusuf: 96] (See vol. 9, p. 259.).

The verse contains a reproach to those among the settlers of the House who associated others with God. That is, this was the condition laid upon your forefather and those after him, and you did not fulfill it but rather associated others with God. A group said: the address in "*an la tushrik*" is to Muhammad (ﷺ), and he was commanded to purify the House and to proclaim the Hajj. The majority hold that this refers to Abraham, and this is the more correct view. The purification of the House is general, covering disbelief, innovations, all impurities, and blood. It has also been said that it means purification from idols, as God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿So shun the abomination of idols﴾ [Al-Hajj: 30] (See p. 53 of this part and following.). This is because Jurhum and the Amalaqah had idols in the location of the House and around it before Abraham (peace be upon him) built it. It has also been said that the meaning is: Keep My House free from being worshipped with an idol in it. This is a command to manifest monotheism in it. What the scholars have said about purifying the Sacred Mosque and other mosques has already been discussed in sufficient detail in *Surat Bara'ah* (See vol. 8, p. 104.).

"Those who stand" (*al-qa'imun*) are those who pray. He, Exalted is He, mentioned among the pillars of prayer the greatest of them, which are standing, bowing, and prostration.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 27:

There are seven issues in it.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage﴾. Most of the reciters read "wa-adhdhin" (وَأَذِّنْ) with the dhal doubled. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Ibn Muhaysin read "wa-ādhin" (وَآذِنْ) with the dhal single and the alif lengthened. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This was garbled for Ibn Jinni, for he related from them "wa-ādhana" (وَآذَنَ) as a past-tense verb, and parsed it on that basis, making it a conjunction with "bawwa'nā" [10:93]. The adhan (أَذَان) means informing, and it has already been discussed in "Bara'ah" [see vol. 8, p. 69].

The second: When Ibrahim, peace be upon him, finished building the House, and it was said to him: "Proclaim to the people the pilgrimage," he said: "O Lord! And how will my voice reach them?" He said: "Proclaim, and upon Me is the conveying." So Ibrahim, the Friend of Allah, climbed Mount Abu Qubays and called out: "O people! Indeed Allah has commanded you to make pilgrimage to this House, so that He may reward you with Paradise and protect you from the punishment of the Fire. So make pilgrimage." Then whoever was in the loins of men and the wombs of women responded: "Labbayka Allahumma labbayk!" Whoever responded that day performed Hajj according to the measure of his response: if he answered once, then once; if he answered twice, then twice. The talbiyah proceeded on that basis. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr.

It is related from Abu al-Tufayl who said: Ibn 'Abbas said to me: "Do you know what was the origin of the talbiyah?" I said: "No." He said: "When Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was commanded to proclaim to the people the pilgrimage, the mountains lowered their peaks and the towns were raised up for him, so he called out to the people for the Hajj, and everything answered him: Labbayka Allahumma labbayk."

It was also said: The address to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, ends at His saying "al-sujud," and then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, addressed Muhammad, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, saying: "And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage," meaning: inform them that the Hajj is obligatory upon them.

A third opinion: the address from His saying "an la tushrik" (that you do not associate) is an address to the Prophet ﷺ. This is the view of the people of reflection, because the Qur'an was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ, so every address within it is to him unless a decisive proof indicates otherwise. Here there is another proof that the address is to the Prophet ﷺ: the word "an la tushrik bi" with the taa (تُشْرِكْ), which is an address to one who is present, whereas Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was absent. The meaning according to this is: "And when We settled for Ibrahim the place of the House, [We said]: ... We made for you the signs of the oneness of Allah, exalted is He, and that Ibrahim worshipped Allah alone."

The reciters, the majority, read "bil-hajj" (بِالْحَجِّ) with a fatha on the ha. Ibn Abi Ishaq read it throughout the Qur'an with a kasra on it. It was also said: Ibrahim's proclamation was among the things he was commanded from the laws of the religion. And Allah knows best.

The third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will come to you on foot and on every lean camel﴾. He promised that people would respond to the call to the pilgrimage to the House, both those who walk and those who ride. He said "they will come to you" (يَأْتُوكَ), although they come to the Ka'bah, because the one who called out was Ibrahim; so whoever comes to the Ka'bah as a pilgrim has in effect come to Ibrahim, since he answered his call. This also honours Ibrahim.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "rijalan" (رِجالًا) is the plural of rajil, like tajir and tijar, and sahib and sihab. It was also said: rijal is the plural of rajul, and rajjal is a plural, as rajil is like tijar, tajr and tajir, and sihab, sahb and sahib. It may also be said in the plural: rujjal with doubled jim, like kafir and kuffar. Ibn Abi Ishaq and Ikrimah read "rujalan" (رُجَالًا) with a damma on the ra and a light jim, which is rare among plural patterns, and it is related from Mujahid. Mujahid also read "rujala" (رُجَالَى) on the pattern of fu'ala, so it is like kusala. Al-Nahhas said: For the plural of rajil there are five forms: rijalah, like rukkab, which is what is related from Ikrimah; rijal, like qiyam; rajlah; rajl; and rijalah. What is related from Mujahid, rujalan, is not well known, and it is more likely that it is not nunated, like kusala and sukara; if it were nunated it would be fu'al, and fu'al in the plural is rare. The men were mentioned before the riders in the mention because of the greater hardship they endure in walking.

(And upon every lean camel they will come) because the meaning of "dhamir" (ضَامِرٍ) is the meaning of dawamir. Al-Farra' said: It is permissible to say "ya'ti" (يَأْتِي) according to the wording. The "dhamir" is the emaciated camel that the journey has worn out; it is said: damura yadmuru dumuran. Allah, exalted is He, described them by the state in which they reached Makkah, and mentioned the cause of the emaciation, saying: "they will come from every deep mountain pass" (مِنْ كُلِّ فَجٍّ عَمِيقٍ), meaning the length of the journey has affected them. He returned the pronoun to the camels as an honour to them, since they set out for Hajj together with their owners, as He said: "And the chargers panting" [100:1], referring to the horses of jihad, as an honour to them when they strove in the way of Allah.

The fourth: Some of them said: He only said "rijalan" because the majority who go out for Hajj are men rather than women. His saying "rijalan" is from your saying "hadha rajul" (this is a man). But this is far-fetched, given His saying "and upon every lean camel," meaning the riders, so men and women are included in it. When He said "rijalan" and began with them, this indicates that the Hajj of one who walks is more excellent than the Hajj of one who rides. Ibn 'Abbas said: I have no regret over anything that escaped me except that I did not perform Hajj on foot, for I heard Allah, Mighty and Majestic, say: "They will come to you on foot." Ibn Abi Najih said: Ibrahim and Isma'il, peace be upon them both, performed Hajj on foot. The companions of Ibn Mas'ud read "yatūna" (يَأْتُونَ), and this is the reading of Ibn Abi 'Ablah and al-Dahhak, with the pronoun referring to the people.

The fifth: There is no disagreement about the permissibility of riding and walking, but they differed about which of them is better. Malik and al-Shafi'i, among others, held that riding is better, following the example of the Prophet ﷺ, and because of the greater expense, and for magnifying the rites of Hajj by the readiness of riding. Others held that walking is better because of the hardship it imposes on the self, and because of the hadith of Abu Sa'id who said: The Prophet ﷺ and his companions performed Hajj on foot from Madinah to Makkah, and he said: "Tie your middles with your waistcloths," and he walked mixing in running (khalt al-harwalah) [meaning a mixture of walking and jogging, sometimes walking and sometimes hurrying, or moderately]. Ibn Majah recorded it in his Sunan. There is no disagreement that according to Malik riding is more excellent in all the rites, following the example of the Prophet ﷺ.

The sixth: Some scholars inferred from the omission of mention of the sea in this verse that the obligation of Hajj does not apply to those who must travel by sea. Malik said in al-Mawaziyyah: "I do not hear any mention of the sea," and this is a matter of inclination, not that the omission of its mention necessarily entails the omission of the obligation in it. This is because Makkah is not on a sea shore where people come by ship; whoever travels by sea must, in reaching Makkah, arrive either on foot or on a lean camel, so only the two states of arrival are mentioned. Dropping the obligation of Hajj merely because of the sea is neither a strong nor a weighty argument. As for when the sea is combined with an enemy, fear, a severe peril, or an illness afflicting a person, then Malik, al-Shafi'i and the majority of scholars hold that the obligation falls because of these excuses, and that it is not a path one is able to take. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The author of al-Istizhar mentioned words on this point, whose apparent meaning is that the obligation does not fall because of any of these excuses, and this is weak. I say: It is weaker than weak, and its explanation has already passed in "al-Baqarah" [vol. 2, p. 195].

"Al-fajj" (الْفَجُّ) is the wide road, and its plural is fijaj. It has already been discussed in "al-Anbiya'" [vol. 11, p. 285]. "Al-'amiq" means the distant.

The reading of the majority is "ya'tina" (يَأْتِينَ). The companions of Abdullah read "ya'tun" (يَأْتُونَ), which refers to the riders, while "ya'tina" refers to the camels, as if he said: "and upon lean camels they will come (from every deep mountain pass)," meaning distant. From this comes "bi'r 'amiqah," meaning a well of deep bottom, and from it the saying:

"And dark of depths, empty of its passage" [This is the first verse of a rajaz poem by Ru'bah ibn al-Ajjaj; after it comes: "Mushtabih al-a'lam, lammA' al-khafaq."]

The seventh: They differed about the one who reaches the House, whether he raises his hands upon seeing it or not. Abu Dawud related that Jabir ibn 'Abdullah was asked about a man who sees the House and raises his hands, and he said: "I did not think anyone did this except the Jews, and we performed Hajj with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and did not do it." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Hands are raised in seven places: at the opening of the prayer, at facing the House, at al-Safa and al-Marwah, at the two standing places, and at the two jamrahs." Al-Thawri, Ibn al-Mubarak, Ahmad and Ishaq followed the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas and weakened the hadith of Jabir, because its narrator Muhajir al-Makki is unknown. Ibn 'Umar used to raise his hands when seeing the House, and it is likewise related from Ibn 'Abbas.

There are twenty-three issues in this passage.

The first issue: God's words ﴿that they may witness﴾. That is, proclaim the Hajj to them, and they will come to you on foot and on mounted animals ﴿that they may witness﴾, meaning, that they may attend. Witnessing (al-shuhud) means attending.

﴿benefits for them﴾: that is, the rites, such as ʿArafat and al-Mashʿar al-Haram. It has also been said that it means forgiveness. It has also been said that it means trade. It has also been said that it is general: that they may attend benefits for them, meaning whatever pleases God, Exalted is He, concerning matters of this world and the Hereafter. This was said by Mujahid and ʿAta, and Ibn al-ʿArabi (Ibn al-ʿArabi) preferred it, because it includes all of these: the rites, trade, forgiveness, and worldly and otherworldly benefit. There is no disagreement that what is meant by God's words ﴿There is no blame on you if you seek bounty from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198] is trade. [See vol. 2, p. 413.]

The second issue: ﴿and mention the name of God on known days﴾. The discussion of the known days and the counted days has already passed in al-Baqarah. [See vol. 3, p. 1.] What is meant by mentioning the name of God is the invocation of the name at the time of slaughter and sacrifice, such as your saying: "In the name of God, God is greatest; O God, from You and for You." And like your saying at the time of slaughter ﴿Indeed, my prayer and my rites and my living and my dying are for God﴾ [al-Anʿam: 162], and so on. The disbelievers used to slaughter in the names of their idols, so the Lord made clear that what is obligatory is slaughter in the name of God. This has already passed in al-Anʿam. [See vol. 7, pp. 152 and 72 onwards.]

The third issue: The scholars differed about the time of slaughter on the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr). Malik, may God be pleased with him, said: after the imam's prayer and his slaughter, unless he delays excessively, so that following him is lost. Abu Hanifa took into account finishing the prayer without the slaughter. Al-Shafiʿi took into account the entry of the time of prayer and the amount of time in which the two sermons could be delivered, so he considered the time rather than the prayer. This is the transmission of al-Muzani from him, and it is the view of al-Tabari. Al-Rabiʿ related from al-Buwayti, who said: al-Shafiʿi said: No one should slaughter until the imam has slaughtered, unless he is one who does not slaughter. So when he has prayed and finished the sermon, slaughter is permitted. This is like the view of Malik. Ahmad said: When the imam has left, slaughter. This is also the view of Ibrahim. The most sound of these views is the view of Malik, because of the hadith of Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ led us in prayer on the day of sacrifice in Medina. Some men advanced and slaughtered, thinking that the Prophet ﷺ had slaughtered. So the Prophet ﷺ commanded whoever had slaughtered to repeat with another slaughter, and not to slaughter until the Prophet ﷺ slaughters. Muslim and al-Tirmidhi related it, and al-Tirmidhi said: "On this topic there are also reports from Jabir, Jundub, Anas, ʿUwaymir ibn Ashqar, Ibn ʿUmar, and Abu Zayd al-Ansari. This is a hasan sahih hadith, and the practice of the people of knowledge is in accordance with it: that no one in the city sacrifices until the imam sacrifices." Abu Hanifa argued with the hadith of al-Bara', in which: "Whoever slaughters after the prayer has completed his rite and has attained the practice of the Muslims." Muslim also related it. So he linked the slaughter to the prayer and did not mention the slaughter, but the hadith of Jabir restricts it. Likewise the hadith of al-Bara' also, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The first thing we begin with on this day of ours is to pray, then we return and slaughter. Whoever does this has attained our practice," and so on. Abu ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: I know of no disagreement among the scholars that whoever slaughters before the prayer, if he is one of the people of the city, is not one who sacrifices, because of his saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever slaughters before the prayer, that is merely a sheep for meat."

The fourth issue: As for the people of the desert and those who have no imam, the well-known position of the school of Malik is that they seek out the time of the imam's slaughter, or the nearest of the imams to them. Rabiʿa and ʿAta said regarding one who has no imam: if he slaughters before sunrise, it does not suffice him, but it suffices him if he slaughters after it. The people of opinion (Ahl al-Ra'y) said it suffices them from after dawn. This is the view of Ibn al-Mubarak, which al-Tirmidhi transmitted from him. They held to God's words: ﴿and mention the name of God on known days over what He has provided them of the livestock of cattle﴾. So He attributed the sacrifice to the day. Whether the day begins at dawn or at sunrise is a matter of two opinions. There is no disagreement that slaughtering the sacrificial animal before dawn of the day of sacrifice does not suffice.

The fifth issue: They differed on how many days of sacrifice there are. Malik said: three, the day of sacrifice and two days after it. Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal said the same. This is related from Abu Hurayrah and Anas ibn Malik without disagreement from them. Al-Shafiʿi said: four, the day of sacrifice and three days after it. Al-Awzaʿi also said this. It is related from ʿAli, may God be pleased with him, Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn ʿUmar, may God be pleased with them, and it is also related from them the same as the view of Malik and Ahmad. It has also been said that it is the day of sacrifice alone, which is the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah. This is related from Ibn Sirin. And from Saʿid ibn Jubayr and Jabir ibn Zayd, that they said: The sacrifice in the cities is one day, and in Mina it is three days. And from al-Hasan al-Basri there are three reports on this: one is as Malik said, the second is as al-Shafiʿi said, and the third is until the last day of Dhu al-Hijjah; so when the new moon of Muharram appears, there is no sacrifice. I say: this is also the view of Sulayman ibn Yasar and Abu Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman, and the two of them related a mursal marfuʿ hadith that al-Daraqutni recorded: "The sacrifices are until the new moon of Dhu al-Hijjah," but it is not sound. Our evidence is God's words: ﴿on known days﴾, the verse, and this is the plural of paucity (jamʿ qillah), but what is certain from it is three, and what is beyond three is not certain, so it is not acted upon. Abu ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: The scholars have agreed that the day of sacrifice is the Eid of sacrifice, and they agreed that there is no sacrifice after the end of Dhu al-Hijjah. In my view, there are only two sound positions on this: one of them is the view of Malik and the Kufans, and the other is the view of al-Shafiʿi and the Syrians. These two views are related from the Companions, so there is no point in occupying oneself with what opposes them, because what opposes them has no basis in the Sunnah or in the statements of the Companions, and whatever departs from these two is abandoned. A sixth view has been related from Qatadah, which is that the sacrifice is the day of sacrifice and six days after it. This too departs from the statements of the Companions, so there is no meaning to it.

The sixth issue: They differed about whether the nights of sacrifice are included with the days, so that slaughter is permitted in them or not. It is related from Malik, according to the well-known view, that they are not included, so slaughter at night is not permitted. This is the position of the majority of his companions and the people of opinion, because of God's words: ﴿and mention the name of God on days﴾. He mentioned the days, and the mention of the days is evidence that slaughter at night is not permitted. Abu Hanifa, al-Shafiʿi, Ahmad, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr said: the nights are included in the days, and slaughter in them is valid. The same is related from Malik and Ashhab, and Ashhab made a distinction between the hady (offering) and the udhiyah (sacrifice): he permitted the hadi at night but did not permit the udhiyah at night.

The seventh issue: God's words ﴿over what He has provided them﴾: that is, over slaughtering what He has provided them.

﴿of the livestock of cattle﴾. The word "al-anʿam" here means camels, cattle, and sheep. "Bahimat al-anʿam" is the same as "al-anʿam," so it is like your saying "the first prayer" (ṣalat al-ula) and "the congregational mosque" (masjid al-jamiʿ).

The eighth issue: ﴿So eat from them﴾ is a command whose meaning, according to the majority, is recommendation (nadb). It is recommended for a man to eat from his offering and his sacrifice and to give the greater part in charity, while they permit giving all of it in charity and eating all of it. A group deviated and made eating and feeding obligatory on the basis of the apparent meaning of the verse [[In B, J and K: "on the apparent meaning of the command."]], and because of the Prophet's saying, peace be upon him: "Eat, store, and give in charity." Al-Kiya said: God's words ﴿So eat from them and feed the poor﴾ indicate that it is not permitted to sell all of it or to give all of it in charity.

The ninth issue: The blood of expiations (kaffarat): its owners do not eat from it. The well-known position of the school of Malik, may God be pleased with him, is that one does not eat from three kinds: the penalty for game hunting, the vow of the needy, and the ransom for injury. He eats from whatever else when it reaches its place of sacrifice, whether it is obligatory or voluntary. A group of the predecessors and the jurists of the cities agreed with him on this.

The tenth issue: If one eats from what is forbidden to him, is he required to compensate for the amount he ate, or must he compensate with a complete offering? There are two views in our school. Ibn al-Majishun held the first view. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: This is the truth; nothing else is incumbent upon him.

Likewise, if someone vows an offering (hadyan) for the needy and then eats from it after it has reached its place of sacrifice, he is liable only for what he ate, contrary to the view in al-Mudawwana (al-Mudawwana, the foundational Maliki legal compendium), because the slaughter has already taken place, and the transgression concerns only the meat. So he compensates for the amount he consumed.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And let them fulfil their vows﴾ indicates the obligation to discharge a vow, whether it is a blood sacrifice (dam), an offering (hady), or something else. This also indicates that one may not eat from a vowed offering as fulfilment of the vow. The same applies to the compensation for hunting (jaza' al-sayd) and the ransom for harm (fidyat al-adha), because what is required is that one bring it complete, without any loss of meat or anything else. If he eats from it, he owes a complete offering. And God knows best.

The eleventh issue: Must one compensate for the value of the meat, or must one provide food? In the Kitab Muhammad, from Abd al-Malik, it is related that he must provide food. The first view is more sound, because food is given in exchange for the whole offering when it cannot be obtained, as an act of worship, whereas the ruling on transgression is not the ruling on worship.

The second issue: If an offering that is guaranteed (al-hady al-madmun), namely the compensation for hunting, the ransom for harm, or a vowed offering for the needy, perishes (atiba) before reaching its place of sacrifice, its owner may eat from it, feed others from it, rich and poor and whomever he wishes, but he may not sell any of its meat, skin, or garlands. Isma'il ibn Ishaq said: Because a guaranteed offering, if it perishes before reaching its place of sacrifice, requires a replacement from him, therefore it is permissible for its owner to eat from it and feed others. But if a voluntary offering (hady al-tatawwu') perishes before reaching its place of sacrifice, it is not permissible to eat from it or feed others from it, because since there is no replacement required for it, it was feared that a person might do this with the offering and slaughter it without its actually perishing. Therefore precaution was taken for the people, and the practice has continued accordingly.

Abu Dawud related from Najiyah al-Aslami that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent with him an offering and said: "If something of it perishes, slaughter it, then dip its sandal in its blood, then leave it between it and the people."

Malik, al-Shafi'i in one of his two opinions, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, the adherents of opinion (ashab al-ra'y), and those who followed them, held, concerning voluntary offerings, in accordance with this hadith: its driver may not eat any of it, and it is left between it and the people, who may eat it.

In Sahih Muslim: "Neither you nor any member of your company may eat from it." Ibn Abbas and al-Shafi'i in his other opinion acted in accordance with the apparent meaning of this prohibition, and Ibn al-Mundhir chose it. They said: Neither its driver [nor any member of his company] may eat from it.

Abu Umar (Ibn Abd al-Barr) said: The Prophet's saying (peace be upon him), "Neither he nor any member of your company may eat from it," is found only in the hadith of Ibn Abbas, and it is not in the hadith of Hisham ibn Urwah from his father from Najiyah. The latter is, in our view, more sound than the hadith of Ibn Abbas, and the practice of the jurists is in accordance with it. And his saying (peace be upon him), "leave it between it and the people," includes the members of his company and others.

Al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr said: Whatever offering is originally obligatory, one does not eat from it; whatever is voluntary and a rite of worship (nusuk), one may eat from it, give it as gifts, store it, and give it in charity. The tamattu' and qiran (types of hajj) are, according to him, rites of worship. The view of al-Awza'i is similar.

Abu Hanifa and his companions said: One may eat from the offering of tamattu' and the voluntary offering, but not from anything other than these that became obligatory by the ruling of the state of ihram.

It is related from Malik: One may not eat from the blood of fasad (a blood sacrifice for violation). By analogy with this, one may not eat from the blood of jabr (a blood sacrifice for compensation), as the view of al-Shafi'i and al-Awza'i holds.

Malik held that God made the compensation for hunting for the needy, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or an expiation of feeding the needy﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 95] (recitation of Nafi', see vol. 6, p. 302). And regarding the ransom for harm He said: ﴿then a ransom of fasting or almsgiving or a rite of sacrifice﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 196] (see vol. 2, p. 365 and following). And the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Ka'b ibn Ujrah: "Feed six needy persons, two mudd for each needy person, or fast three days, or sacrifice a sheep."

The vowed offering for the needy is explicitly stated. As for other offerings, they remain on the original basis of His saying: ﴿And the camels We have made for you among the symbols of God﴾ ... to His saying ﴿so eat from them﴾ [Al-Hajj: 36]. The Prophet (ﷺ) and Ali (may God be pleased with him) ate from the offering he brought and drank from its broth. The Prophet (ﷺ) was a qarin (one performing hajj and umrah together) according to the most sound opinions and reports, so his offering was in this respect obligatory. Therefore what Abu Hanifa relied upon is not sound. And God knows best.

God, glorified is He, permitted eating from the offerings only because the Arabs did not consider it proper to eat from their rites of worship. So God, glorified and exalted is He, commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to oppose them. Accordingly, He legislated and conveyed this, and the Prophet (ﷺ) acted likewise when he gave offerings and entered the state of ihram.

The thirteenth issue: ﴿So eat from them﴾. Some scholars said: God's saying, exalted is He, "so eat from them," abrogates their practice, because they used to forbid the meat of sacrificial animals to themselves and did not eat from them, as we have mentioned concerning the offerings. So God abrogated that by His saying, "so eat from them," and by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever sacrifices, let him eat from his sacrifice." Also, the Prophet (ﷺ) ate from his sacrifice and his offering. Al-Zuhri said: It is from the Sunnah that one eat first from the liver.

The fourteenth issue: Most scholars held that it is recommended to give one third in charity, give one third as gifts, and that he and his family eat one third. Ibn al-Qasim said, from Malik: "We do not have a fixed and specified division for the sacrificial animals." Malik said in his hadith: "It reached me from Ibn Mas'ud, but practice does not follow it." Al-Sahih (Sahih Muslim) and Abu Dawud related that he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) sacrificed a sheep, then said: "O Thawban, prepare the meat of this sheep." He said: "I continued to feed him from it until he arrived at Madinah." This is a text regarding the obligation. The opinion of al-Shafi'i varied: once he said one eats half and gives half in charity, based on His saying, exalted is He: "So eat from them and feed the distressed poor," which mentions two persons. Another time, Muzanni said: one eats a third, gives a third as a gift, and feeds a third, based on His saying: ﴿So eat from them and feed the contented and the beggar﴾ [Al-Hajj: 36], which mentions three.

The fifteenth issue: The traveler is addressed concerning the sacrifice just as the resident is addressed, since the basic principle is the generality of the address concerning it, and this is the view of all scholars. Abu Hanifa and al-Nakha'i disagreed, and it is related from Ali, but the hadith is a proof against them. Malik exempted from the travelers the pilgrim at Mina, so he did not consider a sacrifice obligatory for him, and al-Nakha'i agreed. This is related from the two caliphs Abu Bakr and Umar and a group of the early generations (may God be pleased with them), because the pilgrim is in principle addressed concerning the hady. So when he wishes to sacrifice, he makes it a hady. Other people than the pilgrims were only commanded to sacrifice in order to imitate the people of Mina, so that they obtain a share of their reward.

The sixteenth issue: Scholars differed about storing sacrificial meat (al-idikhar), in four opinions. It is related from Ali and Ibn Umar (may God be pleased with them both), by a sound route, that sacrificial meat may not be stored after three days. They also related this from the Prophet (ﷺ), as will come. A group said: The prohibition of storage that has been reported is abrogated, so one may store it for whatever time one wishes. This was the view of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Buraydah al-Aslami. Another group said: It is permissible to eat from it absolutely. Another group said: If people have need of it, it is not to be stored, because the prohibition was only for a reason, namely his saying (peace be upon him): "I only forbade you for the sake of the dafaf that came in" [The dafaffah: a group of people traveling in a moderate pace, not very fast. And the dafaffah: a group of Bedouins who want to reach the city. He means that they were people who came to Madinah at the time of the Eid al-Adha, so he forbade them to store the meat of the sacrificial animals, so that they would distribute it and give it in charity, and those who came would benefit from it.]

(Ibn al-Athir).]] When it was lifted, the earlier prohibition was lifted with the removal of its cause, not because it was abrogated. Here arises a question of legal theory, which is the Seventeenth issue: the difference between lifting a ruling by abrogation (naskh) and lifting it because its cause (illah) has ceased. Know that what is lifted by abrogation is never again applied, whereas what is lifted because its cause has ceased returns when the cause returns. So if needy people arrived in a town at the time of the Eid al-Adha, and the people of that town had no other provision with which to meet their need except the sacrificed animals, it would be obligatory upon them not to store them beyond three days, as the Prophet ﷺ did.

The Eighteenth issue: the hadiths transmitted on this subject, both prohibiting and permitting, are sound and established. Both the prohibition and the permission have come together, as is stated in the hadiths of ʿAʾisha, Salamah ibn al-Akwaʿ and Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, which the Sahih transmits. The Sahih also transmits from Abu ʿUbayd, client of Ibn Azhar, that he attended the Eid with ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab. He said: "Then I prayed the Eid with ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him. He led us in prayer before the khutbah, then he addressed the people and said: 'The Messenger of Allah ﷺ has forbidden you to eat the meat of your sacrifices after three nights, so do not eat it.'" It is also reported from Ibn ʿUmar that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade that the meat of the sacrificial animals be eaten after three [days]. Salim said: "Ibn ʿUmar would not eat the meat of the sacrificial animals after three [days]." Abu Dawud transmits from Nubaysha that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "We had forbidden you to eat their meat after three [days] so that it might suffice you; now Allah has brought abundance, so eat, store and trade. Beware, these days are days of eating, drinking and remembrance of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic."

Abu Jaʿfar al-Nahhas said: This view is the best that has been said on this matter, so that the hadiths agree and do not contradict one another, and so that the saying of the Commander of the Faithful ʿAli ibn Abi Talib and ʿUthman is restricted, because the people were in hardship and in need, so he acted as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did when the caravan (al-daffa) arrived. The evidence for this is what Ibrahim ibn Sharik narrated to us, saying: Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Layth narrated to us, saying: al-Harith ibn Yaʿqub narrated to me, from Yazid ibn Abi Yazid, from his wife, that she asked ʿAʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, about the meat of the sacrificial animals. She said: "ʿAli ibn Abi Talib came to us from a journey, so we brought him some of it, but he refused to eat until he asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He asked him, and he said: 'Eat from the one of Dhu al-Hijjah to the next Dhu al-Hijjah.'"

Al-Shafiʿi said: Whoever holds the prohibition of storing after three days has not heard the permission; whoever holds the unrestricted permission has not heard the prohibition of storing; and whoever holds both the prohibition and the permission has heard both and acted according to what each requires. And Allah knows best.

It will come in Surat al-Kawthar [see vol. 20, p. 216] the disagreement about the obligation of the sacrifice (udhiyah) and its being recommended, and that it abrogates every earlier slaughter, Allah willing, the Exalted.

The Nineteenth issue: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And feed the miserable, the poor﴾. "Al-faqir" is a description of "al-ba'is" (the miserable), who is the one struck by misery and severe poverty. It is said: "ba'isa, yab'asu, ba'san," when he became poor, so he is ba'is. It may also be used of one who has been struck by a calamity of the age even if he is not poor, and from this is his peace be upon him saying: "But al-ba'is is Saʿd ibn Khawla" [the Prophet ﷺ grieved for him if he died in Mecca, meaning in the land from which he had emigrated; see his biography in al-Istiʿab]. It is said: "a man, ba'is" meaning severe. "Ba'usa, yab'usu, ba'san" when he became severe; and from it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We seized those who did wrong with a severe punishment﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 165], meaning severe. The more the giving of charity from the meat of the sacrifice, the greater the reward. As to the amount that may be eaten there is a difference of opinion which we have mentioned: it is said, half, based on His saying: "eat from it and feed [others]"; and it is said, two-thirds, based on his saying: "Beware, eat, store and trade," meaning seek reward through feeding.

It is disputed whether eating and feeding are obligatory or recommended. It is said: both are obligatory. It is said: both are recommended. It is said: there is a distinction between eating and feeding: eating is recommended and feeding is obligatory, and this is the view of al-Shafiʿi.

The Twentieth issue: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then let them end their unkemptness (tafath)﴾, meaning: then let them, after slaughtering the sacrifices and offerings, complete what remains of the matters of the Hajj, such as shaving, stoning the pillars (ramy al-jimar), and removing disorder (shaʿath) and the like. Ibn ʿArafa said: that is, let them remove their filth (adran). Al-Azhari said: tafath is taking from the moustache, cutting the nails, plucking the armpit hair and shaving the pubic hair, and this is upon exiting the state of ihram. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: in the speech of the Arabs tafath is the removal of disorder (shaʿath). I heard al-Azhari say: tafath in the speech of the Arabs is not known except from the words of Ibn ʿAbbas and the people of tafsir. Al-Hasan said: it is the removal of the austerity (qashaf) of ihram. It is also said: tafath means all the rites of the Hajj; this was transmitted from Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: even if it is authentically from them, it would be a proof because of the nobility of companionship and their comprehensive knowledge of the language. He said: this word is rare; the grammarians have found no poetry about it and have not comprehensively known it. However, I have traced tafath linguistically, and I found that Abu ʿUbayda Maʿmar ibn al-Muthanna said it is the cutting of nails, taking from the moustache, and everything forbidden to the muhrim except marriage. He said: no poetry has come in it that can be cited as evidence. Sahib al-ʿAyn said: tafath is stoning, shaving, shortening, slaughtering, cutting the nails, the moustache and the armpit. Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' mentioned something similar, and I do not think they took it except from the sayings of the scholars. Qutrub said: "tafiha al-rajul" when his filth increased. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:
They shaved their heads, not removing tafath,
and they did not strip from them lice and nits.
What Qutrub pointed to is what Ibn Wahb transmitted from Malik, and it is the correct view regarding tafath. This is the linguistic image of casting off tafath. As for its legal reality: when the pilgrim or the one performing ʿumrah slaughters his offering, shaves his head, removes his filth, purifies and cleanses himself and dresses, he has removed his tafath and fulfilled his vow; and a vow is what binds a person and he commits himself to. I say: what he related from Qutrub and mentioned of poetry was also mentioned by al-Mawardi in his tafsir. He also mentioned another verse, saying:
They ended their tafath and their nahb, then they went on
toward Najd, and they did not wait for ʿAli.
Al-Tha'labi said: the root of tafath in the language is filth; the Arabs say to a man whom they find repugnant: "ma atfathaka," meaning how filthy and repulsive you are. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:
Leaving their armpits, they did not cast off tafath,
nor did they remove from them lice and nits.
Al-Mawardi: It was said to one of the righteous: what is the meaning of the muhrim's unkemptness? He said: so that Allah, Exalted, may witness from you the turning away from caring for yourself, so that He knows your sincerity in giving it up for His obedience.

The Twenty-first issue: ﴿And let them fulfill their vows﴾. They were commanded to fulfill vows in general, except what is disobedience, based on his peace be upon him saying: "There is no fulfilling of a vow in disobedience to Allah," and his saying: "Whoever vows to obey Allah, let him obey Him; and whoever vows to disobey Him, let him not disobey Him."

﴿And let them circle the Ancient House﴾. The circumambulation mentioned in this verse is the circumambulation of ifadah, which is one of the obligatory elements of the Hajj. Al-Tabari said: there is no disagreement among the interpreters on this.

The twenty-second issue: Hajj has three circumambulations (tawaf): the tawaf of arrival (tawaf al-qudum, the circuit made upon entering Makkah), the tawaf of ifadah (the circuit made after 'Arafah), and the tawaf of farewell (tawaf al-wada', the circuit made upon departing). Isma'il ibn Ishaq said: the tawaf of arrival is a sunnah (a recommended practice), and it is dropped for the one who is approaching puberty (al-murahiq), for the Makkan, and for everyone who enters ihram for Hajj from Makkah. He said: the obligatory tawaf (wajib, obligatory act), which does not fall away in any way, is the tawaf of ifadah, which takes place after 'Arafah. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then let them end their state of unkemptness, fulfil their vows, and circumambulate the Ancient House.﴾ He said: this is the tawaf that is prescribed (muftaraḍ) in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and it is the tawaf by which the pilgrim exits the whole of his ihram (the state of consecration).

The Hafiz Abu 'Umar said: what Isma'il mentioned concerning the tawaf of ifadah is the view of Malik among the people of Madinah, and it is the narration of Ibn Wahb, Ibn Nafi' and Ashhab from him. It is also the view of the majority of scholars among the jurists of the Hijaz and Iraq. Ibn al-Qasim and Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam narrated from Malik that the tawaf of arrival is obligatory. Ibn al-Qasim said in more than one place in the Mudawwanah, and he also narrated it from Malik: "The obligatory tawaf is the tawaf of one who arrives in Makkah." He said: whoever forgets the tawaf at the time of entering Makkah, or forgets one circuit of it, or forgets the sa'i (running between al-Safa and al-Marwah) or one circuit of it, until he returns to his country and then remembers, then if he has not had intercourse with his wives, he returns to Makkah until he performs the tawaf around the House, prays the two rak'ahs, runs between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and then offers a sacrifice (hady). If he has had intercourse with his wives, he returns, performs the tawaf and the sa'i, then performs 'umrah and offers a sacrifice. This is the same as his ruling concerning one who forgets the tawaf of ifadah, exactly alike. According to this narration, both circumambulations are obligatory, and the sa'i too.

As for the tawaf of farewell (tawaf al-sadr), which is also called the tawaf of farewell: Ibn al-Qasim and others narrated from Malik concerning one who performed the tawaf of ifadah without wudu' (ritual ablution): he returns from his country and performs it again, unless he had performed a voluntary (tatawwu') tawaf after that. This is among the matters on which Malik and his companions agreed, and that his voluntary tawaf suffices for the obligatory tawaf required of him. Likewise they agreed that whoever does something in his Hajj as a voluntary act, when that act is obligatory in Hajj and its time has passed, his voluntary performance of it becomes counted for the obligation and not as a voluntary act, unlike prayer. If a voluntary act substitutes for the obligatory one in Hajj, then the tawaf upon entering Makkah is more deserving to substitute for the tawaf of ifadah, except for the tawaf after throwing the Jamrat al-'Aqabah on the Day of Sacrifice, or after it, for the farewell. The narration of Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam from Malik differs from this, for in it the tawaf of entry together with the sa'i substitutes for the tawaf of ifadah for one who returns to his country with the hady, just as the tawaf of ifadah together with the sa'i substitutes for one who did not perform the tawaf and the sa'i upon entering Makkah with the hady, and likewise it substitutes for the tawaf of arrival.

Whoever holds this view says: the tawaf of entry is called obligatory, and the tawaf of ifadah is called obligatory, because each of them substitutes for the other; and because it has been narrated from Malik that one who forgets either of them returns from his country, as we have mentioned; and because Allah the Mighty and Majestic did not make obligatory upon the pilgrim except one tawaf, by His saying: ﴿And proclaim to mankind the Hajj﴾; and He said in the context of the verse: ﴿and let them circumambulate the Ancient House﴾. The conjunction "wa" (and) in this verse and others, in their view, does not establish an order unless by a fixed revelation (tawqif).

Al-Tabari transmitted from 'Amr ibn Abi Salamah who said: "I asked Zuhayr about the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿and let them circumambulate the Ancient House﴾, and he said: it is the tawaf of farewell." This indicates that it is obligatory, and it is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i, because the Prophet (peace be upon him) gave a concession to the menstruating woman to depart without performing it, and a concession is granted only for what is obligatory.

The twenty-third issue: the interpreters differed regarding the meaning of describing the House as "Ancient" (al-'Atiq). Mujahid and al-Hasan said: al-'Atiq means the ancient, the old. One says "a sword is 'atiq" and "it has become 'atiq", meaning it has become old. This view is supported by reasoning. And in the Sahih (it is reported): "It is the first mosque that was placed on the earth." It was also said: it is called "ancient" because Allah freed it (a'taqahu) from being dominated by a tyrant (jabbar) with humiliation until the end of time. Ibn al-Zubayr and Mujahid stated this meaning. In al-Tirmidhi, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The House was only named the Ancient House because no tyrant ever prevailed over it." He said: this is a hasan sahih hadith [in the manuscripts B, J, T and K: "gharib" (strange)], and it has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) as a mursal (a narration whose chain omits the companion).

If someone mentions al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf and his setting up the catapult (manjaniq) against the Ka'bah until he broke it, it is said to him: Allah freed it from the arrogant disbelievers, for when they came by themselves rebellious, and not regarding the sanctity of the House, and intended evil toward the Ka'bah, it was protected from them and their hands did not reach it. That was an indication that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, turned them away from it by force. As for the Muslims who believe in its sanctity, if they refrain from it, that refraining does not indicate its station with Allah in the way that its restraint of enemies does. So Allah the Exalted restricted this group to restraint through prohibition and threat, and did not extend it to turning away through compulsion and necessity, and He made the Hour their appointed time, and the Hour is more calamitous and bitter.

A group said: it was called "ancient" because its site was never owned at any time. Another group said: it was called "ancient" because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, frees in it the necks of sinners from punishment. It was also said: it was called "ancient" because it was freed from the flood of Noah, as Ibn Jubayr stated. It was also said: al-'Atiq means the noble, and 'itq means nobility. Tarafah, describing a horse's ear, said:

Two sharp-pointed ears, in which nobility is recognized,
like the two ears of a frightened doe amid a herd of wild cattle.

[Note: al-mu'allal means sharpened. Al-rabrab is a herd of wild cattle, and it was also said gazelles. This version of the verse differs from what is in his Diwan and his Mu'allaqah. The version in both is:
Two sharp-pointed ears, in which nobility is recognized,
like the two ears of a lone ewe at Hawmal.
By "the ewe" here he means the wild bull.]

The freeing of a slave ('itq al-raqiq) is leaving the humiliation of slavery for the dignity of freedom. It is possible that "al-'Atiq" is an adjective of praise indicating the excellence of a thing, as 'Umar said: "I was mounted on a noble horse ('atiq)," the hadith. The first opinion is more correct by reasoning and by the sahih hadith. Mujahid said: Allah created the House two thousand years before the earth, and it was called "Ancient" for this reason. And Allah knows best.

There are twenty-three issues in this passage.

The first issue: God's words ﴿that they may witness﴾. That is, proclaim the Hajj to them, and they will come to you on foot and on mounted animals ﴿that they may witness﴾, meaning, that they may attend. Witnessing (al-shuhud) means attending.

﴿benefits for them﴾: that is, the rites, such as ʿArafat and al-Mashʿar al-Haram. It has also been said that it means forgiveness. It has also been said that it means trade. It has also been said that it is general: that they may attend benefits for them, meaning whatever pleases God, Exalted is He, concerning matters of this world and the Hereafter. This was said by Mujahid and ʿAta, and Ibn al-ʿArabi (Ibn al-ʿArabi) preferred it, because it includes all of these: the rites, trade, forgiveness, and worldly and otherworldly benefit. There is no disagreement that what is meant by God's words ﴿There is no blame on you if you seek bounty from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198] is trade. [See vol. 2, p. 413.]

The second issue: ﴿and mention the name of God on known days﴾. The discussion of the known days and the counted days has already passed in al-Baqarah. [See vol. 3, p. 1.] What is meant by mentioning the name of God is the invocation of the name at the time of slaughter and sacrifice, such as your saying: "In the name of God, God is greatest; O God, from You and for You." And like your saying at the time of slaughter ﴿Indeed, my prayer and my rites and my living and my dying are for God﴾ [al-Anʿam: 162], and so on. The disbelievers used to slaughter in the names of their idols, so the Lord made clear that what is obligatory is slaughter in the name of God. This has already passed in al-Anʿam. [See vol. 7, pp. 152 and 72 onwards.]

The third issue: The scholars differed about the time of slaughter on the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr). Malik, may God be pleased with him, said: after the imam's prayer and his slaughter, unless he delays excessively, so that following him is lost. Abu Hanifa took into account finishing the prayer without the slaughter. Al-Shafiʿi took into account the entry of the time of prayer and the amount of time in which the two sermons could be delivered, so he considered the time rather than the prayer. This is the transmission of al-Muzani from him, and it is the view of al-Tabari. Al-Rabiʿ related from al-Buwayti, who said: al-Shafiʿi said: No one should slaughter until the imam has slaughtered, unless he is one who does not slaughter. So when he has prayed and finished the sermon, slaughter is permitted. This is like the view of Malik. Ahmad said: When the imam has left, slaughter. This is also the view of Ibrahim. The most sound of these views is the view of Malik, because of the hadith of Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ led us in prayer on the day of sacrifice in Medina. Some men advanced and slaughtered, thinking that the Prophet ﷺ had slaughtered. So the Prophet ﷺ commanded whoever had slaughtered to repeat with another slaughter, and not to slaughter until the Prophet ﷺ slaughters. Muslim and al-Tirmidhi related it, and al-Tirmidhi said: "On this topic there are also reports from Jabir, Jundub, Anas, ʿUwaymir ibn Ashqar, Ibn ʿUmar, and Abu Zayd al-Ansari. This is a hasan sahih hadith, and the practice of the people of knowledge is in accordance with it: that no one in the city sacrifices until the imam sacrifices." Abu Hanifa argued with the hadith of al-Bara', in which: "Whoever slaughters after the prayer has completed his rite and has attained the practice of the Muslims." Muslim also related it. So he linked the slaughter to the prayer and did not mention the slaughter, but the hadith of Jabir restricts it. Likewise the hadith of al-Bara' also, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The first thing we begin with on this day of ours is to pray, then we return and slaughter. Whoever does this has attained our practice," and so on. Abu ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: I know of no disagreement among the scholars that whoever slaughters before the prayer, if he is one of the people of the city, is not one who sacrifices, because of his saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever slaughters before the prayer, that is merely a sheep for meat."

The fourth issue: As for the people of the desert and those who have no imam, the well-known position of the school of Malik is that they seek out the time of the imam's slaughter, or the nearest of the imams to them. Rabiʿa and ʿAta said regarding one who has no imam: if he slaughters before sunrise, it does not suffice him, but it suffices him if he slaughters after it. The people of opinion (Ahl al-Ra'y) said it suffices them from after dawn. This is the view of Ibn al-Mubarak, which al-Tirmidhi transmitted from him. They held to God's words: ﴿and mention the name of God on known days over what He has provided them of the livestock of cattle﴾. So He attributed the sacrifice to the day. Whether the day begins at dawn or at sunrise is a matter of two opinions. There is no disagreement that slaughtering the sacrificial animal before dawn of the day of sacrifice does not suffice.

The fifth issue: They differed on how many days of sacrifice there are. Malik said: three, the day of sacrifice and two days after it. Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal said the same. This is related from Abu Hurayrah and Anas ibn Malik without disagreement from them. Al-Shafiʿi said: four, the day of sacrifice and three days after it. Al-Awzaʿi also said this. It is related from ʿAli, may God be pleased with him, Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn ʿUmar, may God be pleased with them, and it is also related from them the same as the view of Malik and Ahmad. It has also been said that it is the day of sacrifice alone, which is the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah. This is related from Ibn Sirin. And from Saʿid ibn Jubayr and Jabir ibn Zayd, that they said: The sacrifice in the cities is one day, and in Mina it is three days. And from al-Hasan al-Basri there are three reports on this: one is as Malik said, the second is as al-Shafiʿi said, and the third is until the last day of Dhu al-Hijjah; so when the new moon of Muharram appears, there is no sacrifice. I say: this is also the view of Sulayman ibn Yasar and Abu Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman, and the two of them related a mursal marfuʿ hadith that al-Daraqutni recorded: "The sacrifices are until the new moon of Dhu al-Hijjah," but it is not sound. Our evidence is God's words: ﴿on known days﴾, the verse, and this is the plural of paucity (jamʿ qillah), but what is certain from it is three, and what is beyond three is not certain, so it is not acted upon. Abu ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: The scholars have agreed that the day of sacrifice is the Eid of sacrifice, and they agreed that there is no sacrifice after the end of Dhu al-Hijjah. In my view, there are only two sound positions on this: one of them is the view of Malik and the Kufans, and the other is the view of al-Shafiʿi and the Syrians. These two views are related from the Companions, so there is no point in occupying oneself with what opposes them, because what opposes them has no basis in the Sunnah or in the statements of the Companions, and whatever departs from these two is abandoned. A sixth view has been related from Qatadah, which is that the sacrifice is the day of sacrifice and six days after it. This too departs from the statements of the Companions, so there is no meaning to it.

The sixth issue: They differed about whether the nights of sacrifice are included with the days, so that slaughter is permitted in them or not. It is related from Malik, according to the well-known view, that they are not included, so slaughter at night is not permitted. This is the position of the majority of his companions and the people of opinion, because of God's words: ﴿and mention the name of God on days﴾. He mentioned the days, and the mention of the days is evidence that slaughter at night is not permitted. Abu Hanifa, al-Shafiʿi, Ahmad, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr said: the nights are included in the days, and slaughter in them is valid. The same is related from Malik and Ashhab, and Ashhab made a distinction between the hady (offering) and the udhiyah (sacrifice): he permitted the hadi at night but did not permit the udhiyah at night.

The seventh issue: God's words ﴿over what He has provided them﴾: that is, over slaughtering what He has provided them.

﴿of the livestock of cattle﴾. The word "al-anʿam" here means camels, cattle, and sheep. "Bahimat al-anʿam" is the same as "al-anʿam," so it is like your saying "the first prayer" (ṣalat al-ula) and "the congregational mosque" (masjid al-jamiʿ).

The eighth issue: ﴿So eat from them﴾ is a command whose meaning, according to the majority, is recommendation (nadb). It is recommended for a man to eat from his offering and his sacrifice and to give the greater part in charity, while they permit giving all of it in charity and eating all of it. A group deviated and made eating and feeding obligatory on the basis of the apparent meaning of the verse [[In B, J and K: "on the apparent meaning of the command."]], and because of the Prophet's saying, peace be upon him: "Eat, store, and give in charity." Al-Kiya said: God's words ﴿So eat from them and feed the poor﴾ indicate that it is not permitted to sell all of it or to give all of it in charity.

The ninth issue: The blood of expiations (kaffarat): its owners do not eat from it. The well-known position of the school of Malik, may God be pleased with him, is that one does not eat from three kinds: the penalty for game hunting, the vow of the needy, and the ransom for injury. He eats from whatever else when it reaches its place of sacrifice, whether it is obligatory or voluntary. A group of the predecessors and the jurists of the cities agreed with him on this.

The tenth issue: If one eats from what is forbidden to him, is he required to compensate for the amount he ate, or must he compensate with a complete offering? There are two views in our school. Ibn al-Majishun held the first view. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: This is the truth; nothing else is incumbent upon him.

Likewise, if someone vows an offering (hadyan) for the needy and then eats from it after it has reached its place of sacrifice, he is liable only for what he ate, contrary to the view in al-Mudawwana (al-Mudawwana, the foundational Maliki legal compendium), because the slaughter has already taken place, and the transgression concerns only the meat. So he compensates for the amount he consumed.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And let them fulfil their vows﴾ indicates the obligation to discharge a vow, whether it is a blood sacrifice (dam), an offering (hady), or something else. This also indicates that one may not eat from a vowed offering as fulfilment of the vow. The same applies to the compensation for hunting (jaza' al-sayd) and the ransom for harm (fidyat al-adha), because what is required is that one bring it complete, without any loss of meat or anything else. If he eats from it, he owes a complete offering. And God knows best.

The eleventh issue: Must one compensate for the value of the meat, or must one provide food? In the Kitab Muhammad, from Abd al-Malik, it is related that he must provide food. The first view is more sound, because food is given in exchange for the whole offering when it cannot be obtained, as an act of worship, whereas the ruling on transgression is not the ruling on worship.

The second issue: If an offering that is guaranteed (al-hady al-madmun), namely the compensation for hunting, the ransom for harm, or a vowed offering for the needy, perishes (atiba) before reaching its place of sacrifice, its owner may eat from it, feed others from it, rich and poor and whomever he wishes, but he may not sell any of its meat, skin, or garlands. Isma'il ibn Ishaq said: Because a guaranteed offering, if it perishes before reaching its place of sacrifice, requires a replacement from him, therefore it is permissible for its owner to eat from it and feed others. But if a voluntary offering (hady al-tatawwu') perishes before reaching its place of sacrifice, it is not permissible to eat from it or feed others from it, because since there is no replacement required for it, it was feared that a person might do this with the offering and slaughter it without its actually perishing. Therefore precaution was taken for the people, and the practice has continued accordingly.

Abu Dawud related from Najiyah al-Aslami that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent with him an offering and said: "If something of it perishes, slaughter it, then dip its sandal in its blood, then leave it between it and the people."

Malik, al-Shafi'i in one of his two opinions, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, the adherents of opinion (ashab al-ra'y), and those who followed them, held, concerning voluntary offerings, in accordance with this hadith: its driver may not eat any of it, and it is left between it and the people, who may eat it.

In Sahih Muslim: "Neither you nor any member of your company may eat from it." Ibn Abbas and al-Shafi'i in his other opinion acted in accordance with the apparent meaning of this prohibition, and Ibn al-Mundhir chose it. They said: Neither its driver [nor any member of his company] may eat from it.
