**The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 22, verse 34:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for every community We have appointed rites (mansak)﴾. When Allah mentioned the sacrificial animals, He made clear that no community was without them. The *ummah* (community) is a people gathered upon one path, meaning: for every believing group We have appointed a *mansak*. The *mansak* is the slaughtering and the shedding of blood, as stated by Mujahid. It is said: "*nasaka*" when one slaughters, "*yansuku*," "*naskan*." The sacrificial animal is a *nasikah*, and its plural is *nusuk*, and from this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or charity or a sacrifice (nusuk)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196]. *Nusuk* also means obedience. Al-Azhari said regarding His saying, "*And for every community We have appointed a mansak*": it indicates the place of sacrifice in this context, meaning a place of *nusk*. It is said: *mansak* and *mansak* are two dialectal forms, and both have been read. The Kufans, except 'Asim, read it with a kasra on the sin (*mansik*), and the rest read it with a fatha (*mansak*). Al-Farra' said: In the speech of the Arabs, the *mansak* is the customary place, whether for good or for evil. It is also said that the *manasik* of the Hajj (the rites of pilgrimage) are so named because people return to them, namely standing at 'Arafat, throwing the pebbles, and the sa'y (the running between al-Safa and al-Marwah).

Ibn 'Arafa said regarding His saying, "*And for every community We have appointed a mansak*": that is, a path (*madhhab*) of obedience to Allah, exalted is He. It is said: "*nasaka nusk qawmihi*" when he followed their path. It is also said: *mansakan* means a festival, as stated by al-Farra'. It is said: it means Hajj, as stated by Qatada. The first opinion is more apparent, due to His saying, exalted is He: (so that they may mention the name of Allah over what He has provided for them of the beast of cattle), meaning: over the slaughtering of what He has provided for them. So Allah, exalted is He, commanded that at the time of slaughter His name be mentioned, and that the slaughter be for Him, since He is the Provider of that. Then the wording shifted from speaking about the communities to informing those present, with a meaning like: "Your God is one for all of you, so likewise the matter regarding the sacrifice should be sincerely directed to Him alone." His saying, exalted is He: (So to Him submit) means: for His right, His face, and His bounty, believe and submit. It may also mean submission, i.e., obey Him and be humbly compliant.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And give good tidings to the mukhbitin﴾. The *mukhbit* is the humble, submissive one among the believers. *Al-khabt* is what is low of the earth, meaning: give them good tidings of a great reward. 'Amr ibn Aws said: The *mukhbitun* are those who do not wrong, and when they are wronged, they do not seek retribution [[al-intisar: revenge.]]. Mujahid said, as narrated from him by Sufyan from Ibn Abi Najih: The *mukhbitun* are those who are at peace with the command of Allah, mighty and majestic.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 35:

There are two issues in this.

The first: His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And their hearts tremble﴾, meaning they fear and are wary of opposing Him. He described them as having fear and trepidation at the mention of Him, and that is due to the strength of their certainty and their vigilance toward their Lord, as if they were standing before Him. He also described them as patient, and as establishing the prayer and maintaining it. It is narrated that this verse, namely His saying: "And give good tidings to the humble (al-mukhbitin)," was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, Umar and Ali, may Allah be pleased with them all. The majority read "al-Salati" with a kasra, as an idafa (genitive construction). Abu 'Amr read "al-Salata" with a fatha, on the basis of the assumption of the nun (of the dual/plural ending), and that its deletion is for lightness because of the length of the noun. Sibawayh recited:

"The guardians of the honour of the tribe..." [[The full line:

al-hafizu 'awrata al-'asheerati la... yatihim min wara'ihim nutaf]] ...

The second: This verse is similar to His saying: ﴿The believers are only those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble, and when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith, and upon their Lord they rely﴾ [al-Anfal: 2][[See vol. 7 p. 365.]], and His saying: ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement, a Book consistent and oft-repeated; the skins shiver therefrom of those who fear their Lord; then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Zumar: 23][[See vol. 15 p. 248.]]. This is the state of those who know Allah, who fear His might and His punishment, not like what the ignorant common folk and the foolish innovators do of shouting and roaring, and of braying like the braying of donkeys. It is said to whoever engages in that and claims it is ecstasy and humility: "You have not reached the point of equalling the state of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ or the state of his Companions in knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, fear of Him and magnifying His majesty." Yet, despite that, their state at admonitions was understanding from Allah and weeping out of fear of Allah. Likewise, Allah the Exalted described the states of the people of knowledge upon hearing His remembrance and reciting His Book, and whoever is not like that is not upon their guidance nor their way. Allah the Exalted said: "And when they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of the truth they recognise; they say, 'Our Lord, we believe, so write us down with the witnesses'" [al-Ma'idah: 83][[See vol. 6 p. 258.]]. This is the description of their state and the report of their speech. Whoever is to follow a precedent, let him follow it; and whoever engages in the states of madmen and the insane, he is of the lowest of them in condition, and madness has many kinds. Al-Sahih reports from Anas ibn Malik that the people asked the Prophet ﷺ persistently until they pressed him (ahfawhu) in the questioning. So he went out one day, ascended the pulpit and said: "Ask me. You will not ask me about anything except that I will explain it to you, as long as I am in this place of mine." When the people heard that, they fell silent (aramma) and feared that some matter had come close. Anas said: "I began looking right and left, and every person had his head wrapped in his garment, weeping." He mentioned the hadith. The discussion of this issue has already passed in more detail than this in surah al-Anfal[[See vol. 7 p. 366.]], and praise be to Allah.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 36:

There are ten issues in this verse.

The first issue: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿wal-budn (and the camels)﴾. Ibn Abi Ishaq read it as "wal-budn." Both are dialectal forms (lughatan), and its singular is badanah, just as one says thamarah, thamar and thumr, and khashabah, khushub and khushub. In the Revelation: "And he had fruit (thamar)" [[See vol. 10, p. 298]]; it has also been recited as "thumr," both being dialectal forms. It is called badanah because it grows fat (tabdun), and al-badanah means fatness. It has been said that this name is specific to camels. It has also been said that al-budn is the plural of "badan" with a fatha on the ba' and the dal. One says badufa al-rajul (with a damma on the dal) when a man became fat, and badden (with a shadda) when he grew old and advanced in years. In the hadith, "Indeed I have become badden," meaning I have grown old and advanced in years. It is also narrated as "badudt," but this has no meaning, since it contradicts his ﷺ description, and its meaning is abundance of flesh. One says: badufa al-rajul yabduru badnan and badanah, so he is badin, meaning bulky.

The second issue: The scholars differed over whether the term budn applies to animals other than camels, such as cattle. Ibn Mas'ud, 'Ata' and al-Shafi'i said no. Malik and Abu Hanifah said yes. The benefit of the disagreement concerns one who vows a badanah but cannot find or afford a badanah, yet can afford a cow: will it suffice for him or not? According to the view of al-Shafi'i and 'Ata', it does not suffice. According to the view of Malik, it suffices. The sound position is that of al-Shafi'i and 'Ata', based on his peace be upon him saying in the sound hadith concerning Friday: "Whoever goes in the first hour, it is as if he has offered a badanah; whoever goes in the second hour, it is as if he has offered a cow..." to the end of the hadith. His ﷺ distinguishing between the cow and the badanah indicates that the cow is not called a badanah, and Allah knows best. Also, His saying, exalted is He, ﴿fa-idha wajabat junubuha (so when they fall on their sides)﴾ indicates this, for the description is specific to camels, while cattle are made to lie down and slaughtered like sheep, as will come. Our evidence is that badanah is derived from badanah, which means bulkiness, and bulkiness is found in both of them together. Also, the cow in drawing near to Allah the Exalted through shedding blood holds the same status as the camel, to the extent that a cow is permissible in sacrifices for seven persons, as with camels. This is a proof for Abu Hanifah, since al-Shafi'i agreed with him on this, though this is not the case in our school. Ibn Shajarah related that badanah is also said of sheep, but this is an anomalous view. Al-budn are the camels that are sent as offerings to the Ka'bah, while al-hady is general, covering camels, cattle and sheep.

The third issue: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿min sha'a'ir Allah (among the rites of Allah)﴾ is explicit that they are part of the rites. As for His saying, ﴿lakum fiha khayr (for you there is good in them)﴾, it means the benefits mentioned earlier, and the correct view is that it includes the good of this world and the Hereafter.

The fourth issue: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿fa-dhkuru ism Allah 'alayha sawaff (so mention the name of Allah over them as they stand in ranks)﴾, meaning slaughter them in the name of Allah. "Sawaff" means that their legs have been arranged in rows. Camels are slaughtered standing and tied. The origin of this description is in horses: one says safana al-faras, so he is safin, when he stands on three legs and bends the hoof of the fourth; al-sunbuk is the edge of the hoof. When they want to slaughter a camel, one of its forelegs is tied, so it stands on three legs. Al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Mujahid, Zayd ibn Aslam and Abu Musa al-Ash'ari read "sawafiya," meaning purified for Allah, exalted and majestic, without associating anyone with Him in the naming over its slaughter. It is also narrated from al-Hasan "sawafin" with a kasra on the fa' and tanwin, lightened, and it has the same meaning as the previous one, but the yaʼ has been dropped for lightness contrary to analogy.

"Sawaff" is the reading of the majority, with a fatha and shadda on the fa', from saffa yasuffu. The singular of sawaff is saffah, and the singular of sawafi is safiyah. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar and Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali read "sawafin" with a nun, the plural of safinah. Its singular is not safin, because fa'il does not take the plural pattern fawa'il except in specific words which are not to be analogized upon: fris (fāris) and fawaris, halik and hawalik, and khalif and khawalif. [[In the Sharh al-Ashmuni on the Alfiyyah of Ibn Malik, it is said that they are: faris, naki, halik, ghaʼib and shahid.]] The safinah is the one whose one foreleg has been raised and tied so that it does not tremble. From this is His saying, exalted is He: "al-safinat al-jiyad (the poised steeds of noble breed)" [[See vol. 15, p. 192]] [Sad 38:31]. 'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

We left the horses clinging to it,
their reins fastened, standing in rows (sufunan).

And it is narrated:

Its steeds lament over it,
their reins fastened, standing in rows.

Another said:

He accustomed the sufun, and it never ceases, as if it were
something that stands on three legs, lame.

Abu 'Amr al-Jarmi said: al-safin is a vein at the front of the leg, so when the horse is struck it raises its leg. al-A'sha said:

And every bay like the trunk of a sahw palm,
when it sees the spear-point, it stands on three legs (safana).

The fifth issue: Ibn Wahb said: Ibn Abi Dhi'b informed me that he asked Ibn Shihab about al-sawaff, and he said: you tie them and then arrange them in rows. Malik ibn Anas said the same to me. The scholars were agreed on the recommendation of this, except Abu Hanifah and al-Thawri, who both permitted slaughtering while kneeling or standing. 'Ata' deviated and preferred slaughtering them kneeling. The sound view is that of the majority, based on His saying, exalted is He: "fa-idha wajabat junubuha (so when they fall on their sides)," meaning they fell after being slaughtered, and from it comes wajabat al-shams (the sun set). In Sahih Muslim, from Ziyad ibn Jubayr: Ibn 'Umar passed by a man who was slaughtering his badanah kneeling, and he said: "Send it up standing, tied, the sunnah of your Prophet ﷺ." Abu Dawud related from Abu al-Zubayr from Jabir, and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit informed me, that the Prophet ﷺ and his companions used to slaughter the badanah standing, with its left foreleg tied, on the remainder of its legs.

The sixth issue: Malik said: If a person is weak, or fears that his badanah will break loose, I see no harm in slaughtering it tied. The preferred practice is that camels be slaughtered standing and untied, unless that is impossible, in which case they are tied, and they are not hamstrung unless one fears he will be too weak to control them. Slaughtering them kneeling is better than hamstringing them. Ibn 'Umar used to take the spear in his hand in the prime of his strength, and slaughter it in its chest, pushing it out at its hump. When he grew old, he would slaughter it kneeling because of his weakness, while another man held the spear with him and another held its halter. Cattle and sheep are made to lie down.

The seventh issue: Slaughter before dawn on the day of sacrifice is not permitted, by consensus. Likewise, the udhiyyah is not permitted before dawn. When dawn rises, slaughter becomes lawful at Mina, and they are not required to wait for the slaughter of their imam, unlike the udhiyyah in the rest of the lands. The place of slaughter is Mina for every pilgrim, and Makkah for every one performing 'umrah. If a pilgrim slaughters in Makkah and the one performing 'umrah slaughters in Mina, neither of them is blameworthy, if Allah the Exalted wills.

The eighth issue: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿fa-idha wajabat junubuha﴾: it is said wajabat al-shams when it set, and wajaba al-ha'it when the wall fell. Qays ibn al-Khatim said:

The Banu 'Awf obeyed a leader who forbade them
from peace, until he became the first to fall.

And Aws ibn Hajar said:

Did the sun not eclipse, and the full moon and the stars,
for the mountain that fell? [[This is the version of the verse as in his Diwan. Its version in the originals is:

Did the sun not eclipse the light of day,
and the full moon, for the falling mountain?

He means by the mountain: Fadalah ibn Kaldah. It is from a poem lamenting him, in which he says:

By the death of Fadalah, the leaders are not equal,
nor the abstinence of the departed.]]

So His saying, exalted is He, ﴿fa-idha wajabat junubuha﴾ means when they fall on their sides dead. He alluded to death by falling on the side, just as He alluded to the slaughter and butchering by His saying, exalted is He: "fa-dhkuru ism Allah 'alayha (mention the name of Allah over them)." Allusions are, in most contexts, more eloquent than explicit statement. The poet said:

So I left him as prey for the beasts, tearing at him,
between the crown of his head and the wrist.
[[The verse is from the Mu'allaqah of 'Antarah. Al-jazr: the plural of jazrah, the sheep or camel that is slaughtered.]]

'Antarah said:

I struck the two horns of its ram, and they both were felled,
and I carried my horse through its midst, and it sped on.
[[This is a half-verse; its second half in his Diwan is:
and I carried my horse through its midst, and it sped on.]]

That is, it fell killed on the ground, al-jadalah, which is the earth, and there are many like this. The falling on the side after slaughter is a sign of the flowing out of blood and the departure of the soul, and this is the time for eating, that is, the time near to eating, because they begin with skinning and cutting a piece of the slaughtered animal, then it is cooked. It is not skinned until it cools, because that would be a form of torture. For this reason 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Do not hasten the souls to depart."

The ninth issue: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿fa-kulu minha (so eat from them)﴾ is a command whose meaning is recommendation. All scholars recommend that a person eat from his hady, and there is reward and compliance in it, especially since the people of the Jahiliyyah did not eat from their offerings, as has passed. Abu al-'Abbas ibn Shurayh said: eating and feeding others are both recommended, and he may suffice with whichever he wishes. Al-Shafi'i said: eating is recommended, and feeding others is obligatory. If he feeds others with all of it, it suffices him, but if he eats all of it, it does not suffice him. This applies to voluntary offerings; as for obligatory blood-offerings, it is not permitted to eat any of them, as its explanation has passed.

The tenth issue: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿wa-at'imu al-qani' wal-mu'tarr (and feed the contented and the beggar)﴾. Mujahid, Ibrahim and al-Tabari said: His saying "wa-at'imu" is a command of permission. "Al-qani'" is the one who asks. One says qana'a al-rajul yaqna'u qunuʼan when he asks, with a fatha on the nun in the past tense and a kasra in the present, yaqna'u qana'ah, so he is qani', when he refrains from asking and is content with his sustenance, like hamida yahmadu, qana'ah, qana'an and qana'anan, as al-Khalil said. From the first meaning is the saying of al-Shammakh:

The wealth of a man sets right his needs and makes him sufficient;
more chaste than begging (qunut).

Ibn al-Sikkit said: among the Arabs there are those who mention qunut in the sense of qana'ah, which is contentment, abstinence and leaving off asking. It is narrated from Abu Raja' that he read "wa-at'imu al-qani'," and the meaning of this is contrary to the first.

One says: qana'a al-rajul fahuwa qani' when he is content. As for al-mu'tarr, it is the one who circles around you seeking what you have, whether he asks or remains silent. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, Mujahid, Ibrahim, al-Kalbi and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: al-mu'tarr is the one who presents himself without asking. Zuhayr said:

Upon their wealthy is the sustenance of whoever comes to them,
and among the poor is generosity and giving.

Malik said: The best I have heard is that al-qani' is the poor person, and al-mu'tarr is the visitor. It is narrated from al-Hasan that he read "wal-mu'tari," and its meaning is like that of al-mu'tarr. One says i'tarrahu, i'tarahu, 'arrahu and 'arrahu when he presented himself for what he had or sought it. Al-Nahhas mentioned this.

**First issue:** ﴿It is not their flesh, nor their blood, that reaches Allah﴾... Ibn Abbas said: The people of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period, *jahiliyyah*) used to smear the House (the Ka'bah) with the blood of the camels (*budn*) offered as sacrifice, and the Muslims wished to do the same, so the verse was revealed. Attaining (*nayl*) is not applicable to the Creator, the Exalted, but it is expressed figuratively (*majaz*) to mean acceptance. The meaning is: it does not reach Him. Ibn Abbas also said: it does not ascend to Him. Ibn 'Isa said: He does not accept their flesh or their blood, but the piety (*taqwa*) from you reaches Him, that is, that which was intended for His Face. That is what He accepts, raises up to Himself, hears, and rewards, and from this is the hadith: "Actions are only by intentions" (*innama al-a'mal bi'l-niyyat*). The recitation is ﴿لَنْ يَنالَ اللَّهَ﴾ and ﴿يَنالُهُ﴾ with *ya'* in both. It is also reported from Ya'qub with *ta'* in both, considering the flesh (as the subject).

**Second issue:** ﴿Thus He has subjected them to you﴾. He, glorified is He, bestowed favour upon us by making them submissive and enabling us to direct them, although they are greater than us in bodies and stronger than us in limbs. This is so that the servant may know that affairs are not as they appear to the servant in terms of management; rather, they are according to what the Mighty, the All-Powerful, wills. Thus the small overcomes the great, so that creation may know that the Victor is Allah, the One, the Subduer over His servants.

**Third issue:** ﴿That you may glorify Allah for having guided you﴾. He, glorified is He, mentioned the mention of His name over them from the verse before it, when He, Mighty is the Speaker, said: ﴿so mention the name of Allah over them﴾, and here He mentioned the *takbir* (saying "Allahu Akbar"). Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, used to combine the two when he slaughtered his offering, saying: "Bismillah, wallahu akbar" ("In the name of Allah, and Allah is greatest"), and this was from his jurisprudence (*fiqh*), may Allah be pleased with him.

In the Sahih, on the authority of Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sacrificed two horned rams, white-mixed (*amlahayn*) [[al-Amlah: the one whose whiteness is greater than its blackness. It is said: the one with predominantly white colour.]]. He said: I saw him slaughter them with his own hand, and I saw him placing his foot on their sides [[al-Sifah (with a *kasrah* on the *sad*): the sides. The intended meaning is one side of the sacrificial animal's body; the dual is used to indicate that he did this to each of them.]], and he said the Basmalah and the takbir.

The scholars differed on this. Abu Thawr said: the mention of Allah's name (*tasmiyah*) is obligatory, like the takbir in prayer. The majority of scholars hold that it is recommended (*mustahabb*). So if one says another phrase containing one of Allah's names and intends by it the *tasmiyah*, it is permissible. Likewise if one says only "Allahu akbar," or "la ilaha illa Allah," as Ibn Habib said. But if one does not intend the *tasmiyah*, it does not suffice in place of the *tasmiyah*, and the animal is not lawful to eat, as Al-Shafi'i and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said. And the majority of scholars among our companions and others disliked invoking blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ) at the time of the *tasmiyah* in slaughter, or mentioning him there, and they said: "Only Allah alone is to be mentioned here." Al-Shafi'i permitted sending blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ) at the time of slaughter.

**Fourth issue:** The majority hold that the offerer's saying "O Allah, accept from me" is permissible. Abu Hanifah disliked this. The proof against him is what the Sahih reports from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, and in it: then he said, "In the name of Allah. O Allah, accept from Muhammad, and the family of Muhammad, and the community of Muhammad," and then he sacrificed it. Some scholars recommended saying this in the words of the verse: ﴿"Our Lord, accept from us; indeed You are the Hearing, the Knowing"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 127] [[See vol. 2, p. 120.]]. Malik disliked their saying: "O Allah, from You and to You," and said: this is an innovation (*bid'ah*). Ibn Habib from among our companions and al-Hasan permitted this, and the proof for them is what Abu Dawud reported from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) slaughtered on the day of sacrifice two horned rams, castrated (*mawju'ayn*) [[i.e., gelded.]], white-mixed. When he turned them toward the qiblah, he said: "Indeed I have turned my face to Him who originated the heavens and the earth, as a *hanif*..." – and he recited up to His words: ﴿and I am the first of the Muslims﴾ [[So it is in all the manuscripts. See vol. 7, pp. 28 and 152.]] – "O Allah, from You and for You, on behalf of Muhammad and his community, in the name of Allah, and Allah is greatest," and then he slaughtered. Perhaps Malik had not received this report, or it was not authenticated according to him, or he saw that practice contradicts it. This is indicated by his saying that it is an innovation. And Allah knows best.

**Fifth issue:** ﴿And give good tidings to the doers of good﴾. It is narrated that it was revealed concerning the four Rightly-Guided Caliphs, as was mentioned in the verse before it. As for the apparent wording, it requires generality, so it includes every doer of good.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 38:

It is narrated that it was revealed concerning the believers when they had multiplied in Makkah and the disbelievers harmed them, and some of them emigrated to the land of Abyssinia. Some of the believers of Makkah wanted to kill whichever disbelievers they could reach, to ambush them, to betray them and to resort to trickery. So this verse was revealed, up to His words: ﴿every treacherous ingrate﴾. In it, Allah, glorified is He, promised defence and forbade treachery and betrayal in the most eloquent prohibition. The severity regarding betrayal has already been mentioned in "al-Anfal" [[See vol. 8, p. 33.]], and that (a banner is raised for the betrayer at his buttocks according to the magnitude of his betrayal, and it is said: this is the betrayal of so-and-so) [[In MS K: "so-and-so son of so-and-so".]]. It is also said: the meaning is that He repels from the believers by continuing their success until faith becomes firmly rooted in their hearts, so that the disbelievers cannot turn them away from their religion, and even if compulsion occurs, He protects them so that they do not apostatise in their hearts. It is also said: He repels from the believers by making them prevail through argument. Then, a disbeliever killing a believer is rare, and if it occurs, Allah repels that harm from that believer by taking him to His mercy. Nafi' read ﴿yudafi'u﴾ and ﴿wa-lawla difa'u﴾. Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read ﴿yadfa'u﴾ and ﴿wa-lawla daf'u﴾. 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿yudafi'u﴾ and ﴿wa-lawla daf'u Allah﴾. Yudafi' has the same meaning as yadfa', like 'aqaba al-lis (he punished the thief) and 'afahu Allah (Allah pardoned him), and the verbal noun is difa'an. Al-Zahrawi related that difa'an is the verbal noun of dafa'a, like hasiba hisaban.

There are two issues here. The first is his saying ﴿Permission has been given to those who are fought against﴾. It is said that this explains His words, ﴿Indeed, God defends those who believe﴾, meaning that He repels the harms of the disbelievers from them by permitting them to fight and by helping them. There is an implied element in it: "Permission has been given to those who are fit for fighting to fight," and it was omitted because the context indicates it. Al-Dahhak said: The Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) asked permission to fight the disbelievers when they harmed them in Makkah. God then revealed, ﴿Indeed, God does not love every treacherous ingrate﴾. When he (ﷺ) emigrated, this was revealed: ﴿Permission has been given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged﴾. This verse abrogates everything in the Qur'an that involves turning away and forgiving without fighting [[In (k) and "Safh" (forgiveness)]]. It is the first verse revealed about fighting [[It should be noted that what preceded in the second part, p. 347, at His words, ﴿And fight in the way of God...﴾ (2:190), differs from what is said here]]. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: it was revealed at the time of the Messenger of God's (ﷺ) emigration to Madinah. Al-Nasa'i and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) was expelled from Makkah, Abu Bakr said: "They have expelled their Prophet; they will surely perish." Then God revealed, ﴿Permission has been given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged. And indeed God is able to give them victory﴾. Abu Bakr then said: "I knew that there would be fighting." Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a good (hasan) hadith." More than one narrator has related it from Sufyan, from al-A'mash, from Muslim al-Batin, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr as a mursal report, and it does not contain "from Ibn 'Abbas."

The second issue: this verse is evidence that permissibility comes from the Shari'ah, contrary to the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school), because His words "Permission has been given" mean "it has been permitted," and this is a word that in the language is established for permitting whatever was forbidden. This meaning was already discussed in al-Baqarah and elsewhere. It is also read as "Udhina" with a fatha on the hamza, meaning "God has permitted." "Yuqatilun" is read with a kasra on the ta, meaning they fight their enemy. It is also read "Yuqatalun" with a fatha on the ta, meaning the polytheists fight them, and they are the believers. For this reason He said, "because they have been wronged," meaning they were expelled from their homes.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on surah 22, verse 40:

There are eight issues in this verse.

**The first issue:** His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿those who have been expelled from their homes﴾ (40). This is one of the ways in which they were wronged. They were expelled only for saying, "Our Lord is Allah alone." So His words, "except that they say, 'Our Lord is Allah'" (40), are a disjunctive exception (*istithna' munqati'*, an exception where the excluded item does not belong to the same category as what precedes it), meaning: "but because they say, 'Our Lord is Allah.'" This is the view of Sibawayh. Al-Farra' said that it may be in the genitive position (*mawdi' khafd*), taking it as coordinated with the preposition *ba'* (by), and this is also the view of Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj. The meaning in his view is: "those who were expelled from their homes without right, except by [reason of] their saying, 'Our Lord is Allah,'" that is, they were expelled for their monotheism; the people of idols expelled them. "Those who have been expelled" (40) is in the genitive position as a substitute (*badal*) for His words, "to those who are fought" (39).

**The second issue:** Ibn al-Arabi said: Our scholars have said that before the Pledge of al-'Aqaba, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was not permitted to fight, and bloodshed was not made lawful for him. He was only commanded to call to Allah, to be patient with harm, and to pardon the ignorant, for a period of ten years, in order to establish the proof of Allah, may He be exalted, against them, and to fulfil His promise, which He bestowed by His grace in His words: ﴿And We would not punish until We sent a messenger﴾ [al-Isra': 15].[[See vol. 10, p. 231.]] People persisted in rebellion and were not guided by clear proof. Quraysh had persecuted those of their people who followed him among the emigrants, until they tempted them away from their religion and drove them from their lands. Some of them fled to the land of Abyssinia; some went out to Medina; and some remained patient under harm. When Quraysh transgressed against Allah, the Exalted, rejected His command, denied His Prophet, peace be upon him, and tortured whoever believed in Him, affirmed His oneness and worshipped Him, and believed in His Prophet, peace be upon him, and held fast to his religion, Allah permitted His Messenger to fight, to defend himself, and to take retribution against those who had wronged them. He revealed: "Permission is given to those who are fought, because they have been wronged" (39), down to His words "the affairs" (41).[[This is conclusive evidence that jihad was legislated to protect the call.]]

**The third issue:** In this verse there is evidence that an act performed by one who has been compelled and forced is attributed to the one who compelled and forced him. This is because Allah, may He be exalted, attributed the expulsion to the disbelievers, since the context concerns establishing and imposing responsibility for the sin. This verse is similar to His words: ﴿when those who disbelieved expelled him﴾ (40) [al-Tawbah: 40]. The discussion regarding both is the same, and it has already been covered in "Bara'ah" (Surat al-Tawbah).

And praise be to Allah.

**The fourth issue:** His, may He be exalted, words: (And had it not been for Allah's repelling some people by means of others) (40). That is: had it not been for what Allah, may He be exalted, legislated for the prophets and believers of fighting the enemies, the people of polytheism would have overpowered them and rendered useless the places of worship where the adherents of the religions mention the name of Allah. But He repelled [the danger] by making fighting obligatory, so that the people of religion could devote themselves to worship. Jihad is a matter that has existed among the nations from earliest times, and through it the laws were made sound and acts of worship were gathered together. It is as if He said: "Permission has been given to fight, so let the believers fight." Then this matter of fighting is reinforced by His words: "And had it not been for Allah's repelling people..." (40), meaning: had it not been for fighting and jihad, the truth would have been overcome in every nation. Therefore, whoever among the Christians and Sabians finds jihad abhorrent contradicts his own creed, for without fighting, the religion that is defended would not remain. Furthermore, these places of worship that were built before their alteration and distortion, and before those religions were abrogated by Islam, were mentioned for this very purpose: had it not been for this repelling, the churches would have been demolished in the time of Moses, the monasteries and churches in the time of Jesus, and the mosques in the time of Muhammad, peace be upon him.

(Surely would have been demolished) (40) [[Read with the light form (*takhfif*) by Nafi'.]] from *hadamtu al-bina'*, meaning I tore down the building, so it collapsed (*infadama*). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is the most correct of what has been said in interpreting the verse. It is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "And had it not been for Allah's repelling, through the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), the disbelievers from the Followers and those after them." Although this involves repelling one group by means of another, the meaning of fighting is more fitting, as has already been mentioned. Mujahid said: "Had it not been for Allah's repelling the oppression of one people by the testimony of trustworthy witnesses." A group said: "Had it not been for Allah's repelling the oppression of oppressors by the justice of rulers." Abu al-Darda' said: "Had it not been that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, repels by means of those in the mosques those who are not in the mosques, and by means of those who fight those who do not fight, the punishment would have come upon them." Another group said: "Had it not been for Allah's repelling punishment through the supplication of the virtuous and the righteous," and other detailed explanations clarifying the meaning of the verse. The verse necessarily implies a repelled party from among the people and a party from whom it is repelled, so consider this carefully.

**The fifth issue:** Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: This verse contains a prohibition against demolishing the churches, synagogues and fire-temples of the protected people (*ahl al-dhimma*, non-Muslim subjects living under Muslim protection). They are not to be left to build what did not exist before, nor to enlarge the buildings either in space or in height. It is not proper for Muslims to enter them or pray in them, and whenever they add something new, it must be demolished. What is found in the lands of war of churches and synagogues is to be demolished. What is in the lands of Islam is not demolished for the protected people, because these are treated like their houses and property, which they were guaranteed protection for by treaty. It is not permissible to allow them to expand, because that would display the causes of disbelief. It is permissible to demolish a mosque in order to rebuild it, and 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, did this with the mosque of the Prophet (ﷺ).

**The sixth issue:** "Lu-hudimat" (would have been demolished) has been recited with the *dal* lightened and with it doubled (*tashdid*).

**Ṣawāmi' (monasteries)** (40) is the plural of *ṣawma'a*, whose form is *fawla'a*. It is a tall building with a pointed top. It is said: *ṣamma'a al-tharida*, meaning he raised its head and sharpened it. A *asma' al-qalb* man is one with sharp understanding. *Al-asma'* among men is one who is sharp in speech. It is also said: it is one with small ears among people and others. Before Islam it was specific to the monks of the Christians and the worshippers of the Sabians, said Qatadah. Then it came to be used for the minaret of the Muslims. **Al-biya' (churches)** is the plural of *bee'a*, which is the church of the Christians. Al-Tabari said: It is said to be the synagogues of the Jews; then Mujahid's view was introduced that does not require this.

**Wa-ṣalawat (and prayer-places)**: Al-Zajjaj and al-Hasan said: they are the synagogues of the Jews, and in Hebrew it is *ṣalūtā*. Abu 'Ubaydah said: The *ṣalawat* are buildings built for the Christians in the deserts, where they pray during their journeys; they are called *ṣalūtā*, which was Arabized and became *ṣalawat*. There are nine readings of "ṣalawat" mentioned by Ibn 'Atiyyah: *ṣulawat*, *ṣalwat*, *ṣilwat*, *ṣulūlī* on the pattern *fu'ūlī*, *ṣulūb* with a single *ba'* (b), the plural of *ṣalīb* (cross), *ṣulūth* with the three-dotted *tha'* on the pattern *fu'ūl*, *ṣulawat* with a *ḍamma* on the *ṣad* and *lam* and an *alif* after the *waw*, *ṣulūthā* with a *ḍamma* on the *ṣad* and *lam* and shortening of the *alif* after the three-dotted *tha'*, [*ṣulawthiyā* with a *kasra* on the *ṣad*, a sukun on the *lam*, a *waw* with a *kasra* after it, a *ya'* after it, a three-dotted *tha'* after it, then an *alif*.[[What is between the brackets is the wording of Abu Hayyan. What is in (ʿAwj) and (B) is: *ṣulawthiyā* with a *kasra* on the *ṣad* and the three-dotted *tha'*.]]]. Al-Nahhas mentioned: It is narrated from 'Asim al-Jahdari that he recited "wa-ṣulūb" (and crosses). It is narrated from al-Dahhak "wa-ṣalūth" with a three-dotted *tha'*, but I do not know whether he pronounced the *ṣad* with a *fatha* or a *ḍamma*. I say: On this basis, there are ten readings here.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The *ṣalawat* are the churches. Abu al-'Aliyah said: The *ṣalawat* are the mosques of the Sabians. Ibn Zayd said: They are the prayers of the Muslims, which are interrupted when the enemy enters upon them and the mosques are demolished. On this view, demolition is used figuratively for prayers, since they are suspended; or he meant the place of prayers and the word was omitted. On the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Zajjaj and others, demolition is literal. Al-Hasan said: The demolition of prayers is abandoning them. Qutrub said: They are the small monasteries, and no singular form of them has been heard. Khusayf held that the purpose of these names is to divide the places of worship of the nations: the *ṣawāmi'* are for the monks, the *biya'* for the Christians, the *ṣalawat* for the Jews, and the *masajid* for the Muslims. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The more apparent view is that the purpose is emphasis in mentioning places of worship. These names are shared by the nations in their referents, except that *bee'a* is specific to the Christians in the language of the Arabs. The meanings of these names apply to the nations that have a scripture from ancient times. The Magians and the polytheists are not mentioned in this verse, because they have nothing that must be protected, and the remembrance of Allah is found only among the people of revealed laws.

Al-Nahhas said: "in which the name of Allah is mentioned" (40): In the Arabic language, on a truly careful analysis, the pronoun in "in which the name of Allah is mentioned" must refer to the mosques and not to other things, since the pronoun is adjacent to them. It is also permissible for it to refer to "monasteries" and what follows, and the meaning would be: at the time of their laws and their upholding of the truth.

**The seventh issue:** If it is asked: why were the mosques and prayer-places of the protected people placed before the mosques of the Muslims? It is said: because they are older in construction. It is also said: because of their nearness to demolition, and the nearness of the mosques to the remembrance of Allah, just as the foremost is placed last in His words: ﴿Then among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾ [Fatir: 32].[[See vol. 14, p. ....]]

**The eighth issue:** His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿And Allah will surely support those who support Him﴾ (40), that is: those who support His religion and His Prophet.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Powerful﴾ (40), that is, Capable. Al-Khattabi said: *al-qawiyy* (the Powerful) can mean the Capable, and whoever is strong at something has the power to do it.

﴿Mighty﴾ means glorious and noble, said al-Zajjaj. It is also said: the one who is invincible, who cannot be sought after. We have explained both in our book *al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna* (The Most Excellent in Explaining the Beautiful Names of Allah).

Al-Zajjaj said: "Alladhina" (those who) is in the accusative position, as a substitution (radd) for "min" (whoever), referring to His words: ﴿And Allah will surely help those who help Him﴾ [22:40].

Others said: "Alladhina" is in the genitive position, as a substitution for His words: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against﴾, and "Alladhina in case We establish them firmly in the land" refers to four of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and no one else in the land was among them.

Ibn Abbas said: (The intended meaning is the Muhajirun (Emigrants), the Ansar (Helpers), and the Tabi'un bi-ihsan (Followers who follow them in goodness).) Qatadah said: They are the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). Ikrimah said: They are the people of the five daily prayers. Al-Hasan and Abu al-Aliyah said: They are this Ummah; when Allah grants them victory, they establish the prayer. Ibn Abi Najih said: It means the rulers. Al-Dahhak said: It is a condition that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, stipulated upon the one to whom He gives dominion, and this is a good (interpretation). Sahl ibn Abd Allah said: Enjoining good and forbidding evil is obligatory upon the ruler and upon the scholars who attend him. It is not incumbent upon the people to command the ruler, because that is binding upon him and obligatory for him, and [the people] should not command the scholars, for the proof has already become binding upon them.

This is a consolation and solace to the Prophet (ﷺ): that is, there were prophets before you who were denied, and they were patient until Allah destroyed those who denied them. So follow their example and be patient.

(And Musa was denied) That is, Pharaoh and his people denied him. As for the Children of Israel, they did not deny him, which is why [the verse] did not join him to what precedes it, so that it would read "and the people of Musa."

(Then I gave the disbelievers respite) That is, I delayed punishment from them.

(Then I seized them) That is, I punished them.

(So how was My rejection?) This is an interrogative meaning change: that is, look at how I changed the blessings they were in by means of punishment and destruction, and so I will do to the deniers among the Quraysh. Al-Jawhari said: al-nakir and al-inkar are the changing of what is disapproved (munkar), and al-munkar is the singular of al-manakir.

This is a consolation and solace to the Prophet (ﷺ): that is, there were prophets before you who were denied, and they were patient until Allah destroyed those who denied them. So follow their example and be patient.

(And Musa was denied) That is, Pharaoh and his people denied him. As for the Children of Israel, they did not deny him, which is why [the verse] did not join him to what precedes it, so that it would read "and the people of Musa."

(Then I gave the disbelievers respite) That is, I delayed punishment from them.

The Qur'an, Surah 22, verse 45, al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿How many a town have We destroyed﴾. That is, We destroyed its people. The discussion of the word *ka-ayyin* ("how many") has already passed in "Al 'Imran" [[See vol. 4, p. 228.]].

(while it was wrongdoing) That is, through disbelief.

(so it lies fallen on its roofs) This was discussed in al-Kahf [[See vol. 10, p. 410.]].

(and a well left idle, and a lofty palace) Al-Zajjaj said: "*wa-bi'rin mu'attalatin*" ("and a well left idle") is coordinated with "*min qaryatin*" ("a town"), meaning "and [how many] of the people of a town and of the people of a well." Al-Farra' holds that "*wa-bi'rin*" is coordinated with "*'urushiha*" ("its roofs"). Al-Asma'i said: I asked Nafi' ibn Abi Nu'aym, "Is *al-bi'r* (the well) and *al-dhi'b* (the wolf) pronounced with a hamza?" He said: "If the Arabs pronounce them with a hamza, then pronounce them with a hamza." Most of Nafi's transmitters recite both with a hamza, except Warsh, whose transmission from him is without a hamza in both words, though the original form is with the hamza. The meaning of *mu'attalah* is "abandoned," as stated by al-Dahhak. It is also said: "empty of its people because of their destruction." It is also said: "its water has sunk." And it is said: "left idle from its buckets and its ropes." The meanings are close.

(and a lofty palace) Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: "high and tall." Ghadi ibn Zayd said:

He raised it, plastering it with marble, and covered it with gypsum (*kils*), so there are nests for birds on its heights.

That is, he raised it. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ata', 'Ikrimah and Mujahid said: "plastered," from *al-shid*, which is lime plaster (*al-jass*). The rajiz (poet) said [[The verse is by al-Shammakh. As in al-Lisan, it is in the basit meter and not rajaz. *Al-ghamr* (with a fatha on the ghayn and a kasra on the mim) is a variant of *al-ghamr* (with a damma on the ghayn and a sukun on the mim), meaning the inexperienced man who has not tested affairs.]]:

Do not think of me, even though I am an inexperienced man, as a puddle of water between the mud and the plaster.

Imru' al-Qays said:

And not a fortress except one built with stone.

[This is the second half of a line whose first half is: "And a desert where no palm trunk was left."]

Ibn 'Abbas said: "*mashid*" means "fortified." Al-Kalbi also said this. It is a *maf'il* in the sense of a *maf'ul*, like *mabi'* meaning *mabyu'* ("sold"). Al-Jawhari said: "*al-mashid*" is that which is made with *al-shid*. And *al-shid* (with a kasra) is anything with which you coat a wall, whether gypsum or flagstone; with a fatha it is the verbal noun. You say: *shadahu yashiduhu shaydan*, meaning he plastered it with gypsum. *Al-mushayyad* (with the shadda) means "lengthened." Al-Kisa'i said: "*al-mashid*" is for the singular, from the words of Allah the Exalted: "*wa-qasrin mashid*" ("and a lofty palace"), and "*al-mushayyad*" is for the plural, from the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿in towers built up high﴾ [An-Nisa': 78] [[See vol. 5, p. 282.]]. In the sentence there is an implied omitted element, its estimated form being: "and a lofty palace like it, left idle." It is said that this well and this palace are well known in Hadramawt. The palace stands over the summit of a mountain that cannot be climbed in any way, and the well is at its foot; the wind does not let anything that falls into it remain, but casts it out. The owners of the palaces were the kings of the settled lands, and the owners of the wells were the kings of the desert. That is, Allah destroyed these and those.

Al-Dahhak and others, among what al-Tha'labi and Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Muqri' and others mentioned, reported that the well is *al-Rass*, and it was in 'Adan in Yemen, in Hadramawt, in a town called Hadhuraa'. Four thousand who had believed in Salih settled there, and they were saved from the punishment, and Salih was with them. Then Salih died, and the place was named Hadramawt, because when Salih was present (*hadara*) there he died (*mata*). They built Hadhuraa' and settled beside this well, and they appointed over themselves a man called al-'Alas ibn Julas ibn Suwayd, as mentioned by al-Ghaznawi. Al-Tha'labi says: Jalhas ibn Julas. He was of good conduct among them and just towards them. They made his minister Sinhareeb ibn Sawada. They remained for a long time and multiplied until they became numerous. The well watered the whole town, its desert, and all the animals, sheep, cattle and other things in it, because there were many pulleys (*bakarat*) set up over it and many men appointed to tend it. And there were many *abazin* (with the nun) of marble, which resembled basins, one filled for the people, another for the animals, another for the cattle, and another for the sheep. The attendants drew water from it by night and by day in turns, and they had no water other than this. The king they had appointed lived a long life. When death came to him, he was anointed with oil so that his image would not change, and they did this whenever one of them died who was among those honored by them. When he died, this grieved them, and they saw that their affairs had been corrupted, and they all wailed in lamentation. Satan seized the opportunity from them and entered the body of the king many days after his death. He spoke to them and said: "I have not died, but I withdrew from you until I could see your conduct." They rejoiced most greatly, and he commanded his close associates to set up a screen between him and them, and he would speak to them from behind it, so that death would not be recognized in his form. They then set up an idol behind the screen which neither ate nor drank. He informed them that he would never die and that he was their god. All of this was spoken by Satan on his tongue. Many of them believed him and some doubted, and the believer who denied him was fewer than the one who affirmed him. Whenever a counselor spoke to them, he was rebuked and suppressed. So they unanimously agreed (*asfaqu*: they gathered together upon it) to worship him. Allah sent to them a prophet to whom revelation came in sleep rather than in waking, named Hanzalah ibn Safwan. He informed them that the image was an idol with no spirit, that Satan had led them astray, that Allah does not take the form of creation, and that the king could not be a partner with Allah. He admonished them, advised them and warned them of the might and vengeance of their Lord. They harmed him and became hostile to him, but he continued to instruct them in admonition and did not cease giving them counsel, until they killed him in the marketplace and threw him into a well. At that moment the punishment befell them. They went to sleep sated and quenched with water, and in the morning the well's water had sunk and its rope had been cut. They all cried out, and the women and children wailed, and the animals cried out from thirst, until death overtook them all and destruction encompassed them. Beasts of prey inherited their land, and foxes and hyenas their dwellings. Their gardens and their wealth were replaced with lote-trees (*sidr*), thorny *'idah* trees and *qatad* [[The *sidr* is a kind of tree and there are two kinds: one is wild, whose fruit is not used and whose leaves are not suitable for washing, its fruit being astringent and not fit for eating; the Arabs call it *al-dal*. The second kind of *sidr* grows in fertile land, its fruit is *nabq* (jujube), and its leaves are used for washing. *Al-'idah* is every tree that is large and has thorns; its singular is *'idahah*, *'ahdah* and *'udah*. *Al-qatad* is a hard tree with thorns like needles.]], so that nothing is heard in them except the howling of the jinn and the roaring of lions. We seek refuge in Allah from His might and from persistence in what brings about His vengeance. Al-Suhayli said: As for the lofty palace, it is a palace built by Shaddad ibn 'Ad ibn Iram; no like of it was built on earth, so they say and claim. Its condition too is like the condition of this well mentioned above, in its desolation after the company of people and its emptiness after being inhabited, and no one can approach it within miles, because of the howling of jinn and the strange sounds heard in it, after the blessings and the abundant life, the splendor of kingship and the order of the people like a string of pearls. They perished and did not return. So Allah, the Exalted, reminded them in this verse as an admonition, a lesson, a reminder, and a warning of the consequences of disobedience and the evil outcome of opposition. We seek refuge in Allah from that, and we ask Him to protect us from a bad end. It is said that the one who destroyed them was Nebuchadnezzar, as mentioned earlier in Surah al-Anbiya' in the words of Allah: ﴿And how many a town have We shattered﴾ [[See vol. 11, p. 274.]] [Al-Anbiya': 11]. Then their well became idle and their palaces were ruined.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary on Surah al-Hajj (22), verse 46:**

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth?﴾ meaning the disbelievers of Makkah, so that they might witness these ruined towns and take warning, and fear the punishment of Allah lest it descend upon them as it descended upon those before them.

(﴿So that they may have hearts with which they understand﴾) He attributed understanding (al-'aql) to the heart because it is its seat, just as hearing's seat is the ear. It has been said that the seat of understanding is the brain, and this is reported from Abu Hanifa, but I do not think that report from him is authentic.

(﴿For indeed, it is not the eyes that go blind﴾) Al-Farra' said: the "hā'" is an 'imād (a dummy pronoun, a pronoun of emphasis or placeholder). It is also permissible to say "fa-innahu," and this is the reading of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud. The meaning is one: the masculine is according to the predicate, and the feminine is according to "al-abṣār" (the eyes) or "al-qiṣṣah" (the matter). That is: "fa-inna al-abṣāra lā ta'mā," or "fa-inna al-qiṣṣah."

(﴿It is not the eyes that go blind﴾) meaning the sight of the eyes remains intact for them.

(﴿But it is the hearts within the breasts that go blind﴾) meaning, they are blind to the perception of truth and to reflection. Qatadah said: the seeing sight was made a means of sustenance and benefit, while the sight that benefits is in the heart. Mujahid said: "For every eye there are four eyes," meaning every person has four eyes: two eyes in his head for his worldly life, and two eyes in his heart for his afterlife. If the two eyes of his head go blind while the two eyes of his heart see, his blindness does not harm him at all; and if the two eyes of his head see while the two eyes of his heart go blind, his sight does not benefit him at all.

Qatadah and Ibn Jubayr said: this verse was revealed concerning Ibn Umm Maktum, the blind man. Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil said: when the verse ﴿And whoever is blind in this [world] will be blind in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Isra' 17:72] was revealed, Ibn Umm Maktum said: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), I am blind in this world; shall I then be blind in the Hereafter?" So this was revealed: "For indeed, it is not the eyes that go blind, but it is the hearts within the breasts that go blind." That is: whoever is blind in this [world] in his heart to Islam, he will be in the Hereafter in the Fire.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 47:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They ask you to hasten the punishment﴾. It was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and this is his saying: ﴿So bring upon us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful﴾ [al-A'raf: 70].[[See vol. 7, p. 237.]] It was also said that it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, and this is his saying: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You﴾ [al-Anfal: 32].[[See vol. 7, p. 398.]]

(﴿And Allah will not fail His promise﴾), i.e., in sending down the punishment. Al-Zajjaj said: They sought to hasten the punishment, so Allah informed them that nothing escapes Him, and it did descend upon them in this world on the Day of Badr.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid said: It means of the days in which Allah created the heavens and the earth. Ikrimah said: It means of the days of the Hereafter. Allah informed them, when they sought to hasten the punishment, that in short days He would bring it upon them in long days. Al-Farra' said: This is a warning to them of the extension of their punishment in the Hereafter, meaning that one day of their punishment in the Hereafter is a thousand years. It was also said: The meaning is that a day of fear and hardship in the Hereafter is like a thousand years of the years of this world in which there is fear and hardship; and likewise the day of bliss, by analogy. Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "مِمَّا يَعُدُّونَ" (mimma ya'uddun) with the yā' (third person), and Abu Ubayd preferred this reading because of the saying "wa-yasta'jiluunaka" (they ask you to hasten). The rest read it with the tā' (second person, addressing them), and Abu Hatim preferred this.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And how many a town did I give respite while it was wrongdoing⁠—﴾ That is, I gave it time and delayed it despite its arrogant defiance.

(Then I seized it.) That is, with punishment.

(And to Me is the final return.)

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verses 49–51:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "O mankind"﴾, meaning the people of Makkah.

(Indeed I am for you only a warner) meaning a warner who instills fear. The meaning of warning (al-indhar) has already been discussed at the beginning of al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 184.]].

(Clear) meaning: I make clear to you what you need to know of the matters of your religion.

(So those who believed and did righteous deeds — for them is forgiveness and an honourable provision) 50, meaning Paradise.

(And those who strove against Our verses) meaning: who strove to nullify Our verses.

(Seeking to frustrate) meaning: contending and opposing. This is what Ibn Abbas said. Al-Farra' said: opposing. Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr said: discouraging people from Islam. Al-Akhfash said: opposing, competing. Al-Zajjaj said: meaning, thinking that they could overcome us, because they thought there would be no resurrection and thought that Allah would not have power over them. Qatadah also said this. Likewise is the meaning of the reading of Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, "mu'ajjizin" without an alif and with a shaddah. It is also possible that its meaning is that they cause the believers to fail in faith in the Prophet, peace be upon him, and in the verses; this was said by al-Suddi. It was also said: meaning they attribute to incapacity whoever follows Muhammad ﷺ, like their saying: "They made him ignorant" and "They called him corrupt."

(Those are the companions of the Hellfire) 10.
