(Those are the companions of the Hellfire) 10.

In it are three issues.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿tamanna﴾ means he recited and recited aloud. And "the Shaytan threw into his wish" means into his recitation and his reading. This was already discussed in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 2, p. 5.]]. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It has come from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to recite: "And We did not send before you any messenger or prophet or muhaddath." Maslamah ibn al-Qasim ibn 'Abd Allah mentioned it, and Sufyan narrated it from 'Amr ibn Dinar from Ibn 'Abbas. Maslamah said: We found the muhaddathun [[Al-muhaddathun (with a fatha on the dal and shadda on it). Ibn al-Athir said: they are the inspired (al-mulhamun), and the mulham is one into whose self a thing is cast, so he reports it by intuition and insight. This is a kind of thing that God, exalted is He, specially gives to whichever of His chosen servants He wills, such as 'Umar. It is as if they were spoken to about something and then said it.]] adhering to prophethood, according to Ibn 'Abbas's reading, because they spoke of lofty matters of the unseen as passing thoughts, and uttered inner wisdom, so they were right in what they said and were protected in what they uttered, like 'Umar ibn al-Khattab in the story of Sariyah [[He is Sariyah ibn Zunaym ibn 'Abd Allah. The story is that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, appointed him over an army and sent it to Persia in the year twenty-three. While 'Umar was delivering the Friday sermon, it came into his mind that the said army had met the enemy while they were in the bottom of a valley and had resolved to flee, with a mountain near them. So in the course of his sermon he said: "O Sariyah, the mountain, the mountain!" and he raised his voice. Allah cast it into Sariyah's hearing, so he turned the people toward the mountain, and they fought the enemy from one side, and Allah granted them victory.
(See his biography in the books on the Companions.)]] and the clear proofs he spoke.

I say: Abu Bakr al-Anbari mentioned this report in his book al-Radd. My father, may Allah have mercy on him, narrated to me: 'Ali ibn Harb narrated to us: Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah narrated to us from 'Amr from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he recited "And We did not send before you any messenger or prophet or muhaddath." Abu Bakr said: This is a report that is not to be relied upon as evidence that this is Qur'an. The muhaddath is the one to whom revelation is given in his sleep, because the dreams of prophets are revelation.

The second: The scholars said: This verse is problematic from two aspects. The first: some hold that prophets, may the blessings of Allah be upon them, include both those who are messengers and those who are not messengers. Others maintain that it is not permissible to say "prophet" until one is a messenger. The proof of the correctness of this view is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger or prophet﴾, so He made prophethood and messengerhood distinct for the Prophet ﷺ. The meaning of "prophet" (nabi) is one who gives news from Allah, exalted and majestic is He, and the meaning of giving news from Allah, exalted and majestic is He, is precisely sending. Al-Farra' said: The messenger is the one sent to the creation by Jibril, peace be upon him, being sent to him face to face, and the prophet is the one whose prophethood is by inspiration or dream. So every messenger is a prophet, but not every prophet is a messenger. Al-Mahdawi said: This is the correct view, that every messenger is a prophet and not every prophet is a messenger. Likewise Qadi 'Iyad mentioned it in his book al-Shifa, saying: The sound view, on which the vast majority agree, is that every messenger is a prophet and not every prophet is a messenger. He cited the hadith of Abu Dharr, that the messengers among the prophets were three hundred and thirteen, the first of them Adam and the last of them Muhammad ﷺ [[In (j): a hasan hadith.]].

The other aspect in which the difficulty lies is the third: the narrations transmitted concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse, none of which is sound. Among the things the disbelievers used to deceive their common people with was their saying: "It is the right of prophets not to be unable to do anything. So why does Muhammad not bring us the punishment, when we have gone to great lengths in enmity toward him?" They also used to say: "It should not be that error and mistake befall them." So the Lord, glorified is He, made clear that they are human, and that the one who brings the punishment is Allah, exalted is He, as He wills, and that for humans, forgetfulness, forgetting and error are permissible until Allah makes His verses firm and abrogates the stratagems of the Shaytan. Al-Layth narrated from Yunus from al-Zuhri from Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited ﴿By the star when it sets﴾ [al-Najm: 1], and when he reached ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza, and Manat, the third, the other?﴾ [al-Najm: 19–20] he slipped and said: "Indeed their intercession is to be hoped for." The polytheists met him, and those in whose hearts there was sickness greeted him and rejoiced. He said: "That was from the Shaytan." Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed: "And We did not send before you any messenger or prophet" to the end of the verse. Al-Nahhas said: This is a broken (munqati') hadith, and in it lies this grave matter. Likewise is the hadith of Qatadah, which adds: "And indeed they are the exalted cranes (al-gharaniq al-'ula)." More monstrous than this is what al-Waqidi narrated from Kathir ibn Zayd from al-Muttalib ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: All the polytheists prostrated except al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, for he took some dust from the earth and raised it to his forehead and prostrated upon it, and he was an old man. It is said he was Abu Uhayhah Sa'id ibn al-'As. Then Jibril, peace be upon him, descended and the Prophet ﷺ recited to him, and he said to him: "I did not bring you that!" And Allah revealed: ﴿You had almost inclined toward them a little﴾ [al-Isra': 74]. Al-Nahhas said: This is a munkar, broken hadith, especially from the narration of al-Waqidi. In al-Bukhari it is reported that the one who took a handful of dust and raised it to his forehead was Umayyah ibn Khalaf. The complete discussion of al-Nahhas on the hadith will come, God willing, at the end of the chapter. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This hadith in which is "they are the exalted cranes" occurs in books of tafsir and the like, but al-Bukhari did not include it, nor Muslim, and no well-known compiler mentions it in my knowledge. Rather, the school of the people of hadith implies that the Shaytan cast, without specifying this cause or any other. There is no disagreement that the Shaytan's casting was only into audible words, by which the trial occurred. Then people differed about the form of this casting. What appears in the tafsirs, and is the well-known view, is that the Prophet ﷺ uttered those words with his tongue. My father, may Allah be pleased with him, told me that he met in the East some shaykhs of scholars and theologians who said: This is not permissible for the Prophet ﷺ, who is protected in conveying the message; rather the matter is that the Shaytan spoke a phrase which he made the disbelievers hear at the moment the Prophet ﷺ said: "Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza, and Manat, the third, the other?" [al-Najm: 19–20], and he brought his voice close to the voice of the Prophet ﷺ until the matter became confused for the polytheists, and they said: "Muhammad recited it." Something similar to this interpretation has been narrated from the Imam Abu al-Ma'ali. It is also said: The one who cast was the devil of mankind, as in His saying, exalted and majestic is He: "And make noise therein" [Fussilat: 26]. Qatadah said: It is what he recited while drowsing.

Qadi 'Iyad said in his book al-Shifa, after mentioning the proof of the truthfulness of the Prophet ﷺ, and that the community unanimously agreed that in matters concerning conveyance he is protected from reporting anything contrary to what it is, whether intentionally, deliberately, or by forgetfulness or error: Know, may Allah honour you, that for us in speaking on the problematic aspect of this hadith there are two approaches. One of them is to discredit its basis, and the second is to accept it. As for the first approach, it suffices you that this is a hadith which none of the people of soundness has transmitted, nor has anyone narrated it through a sound, connected, trustworthy chain. Rather, it is the commentators and historians, who are enamoured of every strange thing and who snatch from pages every sound and unsound report, who have become attached to it and its like. Abu Bakr al-Bazzar said: We do not know of this hadith being narrated from the Prophet ﷺ by a connected chain that is permissible to mention, except what Shu'bah narrated from Abu Bishr from Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, as far as I recall, and the doubt in the hadith is that the Prophet ﷺ was in Mecca ... and he mentioned the story. Only Umayyah ibn Khalid traced it back to Shu'bah, while others transmit it as mursal from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. It is known only from al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. So Abu Bakr, may Allah have mercy on him, has made clear to you that it is not known through any permissible chain other than this, and in it is such weakness as he pointed out, together with the doubt we have mentioned, on which no reliance can be placed and which offers no certainty. As for the hadith of al-Kalbi, it is not permissible to narrate it or mention it, because of the severity of its weakness and falsehood, as al-Bazzar, may Allah have mercy on him, indicated. What is reported in the Sahih is that the Prophet ﷺ recited "By the star" in Mecca, then prostrated, and the Muslims, the polytheists, the jinn and mankind prostrated with him. This is his discrediting from the perspective of transmission. As for the second approach, it is based on accepting the hadith should it be sound. Allah has protected us from its soundness, but in any case the leading imams of the Muslims have answered it with various responses, some weak and some strong. What appears and is preponderant in its interpretation, if we accept it, is that the Prophet ﷺ, as his Lord commanded him, recited the Qur'an in measured recitation and articulated its verses clearly in his recitation, as the trustworthy narrators have transmitted from him. So it is possible that the Shaytan lay in wait for those pauses and inserted into them what he fabricated of those words, imitating the tone of the Prophet ﷺ in such a way that whoever drew near to him among the disbelievers would hear it, so they thought it was from the words of the Prophet ﷺ and spread it.

Al-Qurtubi's ideas are conveyed here through his own words and quotations, so I will translate the passage in full.

And this does not detract, for the Muslims, from the preservation of the surah before that, as God revealed it, and their certainty about the condition of the Prophet ﷺ in censuring the idols and disparaging them, which is known of him. So what is narrated of the Prophet's ﷺ grief at this rumour, this doubt, and the cause of this trial, is [explained]. God Most High said: "And We did not send before you any messenger or prophet..." [[See the Kitab al-Shifa of al-Qadi Iyad, vol. 2, pp. 116, 131, Istanbul edition.]] — the verse. I say: this interpretation is the best that has been said on this matter.

Sulayman ibn Harb said: "inna" in "inna fi..." [[in the position of 10 in the printed text]] means "indahu" ("with him", "in his presence"), i.e., Satan cast into the hearts of the disbelievers at the time of the Prophet's ﷺ recitation, like the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: "And you dwelt among us [fina]" [al-Shu'ara': 18], meaning "with us" ('indana). This is the meaning transmitted by Ibn 'Atiyya from his father, from the scholars of the East, and Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi pointed to it. He said before this: this verse is an explicit text on our purpose, a proof for the soundness of our position, and a basis for the innocence of the Prophet ﷺ from what is attributed to him as having said it. That is because God Most High said: "And We did not send before you any messenger or prophet except that when he wished [tamanna], Satan cast into his wish [umniyyatihi]," i.e., into his recitation. God Most High informs that it is part of His custom with His messengers and His way with His prophets that when they speak on behalf of God Most High a statement, Satan adds to it from his own self, as he does with all sins. You say: "I cast such-and-such into the house," and "I cast such-and-such into the bag." This is a clear text that Satan added to what the Prophet ﷺ said, not that the Prophet ﷺ himself uttered it.

Then he mentioned the meaning of the words of 'Iyad up to his saying: None was guided to this except al-Tabari, because of the greatness of his rank, the clarity of his thought, the breadth of his learning, and the strength of his reasoning. It seems he pointed to this aim, hit this target, and struck the mark, after mentioning many narrations on this matter, all of which are false and have no basis. Had your Lord willed, no one would have related them nor written them down, but He does what He wills. As for other interpretations that some people have related, that Satan compelled him until he said such-and-such, this is impossible, since Satan has no power to strip a person of choice. God Most High said, reporting of him: "I had no authority over you except that I called you, and you responded to me" [Ibrahim: 22]. Had Satan had this power, no one among the children of Adam would have retained any strength in obedience. Whoever imagines that Satan has this power holds the view of the Dualists and the Magians, that good comes from God and evil from Satan. And whoever says that it occurred on his tongue by inadvertence said: it is not far-fetched that he had heard the two phrases from the polytheists, and they were in his memory, so during the recitation of the surah what was in his memory came out by inadvertence. On this view, inadvertence is permissible for them, but they are not left to persist in it. God Almighty revealed this verse as a preparation for his excuse and a consolation to him, lest it be said that he retracted part of his recitation, and it clarified that the like of this occurred to the prophets through inadvertence. Inadvertence is negated only for God Most High.

Ibn 'Abbas said: a devil called al-Abyad had come to the Messenger of God ﷺ in the form of Gabriel, peace be upon him, and cast into the Prophet's ﷺ recitation: "Those are the exalted cranes, and their intercession is indeed to be hoped for." This interpretation, although it is closer to plausibility than what came before it, the first interpretation is the one relied upon, and one should not turn away from it to another, because the verifying scholars have chosen it. The weakness of the hadith is sufficient against every interpretation, and praise be to God. Among what also indicates its weakness and discredits it from the Book is the saying of God Most High: "And they had almost tempted you..." [al-Isra': 73], the two verses, for they reject the report they narrated, because God Most High mentioned that they nearly tempted him so that he would fabricate, and that had He not made him firm he would have inclined towards them. The implication and meaning of this is that God Most High protected him from fabricating and made him firm so that he did not incline towards them even a little, let alone much. Yet they narrate in their feeble reports that he went beyond inclining and fabricating by praising their gods, and that he said, peace be upon him: "I have fabricated against God and said what He did not say." This is the opposite of the meaning of the verse, and the verse weakens the hadith even if it were sound, so how much more so when it has no soundness at all. This is like the saying of God Most High: "Had it not been for the grace of God upon you and His mercy, a group of them would have resolved to lead you astray, but they lead astray none but themselves, and they cannot harm you in the least" [al-Nisa': 113].

Al-Qushayri said: The Quraysh and Thaqif pressed him, when he passed by their idols, to turn his face toward them, and they promised him they would believe in him if he did so, but he did not do it, and he would not have done it. Ibn al-Anbari said: the Messenger came close to it but did not incline. Al-Zajjaj said: i.e., they almost did, and "in" and the lam are for emphasis.

It has also been said that the meaning of "tamanna" is "haddatha" (spoke/related), not "tala" (recited). It is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas regarding the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: "Except when he wished (tamanna)," he said: except when he spoke. "Satan cast into his wish": in his speech. "Then God abrogates what Satan casts": God nullifies what Satan casts. Al-Nahhas said: this is among the best and most excellent of what has been said about the verse. Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Hanbal said in Egypt: a sheet of tafsir narrated by 'Ali ibn Abi Talha — if a man travelled to Egypt intending it alone, it would not be too much. The meaning according to this: that when the Prophet ﷺ spoke to himself, Satan cast into his speech by way of trickery, saying: "If you asked God, Mighty and Majestic, to grant you spoils so that the Muslims would be enriched," and God, Mighty and Majestic, knows that the good lies in other than that, so He nullifies what Satan cast, as Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, said. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' both related that "tamanna" means "he spoke to himself," and this is the well-known usage in the language. They also related that "tamanna" means "recited." It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas also, and said by Mujahid, al-Dahhak and others.

Abu al-Hasan ibn Mahdi said: this wishing is not from the Qur'an or revelation in any way; rather, when the Prophet ﷺ's hands were empty of wealth and he saw what his companions suffered of ill condition, he wished for worldly things in his heart, and Satan's whispering. Al-Mahdawi mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas that the meaning is: when he spoke, Satan cast into his speech, and this is the choice of al-Tabari.

I say: God Most High's saying "so that He may make what Satan casts a trial" (the verse) refutes the interpretation of inner speech. Ibn 'Atiyya said: there is no disagreement that Satan's casting is only into audible words, by which the trial occurred. God knows best.

Al-Nahhas said: Even if the hadith were sound and its chain connected, the meaning in it would be correct, and "sahā" would mean "asqata" (dropped/omitted). Its intended sense would be: "Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza?" and the speech would be complete; then he omitted "And the exalted cranes", meaning the angels, "for their intercession", the pronoun referring to the angels. As for the one who narrates "for they are the exalted cranes", there are answers to his narration, among them that the saying is elided, as the Arabs use in many things, and it may be without elision, serving as a rebuke, since before it is "Have you considered?", and this would be an argument against them. If it was during prayer, then speech was permissible in prayer. It is narrated in this story that among what he recited was: "Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza, and Manat, the third, the other?" and "the exalted cranes", and "their intercession is indeed to be hoped for." Its meaning is related from Mujahid. Al-Hasan said: by "the exalted cranes" he meant the angels, and al-Kalbi explained "al-gharaniqa" as the angels likewise. That is because the disbelievers believed that the idols and the angels were daughters of God, as God Most High related of them, and He refuted them in this surah with His saying: "Is the male yours and the female His?" [[See vol. 17, p. 102.]] Thus God denied all of this from their saying. Hoping for intercession from the angels is sound, but when the polytheists interpreted this mention as referring to their gods, and Satan confused them by it, God abrogated what Satan cast, made His verses firm, and lifted the recitation of those two phrases through which Satan found a way to deception, just as much of the Qur'an was abrogated and its recitation lifted.

Al-Qushayri said: this is not sound, because of His saying: "Then God abrogates what Satan casts," meaning He nullifies it, and the intercession of the angels is not false.

﴿And God is Knowing, Wise.﴾ "Knowing" of what He revealed to His Prophet ﷺ; "Wise" in His creation.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 53:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That He may make what Satan casts a trial﴾, i.e., a misguidance.

(For those in whose hearts is a disease), i.e., shirk and hypocrisy.

(And the hardened of heart), so they do not soften to the command of Allah, exalted is He. Al-Tha'labi said: In the verse there is evidence that the Prophets may be subject to forgetfulness (sahw), oblivion (nisyan), and error (ghalat) through the whisperings of Satan, or when the heart is preoccupied so that he errs, then he is alerted and returns to the correct matter. This is the meaning of His saying: "Then Allah abolishes what Satan casts, then Allah makes His verses firm." However, the error occurs only in the manner in which any one of us errs. As for what is attributed to him of their saying: "Those are the exalted cranes (al-gharaniq al-ula)," it is a lie against the Prophet (ﷺ), because it involves glorifying the idols, and that is not permissible for the Prophets, just as it is not permissible that he recite part of the Qur'an and then recite a poem and say: "I erred and I thought it was Qur'an."

(And indeed the wrongdoers are in extreme opposition), i.e., the disbelievers are in dispute, disobedience, and hostility toward Allah, mighty and majestic, and toward His Messenger (ﷺ). It has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 2, p. 143.]], and all praise is due to Allah alone.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 54:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that those who have been given knowledge may know﴾, i.e., from among the believers. And it has been said: the People of the Book.

(That) i.e., that what has been made firm (muhkam) from the verses of the Quran (ayat) is "the truth from your Lord, so that they believe in it and their hearts humbly submit to it" (fa-tukhbita la-hu qulubuhum), i.e., that they be humbled and settle. And it has been said: that they be sincere.

(And indeed Allah is the Guide of those who believe) Abu Haywa recited: "wa-inna Allaha la-hadin alladhina amanu" with tanwin.

(To a straight path) i.e., He keeps them firm upon guidance.

**Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be in doubt about it﴾**, meaning: in doubt about the Qur'an. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj. Others said: about the religion, which is the Straight Path (al-sirat al-mustaqim). It was also said: about what Satan cast upon the tongue of Muhammad (ﷺ), and they would say: "What is the matter with him, that he mentioned the idols favourably and then turned away from them?" Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read "fi muryah" with a dammah on the letter mim. But the kasrah (fi miryah) is better known, as mentioned by al-Nahhas.

**(Until the Hour comes upon them)**, i.e., the Resurrection (al-qiyamah).

**(Suddenly)**, i.e., unexpectedly.

**(Or there comes upon them the punishment of a barren day)**. Al-Dahhak said: "The punishment of a day that has no night, and it is the Day of Resurrection." Al-Nahhas said: The Day of Resurrection was called "barren" (aqim) because no day follows it that is like it, and this is the meaning of al-Dahhak's statement. In the language, "barren" (al-aqim) describes one who has no child. Since a child comes between two parents, and days follow one another, before and after, the succession of days was likened to birth through the notion of "after"; and since no day came after that day, it was described as barren. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah said: what is meant is the punishment of the Day of Badr, and "barren" means that there is none like it in its magnitude, because the angels fought in it. Ibn Jurayj said: because they did not look at the night in it, rather they were killed before evening, so it became a day with no night. Likewise, the meaning of al-Dahhak's statement is that it is the Day of Resurrection, because it has no night. It was also said: because there was no tenderness or mercy in it, and it was barren of all good. From this is the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿When We sent against them the barren wind﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 41], i.e., the one in which there is no good, and which brings neither rain nor mercy. [[See vol. 17, p. 50.]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 56–57:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The dominion on that Day belongs to Allah; He will judge between them.﴾ That is, on the Day of Resurrection, the dominion belongs to Allah alone, with no one disputing it with Him or contesting it. Al-mulk (dominion) is the breadth of power (ittisa' al-maqdur) and the authority of the one who has the management of affairs. Then He explained His judgment, saying: (So those who believed and did righteous deeds will be in Gardens of Bliss. And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs, for them will be a humiliating punishment.)

I say: It may also be that the reference of "that day" (yawma'idhin) is to the Day of Badr, in which He judged the destruction of the disbeliever and the felicity of the believer. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Umar: (And what makes you know? Perhaps Allah looked upon the people of Badr and said: "Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you.")

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 56–57:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The dominion on that Day belongs to Allah; He will judge between them.﴾ That is, on the Day of Resurrection, the dominion belongs to Allah alone, with no one disputing it with Him or contesting it. Al-mulk (dominion) is the breadth of power (ittisa' al-maqdur) and the authority of the one who has the management of affairs. Then He explained His judgment, saying: (So those who believed and did righteous deeds will be in Gardens of Bliss. And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs, for them will be a humiliating punishment.)

I say: It may also be that the reference of "that day" (yawma'idhin) is to the Day of Badr, in which He judged the destruction of the disbeliever and the felicity of the believer. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Umar: (And what makes you know? Perhaps Allah looked upon the people of Badr and said: "Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you.")

Al-Qurtubi, al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran, commentary on surah 22, verses 58–59:

He singled out the mention of the emigrants (muhajirun) who died or were killed, to honour them and to give them precedence over all others who died. The occasion of revelation of this verse was that when Uthman ibn Maz'un and Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Asad died in Medina, some people said: "One who is killed in the way of Allah is better than one who dies a natural death," so this verse was revealed, placing them on an equal footing, and that Allah provides all of them with a goodly provision.

The apparent meaning of the Shari'ah indicates that the one who is killed is superior. Some scholars ('ulama') have said: the one killed in the way of Allah and the one who dies in the way of Allah are both martyrs (shahid), but the one who is killed has the distinction of what befell him for the sake of Allah. Others said: they are equal. They argued by this verse, and by the words of the Exalted: ﴿And whoever leaves his home as an emigrant to Allah and His Messenger, and then death overtakes him, his reward has indeed become due from Allah﴾ [An-Nisa: 100] [[See vol. 5, p. 347 onward.]], and by the hadith of Umm Haram, for she fell from her mount and died without being killed, and the Prophet ﷺ said to her: "You are among the first (ones)." They also cited the words of the Prophet ﷺ in the hadith of Abdullah ibn Atik: "Whoever leaves his house as an emigrant in the way of Allah, then falls from his mount and dies, or is stung by a snake and dies, or dies a natural death, his reward has indeed become due from Allah. And whoever is struck down (qa'san) [[Qa's: that a person is struck and dies on the spot. He meant by "the obligation of the return" (wujub al-ma'ab) a good final destination after death.]], he has indeed earned the return (al-ma'ab)."

Ibn al-Mubarak related from Fadalah ibn Ubayd, in a report in which he mentioned two men, one of whom was struck by a catapult (manjaniq) in a military campaign and died, and the other died there. Fadalah sat beside the dead man, and it was said to him: "You left the martyr and did not sit beside him?" He said: "I do not care from which of the two graves I am raised," and then he recited the verse in full: "And those who emigrated in the way of Allah and then were killed or died..."

Sulayman ibn Amir said: Fadalah was a commander over the quarters at Rudis. He went out with the funeral processions of two men: one was slain and the other had died naturally. He saw people inclining toward the grave of the slain man, and he said: "I see you, O people, inclining toward the slain man! By Him in whose hand is my soul, I do not care from which of the two graves I am raised. Recite His words, the Exalted: 'And those who emigrated in the way of Allah and then were killed or died.'" Al-Tha'labi mentioned this in his tafsir, and it has the same meaning as what Ibn al-Mubarak related.

Those who held that the one killed has an added excellence argued by what is established from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, that he was asked: "Which jihad is best?" He said: "One whose blood is spilled and whose horse is wounded." And if the one whose blood is spilled and whose horse is wounded is the best of martyrs, it is known that whoever does not have that quality is of lesser rank.

Ibn Amir and the people of Syria read "quttilu" with the doubled letter (tashdid) for intensity (al-taksir). The rest read it without doubling (takhfif).

﴿He will certainly admit them to an entrance which they will be pleased with﴾, meaning the Gardens. The reading of the people of Medina is "madkhalan" with a fatha on the mim, meaning "entry" (dukhulan). The rest read it with a damma. This has been discussed in Surah al-Isra' [[See vol. 10, p. 313.]].

﴿And indeed Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing﴾. Ibn Abbas said: All-Knowing of their intentions, Most Forbearing regarding their punishment.

﴿He will certainly admit them to an entrance which they will be pleased with﴾, meaning the Gardens. ﴿And indeed Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing﴾. Ibn Abbas said: All-Knowing of their intentions, Most Forbearing regarding their punishment.

**The words of Allah, the Exalted: "That [is so]. And whoever retaliates with the like of what he was afflicted with" (22:60).**

"That" is in the nominative position, meaning: that matter which We have related to you. Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning a group of the polytheists of Makkah who met a group of Muslims during the last two nights of al-Muharram. They said: "The Companions of Muhammad dislike fighting in the sacred month, so attack them." The Muslims appealed to them not to fight them in the sacred month, but the polytheists refused except to fight. So they attacked them, the Muslims stood firm, and Allah gave them victory over the polytheists. But something arose in the hearts of the Muslims about fighting in the sacred month, and so this verse was revealed.

It is also said: It was revealed concerning a group of the polytheists who mutilated a group of Muslims whom they had killed on the day of Uhud, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ retaliated against them with the like of it. So the meaning of "whoever retaliates with the like of what he was afflicted with" is: whoever requites the wrongdoer with the like of what he wronged him. The recompense of a punishment is called a punishment because the two acts are alike in form, as in His words: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ (42:40) [see vol. 16, p. 38 onward]. And as in: ﴿So whoever aggresses against you, then aggress against him in the same manner as he has aggressed against you﴾ (2:194) [see vol. 2, p. 354]. This has already been discussed.

**"Then he is wronged"** (22:60): that is, by harsh words and by being driven out of his homeland. For the polytheists denied their Prophet, harmed those who believed in him, and expelled him and them from Makkah, and they backed one another in their expulsion.

**"Surely Allah will help him"** (22:60): that is, Allah will surely help Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions, for the disbelievers transgressed against them.

**"Indeed Allah is Pardoning, Forgiving"** (22:60): that is, He pardoned the believers their sins and their fighting in the sacred month, and He concealed them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 61:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is because Allah causes the night to enter into the day﴾ meaning: that which I have related to you of the victory of the oppressed is because I am the One who causes the night to enter into the day, so none can do what I am able to do. That is, whoever is able to do this is able to grant victory to His servant. The meaning of "causing the night to enter into the day" has already passed in "Al 'Imran" [[See vol. 4, p. 56.]].

(And that Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing) He hears the statements and sees the actions, so there is not hidden from Him the weight of an atom nor the crawling of an ant, except that He knows it, hears it and sees it.

That is because Allah, He is the Truth (al-Haqq), meaning the Possessor of truth: His religion is the truth and His worship is true. The believers deserve His victory by virtue of His true promise.

﴿And that what they call upon besides Him is the falsehood (al-batil)﴾, that is, the idols, which have no entitlement to worship. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read "wa-anna ma tad‘una" (وَأَنَّ مَا تَدْعُونَ) with the letter ta' (ت), in the second person (al-khitab), and Abu Hatim (Abu Hatim al-Sijistani) preferred this reading. The rest read it with the letter ya' (ي), in the third person (al-khabar), here and in Luqman [[See vol. 14, p. 78.]], and Abu 'Ubayd (Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Salam) preferred this.

﴿And that Allah, He is the Most High (al-'Ali)﴾, that is, the one exalted above all things by His power, and exalted above likenesses and rivals, sanctified above the attributes that the wrongdoers ascribe to Him, which are not befitting to His majesty.

﴿The Great (al-Kabir)﴾, that is, the one described with magnificence, majesty, and greatness of station. It has been said: al-Kabir is the Possessor of greatness (al-Kibriya'), and kibriya' is an expression for the perfection of His essence, meaning that He has absolute existence forever and without beginning, so He is the First, the Eternal, and the Last, the One who remains after the annihilation of His creation.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 63:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky, and the earth becomes green?﴾ is evidence of His perfect power, meaning: whoever is able to do this is able to restore life after death, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells﴾ [Fussilat: 39]. And the like of this is many. [[See p. 6 of this part.]]

"Fa-tusbihu" (so it becomes) is not a response (jawab) that would make it in the accusative (mansub); rather, according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh, it is a predicate (khabar). Al-Khalil said: the meaning is "Pay attention! Allah sends down water from the sky, and so it becomes such-and-such," as the poet said:

"Have you not asked the desolate abode, so that it speaks? And will the desert of Sumlaq tell you today?" [[The line is by Jamil ibn Abd Allah, companion of Buthayna. "Al-qawa'" (with a fatha on the qaf) means a barren wasteland. "Al-bayda'" is also a barren wasteland, the kind in which whoever travels perishes (yabid). "Al-Sumlaq" (with a fatha on the sin, a sukun on the mim, and a fatha on the lam) is land that does not grow vegetation, namely the smooth, level plain.

(Shawahid al-Ayni).]] Its meaning: "I have indeed asked it, and it spoke."

It was also said that it is an interrogative for affirmation (istifham tahqiq), meaning: "Indeed you have seen; so reflect on how it becomes!" Or it is a coordinated clause (atf), because the meaning is: "Have you not seen that Allah causes to descend...?" Al-Farra' said: "Have you not seen" is a statement (khabar), as you say in speech: "Know that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sends down water from the sky."

(﴿The earth becomes green﴾) means: possessing greenness, as you say: "mubqilah" and "musbi'ah," meaning: possessing herbage and beasts of prey. It is an expression for its quickly bringing forth plants upon the descent of water, and its continuing in that state customarily. Ibn Atiyyah said: It was narrated from Ikrimah that he said: "This does not happen except in Makkah and Tihamah." The meaning of this is that he took his saying "fa-tusbihu" as intended to refer to the morning after a night of rain, and he held that this greening is delayed in the rest of the lands. I myself have witnessed this in Sus al-Aqsa: rain fell at night after a drought, and by morning that sandy land which the winds had scattered had turned green with a weak, thin vegetation.

(﴿Indeed Allah is Subtle, Acquainted﴾) Ibn Abbas said: "Acquainted" with what the servant conceals of despair when rain is delayed. "Subtle" with the provisions of His servants. It was also said: "Subtle" in bringing forth plants from the earth, and "Acquainted" with their need and poverty.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 64:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, in creation and in dominion, and all of it is in need of His management and perfecting.

(﴿Indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾), so He has no need of anything, and He is the One praised in every state.

Al-Qurtubi, *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*, commentary on Surah 22, verse 65:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do you not see that Allah has subjected to you whatever is on the earth﴾. He mentions another blessing, informing that He has subjected to His servants what they need of animals, trees, and rivers.

(And the ship) means: and He subjected to you the ship while it runs. Abu Abd al-Rahman al-A'raj recited "wal-fulku" (والفلك) in the nominative, as a beginning (*ibtida'*, the subject of the sentence), with what follows it as its predicate (*khabar*). The rest read it in the accusative, in coordination (*nasaq*) with His saying "whatever is on the earth."

(And He holds back the sky from falling upon the earth) means: lest it fall. Al-Kufiyyun (the Kufan grammarians) said: "*li-alla*" (لئلا), meaning "so that it does not fall." His holding it back is the creation of stillness in it, moment after moment.

(Except by His permission) means: except by Allah's permission for it to fall. So it falls by His permission, that is, by His will and His allowing it.[[كذا في ب وط وك وى. وفى أوج: بحيلنه.]]

(Indeed, Allah is Kind and Merciful to people) means: in these things which He has subjected for them.

He it is Who gave you life, i.e., after you had been drops of sperm (nutfan).

(Then He causes you to die) at the expiry of your appointed terms.

(Then He will give you life again) i.e., for the reckoning, the reward and the punishment.

(Indeed, man is ungrateful) i.e., he is truly denying, rejecting the signs that clearly demonstrate His power and His oneness. Ibn Abbas said: he means al-Aswad ibn Abd al-Asad, Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, al-As ibn Hisham, and a group of the polytheists. It was also said: He said this because the predominant trait of man is ingratitude for blessings, as the Exalted says: "And few of My servants are grateful" [Saba': 13].[[See vol. 14, p. 276.]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 67:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For every community We have appointed rites (mansak)﴾ means: a law (shar').

(They perform it) means: they act in accordance with it.

(So let them not dispute with you concerning the matter) means: let none of them dispute with you concerning what is legislated for your community, for the laws have been different in every age. A group has narrated that this verse was revealed on account of the disputes of the disbelievers concerning the slaughter of animals, and their saying to the believers: "You eat what you slaughter yourselves, but you do not eat what God slaughters (i.e., carrion)." So they argued that what God kills is more deserving of being eaten than what you kill with your own knives. Thus the verse was revealed because of this dispute. This has already been discussed in (surah) al-An'am [see vol. 7, p. 72], and praise be to God. And what the scholars have said regarding His saying "mansak" [Qur'an 22:34] has already been mentioned earlier in this surah [p. 58 of this part]. His saying "hum nasikuhu" indicates that mansak is the verbal noun (masdar); had it been the place, He would have said "hum nasikun fihi" (they are performers of rites in it).

Al-Zajjaj said: "So let them not dispute with you concerning the matter" means: let them not argue with you. This is indicated by "and if they argue with you" [Qur'an 22:68]. It may be said: they did dispute with him, so how does He say "let them not dispute with you"? The answer is that the meaning is "so do not dispute with them yourself." The verse was revealed before the command to fight. You say: "So-and-so will not strike you, so do not strike him," and this operates within the pattern of mufa'alah (reciprocal form). One does not say "Zayd will not strike you" while meaning "do not strike Zayd." Abu Mijlaz read: "fa-la yanzi'unnaka fi al-amr" meaning: let them not provoke you (la yastakhiffannaka) and let them not overpower you away from your religion. The reading of the majority is from al-munaza'ah (disputing). In both readings the prohibition is addressed to the disbelievers, while the intended addressee is the Prophet (ﷺ).

(And invite to your Lord) means: to His oneness, His religion, and belief in Him.

(Indeed, you are upon guidance) means: upon a religion.

(Straight) means: upright, with no crookedness in it.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verses 68–69:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if they dispute with you﴾, i.e., they argue with you, O Muhammad, meaning the polytheists of Makkah.

(﴿Say: "Allah knows best what you are doing"﴾) meaning, of their denial of Muhammad ﷺ. This is from Ibn 'Abbas. Muqatil said: this verse was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ on the night of the Isra' (Night Journey), when he was in the seventh heaven, having seen some of the greatest signs of his Lord. So Allah revealed to him: "And if they dispute with you" with falsehood, then repel them with your words: "Allah knows best what you are doing" of disbelief and denial. Allah the Exalted commanded him to turn away from their wrangling, to protect him from being occupied with their obstinacy, for there is no answer for one who is stubbornly contentious.

(﴿Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection﴾) meaning, between the Prophet ﷺ and his people.

(﴿concerning that about which you used to differ﴾) meaning, concerning your disagreement over My signs, so that you will then recognize the truth from falsehood.

Issue: In this verse there is a fine etiquette which Allah taught His servants: in responding to one who disputes out of obstinacy and contention, one should not be answered or debated, and he should be repelled with this statement which Allah taught to His Prophet ﷺ. It has been said that this verse is abrogated by the sword, meaning that one should keep silent about his opponent and suffice with the saying: "Allah will judge between you."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 70:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do you not know that Allah knows whatever is in the heaven and the earth?﴾ (22:70). That is, since you have come to know this, O Muhammad, and have attained certainty of it, then know that He also knows what you differ about, and He will judge between you. It has also been said that it is a rhetorical question (istifham taqrir, a question posed to affirm and establish a fact) addressed to another.

﴿Indeed, that is in a Book﴾ (22:70). That is, whatever occurs in the world is written down with Allah in the Mother of the Book (Umm al-Kitab, the Preserved Tablet).

﴿Indeed, that is easy for Allah﴾ (22:70). That is, the separation between those who differ is easy for Allah. It has also been said that the meaning is: that the Book of the Pen, which He commanded to write whatever is to occur until the Day of Resurrection, is easy for Allah.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they worship﴾, meaning the disbelievers of Quraysh.

(...besides Allah that for which He has sent down no authority) i.e., no proof and evidence. This has already been mentioned in Surat Ali 'Imran [[See vol. 4, p. 232.]].

(And that of which they have no knowledge. And for the wrongdoers there will be no helper.)

﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them﴾: he means the Qur'an.

(You will recognize the denial in the faces of those who disbelieve) that is, the anger and the scowling.

(They almost attack) that is, they assault. Al-satwa (violent force) is intense assault. It is said: "sataa bihi yasţū" when he assaulted him, whether by striking or by insulting, and "sataa 'alayhi" (he attacked him).

(Those who recite Our verses to them) Ibn 'Abbas said: "yasţūna" means they stretch out their hands toward them. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: that is, they fall upon them. Al-Dahhak said: that is, they seize them with the hand. The meaning is the same. The root of satw is subjugation: "Allah is Dhu Satawat," meaning severe seizings.

﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that? The Fire﴾: that is, what you hate more than this Qur'an you hear is the Fire. It is as though they said, "What is worse?" and it was said, "It is the Fire." It is also said: that is, shall I tell you of something worse than what befalls the reciters of the Qur'an from you? It is the Fire. Then this is a threat to them for their assaults upon those who recite the Qur'an.

The word "an-nar" (the Fire) may be read in the nominative, accusative, or genitive. The nominative is "huwa an-nar" (it is the Fire) or "hiya an-nar" (it is the Fire). The accusative carries the sense of "a'nī" (I mean), or it is governed by an implied verb like the second one, or it is treated as governed by the sense, meaning "I inform you of something worse than that: the Fire." The genitive is in apposition (badal).

﴿Allah has promised it to those who disbelieve﴾: in the Resurrection.

﴿And how evil is the destination﴾: that is, the place to which they go, which is the Fire.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 73:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O mankind, a parable has been coined, so listen to it﴾. This is connected to His saying: "And they worship besides Allah that for which He has sent down no authority." He said "a parable has been coined" because Allah's proofs against them through the striking of parables are closer to their understanding. If it is asked: where is the parable that was coined? There are two views. The first: al-Akhfash said: there is no parable here; rather the meaning is "they coined a parable for Allah, so listen to their saying." That is, the disbelievers made a likeness for Allah by worshipping other than Him, as if He said: "They made a likeness to Me in My worship, so listen to the report of this likeness." The second: the saying of al-Qutabi: the meaning is "O mankind, the parable of those who worship gods that cannot create a fly, even if the fly snatches something from them, they cannot rescue it from it." And al-Nahhas said: the meaning is that Allah, mighty and majestic, has coined as a parable what is worshipped besides Him. He said: this is among the best of what has been said about it, i.e., Allah has made clear to you a likeness both for your worshipped ones.

(Indeed those you invoke besides Allah) The reading of the majority is "tad'un" with the ta'. Al-Sulami, Abu al-'Aliyah and Ya'qub read "yad'un" with the ya', as a report. What is meant is the idols that they worshipped besides Allah; they were around the Ka'bah, and they were three hundred and sixty idols. It is said: they are the masters who diverted them from obedience to Allah, mighty and majestic. It is said: the devils led them to disobedience of Allah, the Exalted. The first is more correct.

(Will never create a fly) The dhubab (fly) is a single noun for the male and the female; its small plural is adhibbah and its large plural is dhibban, on the pattern of ghurab, aghribah and ghirban, and it was named so for the abundance of its movement. Al-Jawhari: the dhubab is well known, its singular is dhubabah, and do not say dhibbanah. The midhabbah is that with which flies are driven off. The dhubab of the camels' teeth is their edge. The dhubab of a sword is its tip with which it is struck. The dhubab of the eye is its pupil. The dhubabah is the remaining portion of the religion. Dhabbaba the day when only a remnant of it is left. Al-tadhabdhub is movement. Al-dhabdhabah is the swaying of a suspended thing in the air. Al-dhabdhab is the male organ because of its wavering. In a hadith: "Whoever is protected from the evil of his dhabdhab." [This is among what he did not mention, I mean his saying: "and in the hadith"; what the author, may Allah have mercy on him, transmitted from al-Jawhari is all mentioned in al-Sihah up to his saying: "...the evil of his dhabdhab." It seems that the author's copy of al-Jawhari does not contain these sentences. And in the copy of J: "and in the revelation" and "in the hadith".]

(And if the fly snatches anything from them, they cannot rescue it from it) Al-istinqadh and al-inqadh mean deliverance. Ibn 'Abbas said: they used to smear their idols with saffron, and it would dry, and the fly would come and snatch it away. Al-Suddi said: they used to place food for the idols, and the fly would settle on it and eat it.

(Weak are the seeker and the sought) It is said: the seeker is the gods and the sought is the fly. It is said conversely. It is said: the seeker is the worshipper of the idol and the sought is the idol; the seeker petitions this idol by drawing near to it, and the idol is the one petitioned. It has also been said: "And if the fly snatches anything from them" refers to its pain in stinging their bodies, until it snatches from them patience and dignity along with it. The fly was singled out for four matters that belong to it: for its lowliness, its weakness, its repulsiveness, and its abundance. If this, which is the weakest and most contemptible of animals, cannot be created by those they worship besides Allah, mighty and majestic, nor can they repel its harm, how could it be permissible that they be gods worshipped and lords obeyed? This is among the strongest proofs and clearest demonstrations.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 22, verse 74:**

His words, exalted is He: ﴿They have not measured Allah with His true measure﴾, meaning they did not magnify Him with His true magnificence, in that they made these idols partners to Him. This has already been discussed in Al-An'am [[See vol. 7, p. 36.]].

(﴿Indeed, Allah is Strong, Mighty﴾) 40. Already mentioned.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verses 75–76:**

Allah's words: ﴿Allah chooses messengers from among the angels and from among mankind﴾. He concluded the surah by stating that Allah chose Muhammad (ﷺ) to convey the message, meaning that sending Muhammad was not an innovation. It was said that al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said: "Was the Reminder sent down to him from among us?" So the verse was revealed. It also informs that the choice belongs to Allah, glorified and exalted be He.

(Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing) of His servants' statements (All-Seeing) of whom He chooses from His creation for His message.

(He knows what is before them) means what they have sent forward.

(And what is behind them) means what they have left behind. Like His words in Ya-Sin: "Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life and record what they have sent forward" [Ya-Sin: 12], meaning what is before them, "and their traces" meaning what they have left behind. [See vol. 15, p. 11.]

(And to Allah are all matters returned) 210.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 77:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, bow and prostrate yourselves﴾. It has already been mentioned at the beginning of the surah that it is distinguished by two prostrations. Malik and Abu Hanifa did not regard this second prostration as one of the obligatory prostrations (ʿazaʾim), because He joined bowing (ruku') with prostration (sujud), and because the intended meaning is the obligatory prayer (salah al-mafrudah). He singled out bowing and prostration to honour the prayer. The discussion of bowing and prostration has already been explained in full in (surat) al-Baqarah. [See vol. 1, p. 344.] And all praise is due to Allah alone.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and worship your Lord﴾, that is, carry out His command.

(And do good) is recommended in matters other than the obligatory duties whose obligation is established from elsewhere than this passage.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on surah 22, verse 78:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And strive for Allah with the striving due to Him.﴾ It has been said that it refers to fighting the disbelievers (*jihad*, struggle). It has also been said that it is an indication of carrying out everything Allah has commanded and refraining from everything Allah has forbidden. That is, strive against yourselves in obedience to Allah and restrain them from desire; strive against Satan by repelling his whispering; strive against the oppressors by repelling their oppression; and strive against the disbelievers by repelling their disbelief. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: Muqatil said, "This verse is abrogated (*mansukh*, from *naskh*, abrogation) by the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16] [See vol. 18, p. 144.]. Likewise, Hibat Allah said that His words ﴿with the striving due to Him﴾ and His words in the other verse ﴿with the fear due to Him﴾ [Al ʿImran: 102] [See vol. 4, p. 157.] are abrogated by the easing to what is within one's capacity in these commands. There is no need to posit abrogation, for this is what is meant from the outset of the ruling, since 'the striving due to Him' is that from which hardship has been lifted." Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The best of your religion is the easiest of it." Abu Jaʿfar al-Nahhas said: "This is among the things in which abrogation cannot occur, because it is obligatory upon a person." As Hayawa ibn Shurayh narrated, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "The mujahid is one who struggles against his own self for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic." And as Abu Ghalib narrated from Abu Umama: a man asked the Prophet (ﷺ), "Which jihad is best?" He did not answer him at the first pillar (*jamra*, a stone pillar at Mina). Then he asked him at the second pillar, and he did not answer him. Then he asked him at the Jamrat al-ʿAqaba, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Where is the questioner?" He said, "Here I am." He (ﷺ) said: "A word of justice in the presence of an oppressive ruler."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He has chosen you﴾, that is, He has selected you to defend His religion and to adhere to His command. This is an emphasis on the command to striving: that is, it is obligatory upon you to strive because Allah has chosen you for it.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And He has not placed upon you in the religion any difficulty﴾. In this there are three issues.

The first: Allah the Exalted's words ﴿any difficulty﴾, that is, any constriction. This was discussed previously in *al-Anʿam*. This verse applies to many rulings, and it is among the things Allah has particularly granted to this nation. Maʿmar narrated from Qatada, who said: "This nation was given three things that no prophet was given. It was said to the Prophet, 'Go, there is no blame upon you,' and it was said to this nation: ﴿And He has not placed upon you in the religion any difficulty﴾. The Prophet is a witness over his nation, and it was said to this nation: ﴿that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾. It was said to the Prophet, 'Ask and it will be given to you,' and it was said to this nation: ﴿Call upon Me; I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir: 60] [See vol. 15, p. 326.]."

The second: The scholars differed regarding this difficulty that Allah the Exalted has lifted. Ikrima said: it is what He has made lawful of women, two, three, or four, and what your right hand possesses. It was also said: what is meant is the shortening of the prayer and breaking the fast for the traveler, the prayer of gesture (*salat al-iyma'*) for one who is unable to perform it otherwise, the exemption from jihad for the blind, the lame, the sick, the destitute who cannot find what to spend on his campaign, the debtor, and the one who has parents, and the lifting of the burden (*isr*) that was upon the Children of Israel. The detailed discussion of most of these matters has already passed [See vol. 2, p. 155, and vol. 3, p. 430.]. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan al-Basri that this (verse) concerns the advancing and postponing of the crescent moons for the Fitr, the Adha, and the fasting. So if the community erred regarding the crescent of Dhu al-Hijja, and they stood at ʿArafa a day before, or stood on the day of sacrifice, it suffices them. There is a difference of opinion on this which we explained in the book *al-Muqtabas fi Sharh Muwatta' Malik ibn Anas*, may Allah be pleased with him. What we have mentioned is the correct view on this matter. And likewise the Fitr and the Adha, due to what Hammad ibn Zayd narrated from Ayyub, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Abu Hurayra, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Your Fitr is the day you break your fast, and your Adha is the day you sacrifice." Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni recorded it, and this is its wording as we have mentioned. The meaning is: by your own judgment, without any hardship befalling you. The imams have also narrated that on the day of sacrifice he (ﷺ) was asked about various things, and he was never asked about a matter that a person forgets or is ignorant of, such as the order of some acts before others and similar things, without his replying: "Do it, and there is no hardship."

The third: The scholars said: the lifting of hardship applies only to one who adheres to the path of the Sharia. As for highway robbers, thieves, and those liable to the prescribed punishments (*hudud*), hardship is upon them, and they have brought it upon themselves by abandoning the religion. There is no greater hardship in the Sharia than requiring a man to stand firm against two in the way of Allah the Exalted; yet with sound certainty and firm resolve, it is not hardship.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿The religion of your father﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, follow the religion of your father. Al-Farra' said: it is in the accusative by way of omitting the particle of comparison (*kaf*), as if he had said "like the religion of." It was also said: the meaning is, do the good deed as your father did, so the act is put in place of the religion. Ibrahim is the father of all the Arabs. It was also said: the address is to all Muslims, even though not all of them are his descendants, because the sanctity of Ibrahim upon the Muslims is like the sanctity of a father upon his child.

(He named you Muslims before) — Ibn Zayd and al-Hasan said: "He" refers back to Ibrahim, and the meaning is: he named you Muslims before the Prophet (ﷺ).

(And in this) — that is, in His ruling that whoever follows Muhammad (ﷺ) is a Muslim. Ibn Zayd said: this is the meaning of His words: ﴿Our Lord, make us submitting to You, and of our descendants a Muslim nation submitting to You﴾ [al-Baqara: 128] [See vol. 2, p. 126 onward.]. Al-Nahhas said: this view contradicts the view of the great scholars of the community (in manuscript K: "the scholars"). ʿAli ibn Abi Talha narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: Allah the Mighty and Majestic named you Muslims before, that is, in the earlier books and in this Qur'an. Mujahid and others said likewise.

(That the Messenger may be a witness over you) — that is, by his conveying (the message) to you.

(And that you may be witnesses over mankind) — that their messengers have conveyed to them, as was mentioned previously in *al-Baqara* [See vol. 2, p. 126 and p. 153 onward.].

(So establish prayer and give zakat and hold fast to Allah; He is your protector—and excellent is the protector and excellent is the helper) — this has been discussed previously in full [See vol. 1, and vol. 4, p. 156.], and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds [added from manuscript K].
